Issue #2489: Feature: expose connected components and cycles — networkx is already bundled

**Version:** graphify 0.9.33 (pipx, Python 3.14.5, Windows)

## The gap

graphify already builds a directed graph and already ships `networkx` 3.6.1, but never
calls its connectivity primitives. Searching the installed package (80 `.py` files):

| symbol | files containing it |
|---|---|
| `connected_component` | **0** |
| `strongly_connected` | **0** |
| `in_degree` / `out_degree` | **0** |
| `dijkstra` | **0** |
| `leiden` / `louvain` | 7 / 6 |
| `betweenness` | 2 |

So community detection and centrality are covered, but connectivity is not — even though
`nx.weakly_connected_components` and `nx.strongly_connected_components` would run on the
graph already in memory, with no new dependency and no LLM.

## Two questions this would answer

**1. Weakly connected components → orphaned code.**
Nodes that no path reaches from the rest of the project. Running this externally on a
graphify graph of a Next.js repo (229 nodes) surfaced a component of 3 containing a React
component that nothing imports, and an isolated script — neither visible from `god-nodes`
or from community labels, because both metrics describe nodes that *are* connected.

**2. Strongly connected components → circular dependencies.**
A cycle means no member can be read, tested or replaced on its own. On a markdown-heavy
repo the same external run found a 9-file cycle spanning docs and automation:

```
STATUS.md -> fila.yml -> fila.py -> POST_02.md -> PAUTA_01.md -> CONTA.md -> STATUS.md
```

Five of the six edges were `EXTRACTED`. This is the kind of finding an onboarding agent
benefits from, and `GRAPH_REPORT.md` is the natural place for it.

## Suggested shape

```
graphify components         # weakly connected; flags the ones with no source files
graphify cycles             # strongly connected components of size > 1
```

and a short section in `GRAPH_REPORT.md`:

```
Components: 7 (largest 150 nodes, 66%)
Circular dependencies: 0
```

## One caveat worth designing around

Config files distort the count. In the Next.js repo above, 4 of the 7 components were
`package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `eslint.config.mjs` and `postcss.config.mjs` — each parses
into its own tree with no edge to source code, so they read as "orphans" while being
nothing of the sort. A component containing no `file_type: code` node could be labelled as
config rather than counted as orphaned code.

## Context

This came out of building a small external layer that post-processes `graph.json` for
exactly these questions, and then checking whether graphify already answered them. It does
not, but it is one import away from doing so — the extraction quality is already there, and
these would be a thin analysis pass on top rather than new machinery.

Happy to send a PR if the direction is welcome.

```
        for neighbor in neighbors:

                visited_set.add(neighbor)
```

The reproduction requirement is the point: someone who clones the repository and runs one command must get

```
bench/run.sh --suite <name>
             [--cell <id>...]
             [--competitor <name>...]
             [--repeat N]            # default 5
             [--duration S]          # default 60
             [--warmup S]            # default 30

             [--baseline <git-ref>]  # interleaved A/B against that ref
```

Behaviour contract:

- Captures provenance **first** and fails fast if it cannot. No kernel version, no run.
- Refuses to run on a dirty worktree unless `--allow-dirty`, and then stamps `dirty: true` into provenance;
  `dirty: true` results can never be published.
- Prints and records the exact command line of every tool invocation it makes.
- Writes one JSON per cell plus the raw `.hgrm` histograms.
- `--suite <name>` resolves through `matrix::suite(name)` from `{{bench-matrix-cells-and-corpora}}` and

  unrecognised name exits 2 printing all four. The suite vocabulary is deliberately NOT defined in this
  argument parser: it is a property of the registry, and a second definition here would drift from it.
  `--cell <id>` intersects the resolved set and names a cell that is not in it as an exit-2 error.
- `--baseline <ref>` builds that ref into a second binary in the same invocation and runs the interleaved
  A/B, emitting `ab.json` with the U statistic and p value. That flag is **declared but refused** in this
  issue with a message naming `{{perf-ab-interleaved-ratio-gate}}`, which implements it; a flag that
  silently does nothing is worse than one that says it is not wired yet.
- `--competitor <name>...` is part of the committed interface above and is **declared and permanently
  refused here**, with a message naming `scripts/bench/compare.sh` and `{{bench-competitor-compare-script}}`

  belong to that script, and because a second entry point for one capability is how the two acquire
  different defaults. This refusal is permanent: unlike `--baseline`, no later issue implements it.
- Exit codes: `0` all cells valid; `1` harness error; `2` one or more cells invalid; `3` a budget was
  exceeded. Exit code 3 is reachable only once `{{perf-budgets-file-and-raise-lint}}` lands; until then the
  budget check is a no-op that returns 0 budgets checked, and `--json` reports that count so its absence is

Issue #451: feat(python): class-field nodes, type-annotation edges, and enum members

## What problem does this solve?

Python class **bodies** are not extracted: class-level field/attribute assignments produce no nodes, type annotations are not projected as edges, and enums are not typed. The internal object model of every Python codebase is invisible to the graph.

Evidence from an indexed Django project (~82.6k nodes):
- `Field` label total = **9** across the entire graph — and all 9 are **Rust** struct fields; **zero Python**. `MATCH (c:Class)-[:DEFINES]->(f:Field)` -> **0 rows**.
- The core `Inventory` model (`base_api/observations/models/models_shared.py`) has **out_degree = 0** despite **in_degree = 1235** — heavily referenced, but its own body (every `CharField`/`ForeignKey`/etc.) contributes nothing.
- Type annotations live only as **string properties** (`return_type`/`param_types`): **219** methods carry `return_type` containing `Inventory`, but there is **no edge** to that `Class` node — "who returns/accepts `X`?" is not traversable.
- Enums: `Enum` label = **2** (both Rust); **493** Python enums (`Enum`/`TextChoices`/`IntegerChoices` bases) are bare `Class` nodes with no member representation.

Functions, methods, decorators (`DECORATES` 11,773) and inheritance (`INHERITS` 5,712) are already well modeled — the missing layer is **class fields + type-annotation edges + enum members**.

## Proposed solution

The tree-sitter Python grammar already exposes class-body assignments and `typed_parameter`/annotation nodes; the Rust path already emits `Field`. Extend the existing extractors (`internal/cbm/extract_defs.c`, `extract_type_refs.c` / `extract_type_assigns.c`):

1. **`Field` nodes** per class-level assignment / annotated attribute (plain assignment, `@dataclass`, `attrs`, Pydantic, Django `x = models.CharField(...)`), with `Class -[:DEFINES]-> Field` and `parent_class` (label + prop already exist in the schema).
2. **Generic symbol resolution** (NOT framework-specific): when a field's RHS callable argument or its annotation resolves to a known `Class`, emit `Field -[:REFERENCES]-> Class` — e.g. `ForeignKey(Inventory)`, `x: Inventory`, `list[Target]`. This is plain AST symbol resolution; the model-relationship graph people want emerges as a side effect, without modeling ORM semantics.
3. **Type-annotation edges:** project the already-parsed param/return annotation strings into `DEPENDS_ON`/`USAGE` edges to their `Class` nodes (today they are dead string props).
4. **Enums:** type enum classes as `Enum` and emit their members as `Field`s.

**Scope note:** this deliberately does NOT introduce Django-ORM-semantic FK/M2M/O2O edge *types* (framework-specific, out of scope for a generic AST tool) — only generic field nodes and symbol/type resolution. Relationship traversal falls out of (2) generically.

## Public OSS test beds

- `django/django` (its own `tests/` app models) and `wagtail/wagtail` — FK/M2M/O2O-heavy.
- `pydantic/pydantic`, `tiangolo/sqlmodel`, `tiangolo/fastapi` — annotated-attribute models and typed params.
- `python/cpython` `Lib/enum.py` + tests — enum members.

## Alternatives considered

- *Treat field assignments as generic `Variable`s:* loses parent-class scoping and the type target, so no reference/type edges — the key value.
- *`search_code` grep for `ForeignKey`/type names:* finds text, no graph edges; `trace_path` can't traverse.
- *LSP go-to-def on attributes:* intra-symbol resolution only; does not populate field/type graph structure.

## Confirmations
- [x] I searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate. Framework-semantic ORM relationship edges are intentionally excluded (generic field + type resolution only). Distinct from #292 (cross-repo protocol matching).

Issue #1521: Emit HLSL helper declarations before their call sites

## Problem

Materialized helper definitions can be emitted after HLSL functions that call them. HLSL does not provide C-style implicit function declarations, so DXC reports the call as an undeclared identifier even when an exact definition appears later in the same artifact.

This is separate from helper materialization and overload binding: the concrete symbol and body both exist, but declaration order makes the artifact invalid.

## Expected behavior

Emit HLSL functions in dependency order or generate legal forward declarations for reachable helpers. Preserve overload identity, parameter direction, arrays, resources, and generated names exactly between declarations, definitions, and calls.

## Acceptance criteria

- Build a call dependency graph for generated HLSL helpers and emit callees before callers when acyclic.
- Emit deterministic forward declarations for recursion and mutually recursive strongly connected components where HLSL supports the signature.
- Keep overload sets, generated mangled names, resource parameter types, fixed-array extents, and `in`/`out`/`inout` qualifiers identical.
- Scope each declaration to the entry-point package that uses it and avoid duplicate or conflicting prototypes.
- Reject signatures that cannot be declared legally in HLSL with a structured target diagnostic.
- Add DXC coverage for a late-defined helper, nested dependencies, overloads, and mutual recursion.

## Real-world impact

At MLX commit `968d264f2903d578e699c4452a4dbf48633921aa`, generated GEMV `run` helpers call specialized `load_safe` and `load_unsafe` functions around lines 6,480-16,000, while the exact definitions begin around line 16,506. Official DXC reports hundreds of undeclared helper calls even though the concrete definitions are present. Resolving the separate pointer and array contracts must not leave these declaration-order failures behind.

## Related work

- #1495 materializes the concrete sibling helpers and binds their canonical symbols; this issue covers legal HLSL declaration order after those bodies exist.

A bounded `phase-loop resume` repair child recursively invoked `phase-loop resume`, which launched another repair child instead of reconciling the trusted closeout. - repo: ReGenesis v63 FOUND phase
- original durable terminal: `awaiting_phase_closeout`, verification `passed`, 27 staged paths, all exactly in active plan ownership, four IF gates, valid browser evidence

## Reproduction

Run:

```text
PHASE_LOOP_REVIEW=block PHASE_LOOP_RUNNER_REPO_ROOT=/home/viperjuice/code/agent-harness \
  codex-phase-loop resume --phase FOUND --max-phases 1 --governed \
  --closeout-mode push --closeout-allow-unowned "<reason>" \
  --executor codex --model gpt-5.6-terra --effort high \
  --bypass-approvals --stream-output
```

The first repair child correctly established that every staged path matched the plan, then executed:

```text
phase-loop resume --repo <repo> --phase FOUND --max-phases 1 --closeout-mode push --json
```

- Recursive repair fan-out rather than closeout reconciliation.
- Operator SIGINT was required to stop it.
- Final state became `blocked`, verification `blocked`, blocker `repeated_verification_failure`, summary `Codex live launch for FOUND was interrupted and required process-group cleanup.`
- The staged application index remained intact.

## Expected result

A repair child must not be able to launch another repair for the same repo/phase/run lineage. It should emit a valid repair closeout to the parent, or the runtime should detect repair depth > 1 and reconcile/fail closed without recursive dispatch. Operator interruption of recursive cleanup should preserve the prior trusted terminal summary rather than superseding it with a less accurate blocker.

## Suggested guard

- Propagate a repair-lineage/depth environment marker and reject nested repair dispatch for the same repo+phase.
- Teach repair prompts not to invoke `phase-loop resume/run`; they should emit the shared closeout for parent reconciliation.
- On process-group cleanup, preserve the last verified terminal summary when the interrupted work unit was only a repair coordinator and made no repo changes.

# Issue: Stage 1d — IP-filter minus-strand window, memory footprint (280 GiB on PBMC), and three output-bookkeeping defects

**Labels:** bug, performance, Stage-1d. Found by the independent verifier of the final benchmark run (code `4efeb125`, 2026-08-21).

## 1. Internal-priming filter tests the wrong side on the minus strand
`ema/experimental/internal_priming.py` uses one forward-coordinate window `[pos-10, pos+30)` for both
strands. On `+` that is 10 bp upstream / 30 bp downstream of the cleavage site (correct: the
genomic A-stretch that primes oligo-dT sits downstream). On `-` the same genomic window is 30 bp
*upstream* / 10 bp downstream in transcript orientation, so the filter mostly tests upstream T-runs.
Re-applying a strand-symmetric rule to the survivors of the final run flags 3.5% (PBMC), 4.2% / 3.6%
(mice) of minus-strand sites that passed, and the current rule removed ~2,500 PBMC sites the
symmetric rule would keep. Benchmark effect is negligible (P@100 0.7167 → 0.7182) but the rule is
wrong. Fix: reflect the window on `-` (`[pos-30, pos+10)` genomic) and scan the reverse complement;
add a minus-strand unit test with an implanted downstream (transcript-wise) A-run.

## 2. Memory / CPU
Final PBMC 10k run: peak RSS **293.7 GB (280.1 GiB)** without IP filter, 239.5 GB with, wall 3:45 h,
~1.4 cores used despite `--threads 16`. That is 2.1× the pre-1b run (140 GB) and 2.8× the shipped
caller (105.6 GB); the tier-1 quantification changes (1b/1c) roughly doubled memory. Mice: 23 GB.
Please profile `ema/countmatrix/polya.py` ClipStream/ClipAccumulator (+ `{end1: {cb: n}}` maps) and
the candidate-partition path; likely wins: stream per chromosome, drop per-end1 maps after flush,
use array-backed counters. Also: peak calling is effectively serial — `--threads` only helps
downstream.

## 3. Output bookkeeping
- In `--ip-filter-mode filter`, `annotatedpas.bed` has no per-site IP column (9 columns); only
  `04_pas_gene_assignment/peak_filters_stats.json` counts. Downstream "trusted novel PAS" needs a
  per-site flag: write it in both modes (or always emit `ip_flags.tsv`).
- `pasbed.bed` silently drops gene-assigned PAS with zero counts after the CB filter
  (PBMC 1,814 = 0.45%; mouse1 2,809 = 3.7% of `annotatedpas.bed`). Document, or record them with
  count 0.
- `ema/cli/run.py` logs "--seq-len / yaml seqlen not set; defaulting to 150" before the Click value
  is merged, although the resolved config has 91/98. Misleading.
- In multi-dataset runs `unified/multi_sample_merged.bed` col 5 is the *first* merged member's
  clip-molecule count (`bedtools merge -o first`), not cohort support; a unified PAS can merge a
  tier-1 member with a tier-2 member. Please emit cohort-level `clip_umis_sum` / `any_tier1` per
  unified PAS (we currently recompute from the per-dataset `*.support.tsv` via
  `multi_sample_pas_mapping.tsv`).

Issue #41: [RELIABILITY][P1] Restore PostgreSQL tables in dependency-safe order

## Severity
**P1 / High**

## Summary
PostgreSQL backup data is ordered alphabetically by schema/table and restored in that same order. The restore does not account for foreign-key dependencies or defer constraints, so a child table can be imported before the parent rows it references.

## Evidence
`PostgresBackupEngine.CreateBackupAsync(...)` obtains tables with `ORDER BY table_schema, table_name` and serializes one `COPY` block per table.

`RestoreBackupAsync(...)` replays those blocks sequentially with ordinary constraint enforcement. There is no dependency graph, constraint deferral/disable strategy or native `pg_restore` ordering.

## Impact
A logically valid backup can fail to restore solely because alphabetical order does not match referential dependency order. Combined with a non-atomic restore, this can also leave earlier tables modified before the FK failure occurs.

## Recommended remediation
1. Prefer native PostgreSQL dump/restore ordering where possible.
2. Otherwise build a dependency-aware table order from foreign-key metadata.
3. Where appropriate, use transaction-scoped deferred constraints with explicit validation before commit.
4. Detect cycles and define a safe strategy rather than relying on incidental naming.
5. Add multi-schema parent/child and cyclic-FK restore tests.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Parent/child tables restore successfully regardless of alphabetical names.
- [ ] Multi-schema foreign keys are handled.
- [ ] Cyclic dependencies have an explicit tested strategy.
- [ ] Constraints are validated before a restore is considered successful.
- [ ] Integration tests include a schema where the child sorts before its parent.

Issue #138: AI Assistant sessions don't use ToolsetResolver — nested toolsets silently broken

## Summary

The `AssistantSessionManager` has its own inline toolset expansion (`expandToolset()`,
lines 866-879) instead of using the existing `ToolsetResolver` service. The inline
implementation lacks recursive expansion, so nested `@ToolsetName` references within
toolsets are passed as literal strings to `--allowedTools` rather than being expanded.

## How it works today

There are two separate code paths for resolving `@ToolsetName` references:

### `ToolsetResolver` (used by task execution and reports)

`core/src/main/java/.../ToolsetResolver.java` is an `@ApplicationScoped` CDI bean with:

- **Recursive expansion** — if toolset "Dev" contains `@Base`, it recursively expands "Base"
- **Cycle detection** — a `visited` set prevents infinite loops
- **Deduplication** — uses `LinkedHashSet` to remove duplicates while preserving order

Used by `TaskExecutionService` (line 265) and `ReportExecutionService` (line 325).

### `AssistantSessionManager.expandToolset()` (used by AI Assistant sessions)

`app/src/main/java/.../AssistantSessionManager.java` lines 866-879 has its own inline
implementation that:

- Does **NOT** recurse — `@AnotherToolset` references inside a toolset are added as literal
  strings
- **No cycle detection**
- **No deduplication** — uses plain `ArrayList`

## Why nesting matters

The UI explicitly supports nesting. `ToolsetDetailPage.tsx` (line 146-148) tells users:

> *"Define the tools in this toolset. You can add individual tool patterns like
> `Bash(git log *)` or reference other toolsets using the `@ToolsetName` syntax."*

A user could reasonably create:

- **Toolset "Base Read"** = `Read, Grep, Glob`
- **Toolset "Dev"** = `@Base Read, Edit, Write, Bash(git *)`

When a session template uses `@Dev`:

| Path | Result |
|------|--------|
| Task execution (`ToolsetResolver`) | `Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash(git *)` |
| AI Assistant (`expandToolset`) | `@Base Read, Edit, Write, Bash(git *)` |

In the assistant path, `@Base Read` ends up as a literal argument to `--allowedTools`,
which Claude Code doesn't recognize as a valid tool pattern.

## Root cause

Input format mismatch. `ToolsetResolver.resolve()` takes a comma-separated `String`
(matching `ActionTypeEntity.allowedTools`, a single TEXT column). But
`SessionTemplateEntity.allowedTools` is a `@ElementCollection` (`List<String>`). Rather
than adapting `ToolsetResolver` to accept a `List<String>`, an inline implementation was
written that omitted recursion, cycle detection, and deduplication.

## Fix

Add a `resolve(List<String>)` overload to `ToolsetResolver`, inject it into
`AssistantSessionManager`, and delete the private `expandToolset()` and
`resolveAllowedTools()` methods.

Issue #7875: feat: Transitive compatibility impact analysis via reference graph

## Description

Compatibility checks are pairwise: "is PaymentInfo v2 compatible with v1?" But schemas reference each other in a DAG. A compatible change to `PaymentInfo` can silently break `OrderEvent` or `UserEvent` which reference it — and the pairwise check doesn't warn about this.

No schema registry evaluates compatibility transitively across the reference graph.

## Proposed Feature

A `/compatibility/impact` endpoint that, given a proposed schema change, reports the full blast radius.

### API

```
POST /apis/registry/v3/compatibility/impact

{
  "groupId": "com.example",
  "artifactId": "PaymentInfo",
  "content": "<proposed new schema>",
  "contentType": "application/json"
}
```

Response:
```json
{
  "directlyAffected": 3,
  "transitivelyAffected": 7,
  "breaking": 1,
  "results": [
    {
      "artifact": "com.example/OrderEvent",
      "version": "3",
      "depth": 1,
      "result": "COMPATIBLE",
      "rule": "BACKWARD"
    },
    {
      "artifact": "com.example/UserEvent",
      "version": "5",
      "depth": 1,
      "result": "INCOMPATIBLE",
      "rule": "BACKWARD",
      "violations": ["Field 'payment' default references removed field 'legacyCode'"]
    }
  ]
}
```

### How It Works

1. **Reverse reference lookup**: Query `artifact_references` for all schemas referencing the changed artifact. Walk transitively via BFS up to configurable depth (default 5).
2. **Resolved compatibility**: For each affected schema, resolve references using current versions AND proposed change, then compare using the affected schema's compatibility rule.
3. **Impact report**: Aggregate into structured report with blast radius metrics.

### Enforcement Modes

| Mode | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| `REPORT` (default) | Return impact report, allow registration |
| `WARN` | Return report with warnings in response headers |
| `ENFORCE` | Reject registration if any affected schema breaks |

### Configuration

```properties
apicurio.compatibility.transitive.mode=REPORT
apicurio.compatibility.transitive.max-depth=5
```

### UI Integration

- Impact report surfaced when creating a new version: "This change affects 7 schemas. 1 would become incompatible."
- Visual reference graph with red/green compatibility indicators.

## Priority

High — most impactful for organizations with >100 schemas and cross-references. Debezium deployments (one schema per table, shared referenced types) would benefit immediately.

## Related

- #6948 — Improved support for artifact references
- #5297 — Branch transitive compatibility (different concept — within-artifact vs across-artifacts)

Two aggregations in `app/repositories/sla_repository.py` disagree about what "an outage's result" means:

```python
# aggregate_dashboard_kpis: counts every SLAResultORM row
query = select(func.count(SLAResultORM.id).label("total_outages"), ...)
# no filter on is_latest

# aggregate_performance: picks one row per outage via row_number
.row_number().over(partition_by=outage_id, order_by=(created_at.desc(), id.desc()))
```

`SLARepository.create` appends a NEW row on every recompute (demoting the previous `is_latest`). Consequences:

- **KPI inflation**: `GET /sla/analytics/dashboard` counts every historical recompute as a separate outage. A single outage recomputed 5 times after config changes contributes 5 to `total_outages` and any violated variant to `total_violations`, while `GET /sla/analytics/performance` reports it once. The two endpoints answer the same question with different denominators.
- **Snapshot inconsistency**: `create_snapshot`/`rebuild_snapshot` mix the two aggregations (KPIs for counts, `avg_mttr` from performance), producing snapshots whose `total_outages` cannot be reconciled with the reported violation rate.
- **Drift detection is self-consistent but misleading**: `reconcile_snapshots` compares live KPIs to snapshot KPIs, so both can agree while both are wrong.

## Root cause

The `is_latest` flag (`app/models/orm/sla.py`) exists and is maintained, but the KPI aggregation never uses it.

## Why this is architecturally hard

1. The correct fix is to add `.filter(SLAResultORM.is_latest.is_(True))` (or a `DISTINCT ON (outage_id)`) to the KPI query, but that changes historical dashboard values, so the change needs a documented migration note and updated golden values in the dashboard tests.
2. The dispute flow writes proposed rows with `is_latest=False` that are newer by `created_at` than the real latest — any "latest by created_at" strategy must also respect the flag, which the performance aggregation currently ignores (see the related rejected-dispute issue).
3. The frontend dashboard (`src/features/dashboard/` and `src/components/dashboard/sla-dashboard-view.tsx` in ApexChainx-Frontend) displays these KPIs; changing semantics changes what operators see, so the change must be coordinated and versioned.

## Proposed design

Make `aggregate_dashboard_kpis` count only `is_latest` rows (with a `DISTINCT ON` fallback for pre-migration data, mirroring `get_by_outage`), and add a regression test that recomputes one outage N times and asserts KPI counts stay at 1. Add a `method` field to the snapshot schema noting the counting rule.

## Downstream impact

Frontend dashboard KPI values change; no schema change. Backend OpenAPI snapshot unchanged unless the response shape gains the `method` field.

## Acceptance criteria

### Service
- [ ] Dashboard KPIs count each outage once regardless of recompute history.
- [ ] KPIs and performance aggregation agree on `total_outages` for the same filter.

### Tests
- [ ] A test creates one outage, computes SLA twice with changed config, and asserts KPIs report 1 outage.
- [ ] Snapshot reconciliation tests pass with the corrected counts.

## Out of scope

The rejected-dispute row pollution (tracked separately) and analytics caching.

## Getting started

```bash
pytest tests/test_sla_typing.py -q
make typecheck
```

Good first files to read: `app/repositories/sla_repository.py`, `app/models/orm/sla.py`, `tests/test_sla_typing.py`.

[View Post on Blog](https://allanchain.github.io/blog/post/pipenv-and-poetry)

> Strange as the title is, they just don't work conveniently "out of box"

---

## Preface

> I am not an expert. Wrote this section just for completion.

### Why not simply pip

`pip install` is simple and naive. You will get crazy if you come from JavaScript world where both npm and yarn are excellent package managers. It even takes effort to manage production and development dependecies in two separate list. A tool for handling all the dependencies and virtual env works is handy, and can simplify workflows.

### What do they actuallly do

Pretty much like mentioned above. Quoting from pipenv's doc for some detailed feature:

> - Enables truly deterministic builds, while easily specifying only what you want.
> - Generates and checks file hashes for locked dependencies.
> - Automatically install required Pythons, if pyenv is available.
> - Automatically finds your project home, recursively, by looking for a Pipfile.
> - Automatically generates a Pipfile, if one doesn’t exist.
> - Automatically creates a virtualenv in a standard location.
> - Automatically adds/removes packages to a Pipfile when they are installed or uninstalled.
> - Automatically loads .env files, if they exist.

## Major Problem: Speed

Resolving and locking dependencies are **too slow**. A typical jupyterlab workspace takes hours to finish.

### Why this happens

In node package ecosystem a project has hundreds of dependencies to resolve, install and lock, but still faster than pipenv or poetry. That's because in python package ecosystem, many packages are not properly formed and it's impossible to get it's dependencies without downloading it.

See also https://python-poetry.org/docs/faq/#why-is-the-dependency-resolution-process-slow

### How to solve in pipenv

pipenv is slow at locking, so you may want use `--skip-lock` flag or set `PIPENV_SKIP_LOCK` env when the network is poor, then `pipenv lock` when network connection is good.

### How to solve in poetry

Poetry is slow at dependency resolution. Quoting from poetry doc:

> At the moment there is no way around it.

## Other pipenv problems

### Lock file not cross platform

Ironically, _deterministic builds_ actually leads to wrong packages installed on different platforms.

Lock files may be version-dependent. Take `pytest` for example, if you install and lock on python 3.8, the `importlib_metadata` is not installed because py3.8 already have `importlib.metadata` included. But when you install based on the lock file on py3.6, `importlib_metadata` is not found. This is not happening when directly install `pytest` on py3.6

#### How to solve

1. Use markers for subdependencies: `importlib_metadata = {version="~=1.7.0", python_version="<'3.8'"}`
2. Or use [`pyenv`](https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv) / [`pyenv-win`](https://github.com/pyenv-win/pyenv-win)

### apt install may be outdated

Better install via pip(x)

### Script shortcut cannot combine multi commands

pypa/pipenv#2283

You can write `command A && command B` in `package.json`, but not `Pipfile`. All you can do is write in a shell script.

### No python version range

pypa/pipenv#1050

If you are sure that your program and `Pipfile.lock` works for python > 3.5.2, remove python requirement :smirk:

### No extra denpendencies

This can be frustrating if you want uWSGI to be installed only on production machine, but not on your PC.

## Other poetry problems

### Prefer `python`

**Use poetry with pyenv if `python -V` outputs `2.7.x`.** Or it will be an awful develop experience.

Or if you are sure you just need to create venv with system's python3, you can choose pip(x) install it.

Issue #5: Feat: Memory Layer

Implement a persistent memory layer to allow the AI assistant to learn and remember information across sessions.

## Overview
- Store and retrieve contextual information between sessions
- Remember user preferences and coding patterns
- Build knowledge about the project over time
- Create a searchable memory database
- Support different memory scopes (project, global, session)

This will enable the AI to provide more personalized assistance and maintain context about projects and user preferences across multiple interactions.

## Implementation Approaches

### Approach 1: SQLite + In-Memory Cache

A lightweight approach using SQLite (already in the project) with an intelligent caching layer for performance.

**Pros:**
- No external dependencies
- Good performance for small-medium datasets (< 10k memories)
- Simple to implement and maintain
- Transactional consistency

**Architecture:**
- SQLite for persistent storage with denormalized schema
- LRU cache for hot memories
- In-memory graph index for relationship traversal
- Lightweight embeddings using TF-IDF or keyword extraction

**Key Components:**
- Memory types: facts, insights, patterns, preferences
- Smart pruning based on importance scores
- Async memory extraction from interactions
- Simple relationship tracking without complex graph queries

### Approach 2: Embedded Graph Database

Use a purpose-built embedded graph database for more sophisticated memory relationships.

**Options:**

1. **Cayley** (github.com/cayleygraph/cayley)
   - Pure Go graph database inspired by Google's Knowledge Graph
   - Supports multiple backends including BoltDB
   - Built-in graph query language (Gizmo)
   - Good for complex relationship queries

2. **BadgerDB + Graph Layer** (github.com/dgraph-io/badger)
   - High-performance key-value store from Dgraph team
   - Build custom graph layer on top
   - Excellent performance for large datasets
   - Used in production at scale

3. **BoltDB/BBolt + Graph Layer** (github.com/etcd-io/bbolt)
   - Simple, reliable embedded key-value database
   - Mature and battle-tested
   - Build lightweight graph operations on top
   - Good for moderate datasets

4. **EliasDB** (github.com/krotik/eliasdb)
   - Pure Go graph database
   - Built-in REST API and query language
   - Standalone or embedded usage
   - Includes graph traversal features

**Pros:**
- Better performance for complex graph operations
- Native graph traversal capabilities
- Scales better for larger memory stores
- More sophisticated relationship modeling

**Cons:**
- Additional dependency
- More complex to implement
- Potentially overkill for simple use cases

Issue #92: chore(repo): define branch lifecycle and cleanup automation

## Context

A branch audit found that squash-merged PR branches continue to appear ahead of `main` even when their exact reviewed content has already landed. The repository also accumulates short-lived `automation/*` result refs and `research/*` diagnostic refs.

This is low-priority repository housekeeping. It must not displace H02A, physical validation, or other product-critical work.

## Proposed outcome

Define and implement a conservative branch-lifecycle policy that keeps useful provenance while preventing stale refs from accumulating indefinitely.

## Candidate policy

- Automatically delete ordinary same-repository PR head branches after a confirmed merge.
- Give `automation/*` branches a short retention window after their result has been incorporated or linked from the owning PR/experiment record.
- Give `research/*` branches a longer retention window, requiring useful conclusions or evidence references to be summarized before deletion.
- Preserve `main`, active PR heads, `archive/*`, explicitly pinned refs, and branches referenced by unresolved review/evidence work.
- Never infer safety from GitHub's ahead/behind badge alone; verify merge/PR identity or use an explicit allowlist.
- Provide a dry-run/report mode and an easy manual retention override before enabling destructive cleanup.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A documented lifecycle policy defines branch classes, retention periods, exclusions, and ownership.
- [ ] Ordinary merged branches can be deleted automatically or through a safe repeatable command/workflow.
- [ ] `automation/*` and `research/*` cleanup checks verify that relevant results have been incorporated or referenced.
- [ ] The cleanup path refuses active PR heads, protected/default branches, archived refs, and ambiguous branches.
- [ ] A dry-run produces a human-reviewable deletion plan before any scheduled destructive run.
- [ ] Tests cover squash-merged branches, post-merge commits, active PRs, failed research runs, pinned refs, and repeated idempotent execution.

## Non-goals

- No immediate deletion of existing research or diagnostic history.
- No change to product behavior, acceptance gates, roadmap authorization, or release status.
- No aggressive cleanup based solely on branch age.

Issue #106831: RFC: Fast GPIO API Extension

### Problem Description

`ws2812_gpio` and similar bit-bang drivers require sub-microsecond GPIO toggling. The standard `gpio_pin_set_raw()` is too slow for this — it goes through two indirect pointer dereferences and a non-inlinable function call (~10–20 cycles), while WS2812 allows only ~20–40 cycles per phase at typical MCU speeds.

The current solution is vendor-specific inline assembly hardcoded into `ws2812_gpio.c`, locking the driver to nRF51/52/53/91 only:

```c
/* ws2812_gpio.c today */
volatile uint32_t *base = (volatile uint32_t *)&NRF_GPIO->OUTSET;
#define SET_HIGH "str %[p], [%[r], #0]\n"
#define SET_LOW  "str %[p], [%[r], #4]\n"
```

Every new platform (SAM0, STM32, MSPM0, ...) must add another `#ifdef` branch to `ws2812_gpio.c`. This is the root problem this RFC addresses.

---

### Why not #105263 (`GPIO_GET_REGS`)

PR #105263 solves the performance problem but leaks raw MMIO register addresses across the subsystem boundary into `ws2812_gpio.c`:

```c
/* With GPIO_GET_REGS — ws2812_gpio still does MMIO manipulation */
sys_write32(pin_mask, regs.set);   /* regs.set is a raw register pointer */
```

Additionally `regs.set` and `regs.clear` can be NULL on platforms without dedicated SET/CLEAR registers, pushing fallback logic onto every consumer.

### Proposed Change (Summary)

Extend the GPIO API with a fast path for pin operations. The extension has three parts: vendor-owned headers, Kconfig-driven selection, and a small addition to `gpio.h`.

### Proposed Change (Detailed)

## Design rules

- **One `gpio_fast_spec` represents one port** with a mask of one or more pins on that port. All masked pins are operated atomically in a single register write.
  Pins on different ports require separate specs and are operated sequentially by the consumer — cross-port atomicity is not a goal of this API.
- **`gpio_fast_spec` is opaque to consumers.** Its fields are vendor-defined and must not be accessed directly. It is fully pre-computed by `gpio_fast_configure()` and treated as `const` thereafter — never mutated during operation.
- **`__ramfunc` is owned by the vendor header.** If a platform requires the fast path to run from RAM (e.g. to avoid flash wait-state jitter), the vendor marks its inline functions accordingly. The requirement propagates automatically up the inlined call chain to the first non-inlined boundary in the consumer. No `__ramfunc` annotation is ever needed in consumer code.
- **IRQ locking for stream operations is owned by the API.** `gpio_fast_send_stream()` acquires and releases the IRQ lock internally. Consumers do not manage locks for stream transmission.

---

## API

### Configure

```c
/**
 * @brief Populate a gpio_fast_spec for one or more pins on a port.
 *
 * Pre-computes all vendor-specific state needed for fast operations
 * (register addresses, pin mask, direction registers for fast
 * reconfiguration). Must be called once at init before any fast
 * operation.
 *
 * All pins in pin_mask must belong to the same port.
 *
 * @param fast      Output. Opaque fast path descriptor.
 * @param port      GPIO port device.
 * @param pin_mask  Mask of one or more pins on that port.
 * @param flags     GPIO configuration flags (e.g. GPIO_OUTPUT).
 * @return 0 on success, negative errno on failure.
 */
int gpio_fast_configure(struct gpio_fast_spec *fast,
                        const struct device *port,
                        gpio_port_pins_t pin_mask,
                        gpio_flags_t flags);

/**
 * @brief Single-pin convenience wrapper using a gpio_dt_spec.
 *
 * Equivalent to gpio_fast_configure() with pin_mask = BIT(spec->pin).
 */
static inline int gpio_fast_configure_dt(struct gpio_fast_spec *fast,
                                         const struct gpio_dt_spec *spec,
                                         gpio_flags_t flags)
{
    return gpio_fast_configure(fast, spec->port, BIT(spec->pin), flags);
}
```

## Problem

CLI has placeholder commands for managing analyzed packages, but they're not implemented. Users can analyze code but can't:
- List what packages are stored
- View package details/statistics
- Export graph data
- Delete packages from database

### Current State

```bash
mapper analyse list          # Shows "Not implemented yet"
mapper analyse get my-pkg    # Shows "Not implemented yet"  
mapper analyse export my-pkg # Shows "Not implemented yet"
mapper analyse delete my-pkg # Shows "Not implemented yet"
```

## Required Commands

### `mapper analyse list`

List all analyzed packages in database.

**Options**:
- `--detailed` - Show full stats (node counts, relationships, timestamps)
- `--json` - Output as JSON

**Output**:
```
Analyzed Packages:
  my-app       50 modules, 200 classes, 500 functions    2026-03-26
  utils        10 modules,  30 classes, 100 functions    2026-03-25
  service      25 modules, 120 classes, 300 functions    2026-03-24
```

### `mapper analyse get <package>`

Show detailed package statistics.

**Options**:
- `--depth N` - Max depth for relationship traversal (default: 3)
- `--stats-only` - Show only statistics, no graph details

**Output**:
```
Package: my-app
Analyzed: 2026-03-26 14:30:00

Nodes:
  Modules:     50
  Classes:    200
  Functions:  500
  Methods:   1200

Relationships:
  DEFINES:    750
  CONTAINS:  1200
  CALLS:     3500
  IMPORTS:    200
  INHERITS:    50

Most Connected:
  utils.helpers.format_data (45 incoming calls)
  models.Base (30 child classes)
```

Export graph data in various formats.

**Options**:
- `--format <fmt>` - Export format: `json`, `cypher`, `graphml`, `dot`, `csv` (default: json)
- `--output <path>` - Output file path (default: stdout)
- `--only <type>` - Export only `nodes` or `relationships`
- `--node-type <type>` - Filter by node type (Module, Class, Function, Method)
- `--relationship-type <type>` - Filter by relationship type
- `--pretty` - Pretty-print output

**Formats**:

**JSON**:
```json
{
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "...", "label": "Class", "properties": {...}},
    ...
  ],
  "relationships": [
    {"from": "...", "to": "...", "type": "CALLS"},
```

```cypher
CREATE (n2:Class {name: "App", fqn: "main.App", ...});
CREATE (n1)-[:DEFINES]->(n2);
```

Issue #14789: [Perf]: nativeWatcher registers ignored descendants for recursive context dependencies

### Summary

On Linux, `experiments.nativeWatcher` registers every ignored descendant of a
recursive context dependency before applying `watchOptions.ignored`. This
adds avoidable lazy-startup work, consumes inotify descriptors, and can reach
`max_user_watches` on large repositories. Watchpack prunes the same tree and
keeps the descriptor count flat.

### Reproduction and measurements

Create an entry plus eight live nested directories and an ignored tree, add
their common parent to `compilation.contextDependencies`, enable
`experiments.nativeWatcher`, and set `watchOptions.ignored` to
`'**/ignored/**'`. Count `inotify wd:` lines in `/proc/<pid>/fdinfo/*` after
the first watch callback, then write one ignored file and one live nested file.

| ignored top-level dirs | physical ignored dirs | native watches | native ready | Watchpack watches | Watchpack ready |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 1 | 23 | ~0.20 s | 23 | ~0.29 s |
| 100 | 201 | 223 | ~0.22 s | 23 | ~0.29 s |
| 1,000 | 2,001 | 2,023 | ~0.34 s | 23 | ~0.30 s |
| 5,000 | 10,001 | 10,023 | ~1.25 s | 23 | ~0.32 s |

The native no-ignore run has the same registration counts. Ignored writes do
not rebuild and live nested writes do, so event filtering is correct; the
problem is specifically registration/traversal cost.

### Cause and suggested direction

The inotify backend recursively walks/registers descendants for a recursive
watch and also recursively registers newly created or moved-in directories.
Rspack currently filters in the event trigger, after that work is complete.
A single non-recursive context watch is not sufficient because it would miss
changes in pre-existing children.

The maintainable fix is an ignored-aware recursive registration path (ideally
a prune predicate in the watcher backend) that applies the same filter during
both the initial walk and later create/rename registration. An in-Rspack Linux
registration actor could alternatively register retained directories
non-recursively, process directory create/rename/remove events without calling
synchronous `watch()` from the notify callback, and preserve symlink,
watch-limit, and close/rebuild semantics. This should have focused tests for
ignored/live siblings, nested creation, rename in/out, symlinks, and races.

This was found while validating the consolidated HMR/lazy-compilation work in
#14772; it is intentionally separate from the correctness fixes in that PR.

# [RFC / Research Plan] Benchmarking Protocol Adherence, Model Performance, and Citation Fidelity across AI Coding Agents

## Summary

We propose a comprehensive benchmarking framework and study to evaluate how AI coding agents execute standardized computational biology protocols. Specifically, this plan investigates:
1. **Model Generalizability:** How protocol execution varies across a range of frontier, reasoning, lightweight, and open-weight LLMs.
2. **Behavioral & Performance Delta:** How the presence of a structured `protocol.md` alters agent behavior, accuracy, and efficiency compared to unguided baselines.
3. **Citation & Provenance Fidelity:** Whether agents faithfully report primary literature citations (DOIs/PMIDs) from atomic (1 citation) and composite (1+ aggregated citations) protocols, and how an invoking agent skill can reinforce this behavior.

---

## Motivation & Core Questions

As we develop AI-agent-executable protocols (ADR 0001, ADR 0004), we must systematically measure how effectively agents consume these specifications and whether they maintain scientific rigor during execution.

### 1. Performance Across a Range of Models
* **Question:** Do lightweight or cost-effective models (e.g., Gemini 2.0 Flash, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o-mini) follow protocols as effectively as flagship reasoning models (e.g., Gemini Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet with Thinking, o1/o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1)?
* **Implication:** Understanding model tier requirements helps users balance computational cost with execution reliability when dispatching agents on automated workflows.

### 2. Behavioral & Performance Impact of Protocols
* **Question:** How does providing an explicit `protocol.md` change agent behavior compared to open-ended coding prompts?
* **Hypotheses to Test:**
  * Protocols will significantly reduce trial-and-error loops, non-existent parameter hallucinations, and deprecated API calls.
  * Protocols will improve deterministic step completion and reproducibility.
  * Protocols will reduce overall token usage and runtime by eliminating exploratory search.

### 3. Primary Literature Citation Fidelity in a1+ Protocols
* **Question:** Do coding agents faithfully attribute and cite primary literature when executing atomic (single-citation) and composite (multi-citation aggregated) protocols?
* **Challenges:**
  * LLMs frequently hallucinate DOIs, omit citations for sub-steps, or substitute general review papers for the specific primary method citations defined in the protocol YAML frontmatter.
  * In **atomic protocols** (1 citation), the agent must precisely report the single primary method DOI (e.g., the original tool paper).
  * In **composite protocols** (1+ citations), the agent must trace the entire `protocols_used` dependency graph and aggregate all constituent atomic citations into the final run provenance and manuscript methods.
* **Skill Reinforcement:** We hypothesize that wrapping protocol execution in an invoking agent skill (e.g., `bioc-protocol-runner` / `run-protocol`) with explicit citation schemas and tool-level provenance enforcement will bring citation fidelity to ~100%.

---

### 1. Test Conditions (A / B / C Testing)

* **Condition B (Protocol in Context):** Agent is given the prompt + the raw `protocol.md` (frontmatter + instructions) in context.
* **Condition C (Protocol + Invoking Skill):** Agent executes the protocol via an invoking skill that enforces step validation, environment setup, and structured provenance citation logging.

### Describe the bug

## Summary

`sparse_attn_sharedkv` in the PA_ND compressed-KV path can produce different BF16 outputs when only the physical paged-KV block allocation changes. The logical query, K/V values, sparse indices, and attention metadata remain identical.

This makes DeepSeek V4 logits and selected tokens depend on allocator state. It reproduces without PD separation, graph mode, EP, MTP, prefix caching, or DSpark. Higher concurrency can exercise block reuse and fragmentation more often, but this issue does not make a quantitative failure-rate claim.

The operator defect and its fix are independently demonstrated below. Premature EOS and `stop_without_tool_call` are not used as correctness criteria for this issue because a separate frontend rendering defect in #14035 materially changes that boundary; see [Scope](#scope).

## Root cause

The first incorrect boundary is [`SASVectorBlock<SAST>::CopyInKv`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/blob/50e0ce60849a7b6fe6f94e1de085b6fc06e7006d/csrc/attention/sparse_attn_sharedkv/op_kernel/arch32/sparse_attn_sharedkv_scfa_block_vector.h#L589-L643).

For a pair of compressed-KV blocks, the PA_ND fast path derives `srcStride` from the absolute difference between two physical GM offsets, starts from the lower physical address, and issues one strided DMA:

```cpp
int64_t blkTableSrcStride =
    Abs(keyOffset1 - keyOffset2) - sparseBlockSize * headDim;
int64_t startGmOffset = MinValid(keyOffset1, keyOffset2);
intriParams.blockCount = (keyOffset1 >= 0) + (keyOffset2 >= 0);
intriParams.srcStride = blkTableSrcStride * sizeof(KV_T);
DataCopyPad(kvMergUb_[...], cmpKvGm_[startGmOffset], intriParams, padParams);
```

The DMA therefore copies the lower physical address first instead of preserving the logical order supplied by `cmp_sparse_indices`. Paged allocation is runtime state and must not change the semantic operator result, but here it changes the merged K/V row order consumed by matmul and softmax.

The K/V values themselves are intact. A diagnostic kernel mirrored the merged BF16 rows after `CopyInKv`, and a CPU reconstruction followed the source code's exact addressing and fallback rules. For rank-4 query row 629, changing only the physical block table reversed 61 of 79 pair slots, or 122 row positions, while preserving the exact K/V row multiset. Both captured DMA buffers matched the CPU reconstruction bitwise.

The row permutation changes finite-precision reduction order. The first observed tensor difference is in `sparse_attn_sharedkv`, before it propagates through `wo_a`, `wo_b`, all-reduce, later layers, logits, and token selection.

BSND and TND do not use this paged physical-address ordering rule.

## Proposed fix

For PA_ND, copy the two blocks separately with `CopyInSingleKv` in the order supplied by `cmp_sparse_indices`. BSND and TND keep the existing path.

This is preferable to sorting each pair by logical sparse index because `cmp_sparse_indices` already defines the operator input order. A conditional implementation that retained the dual DMA when physical and logical order happened to agree was also allocation-invariant, but compiled slower than the simpler unconditional implementation.

Issue #20743: Bug Report: recursive CTEs with an unexpandable star seed panic during semantic analysis

> **Not looking for external contributions on this one.** We're already working in this area and intend to fix it ourselves. Please don't open a PR against this issue — it's filed to track the problem and record the analysis, not as an invitation. Comments and additional repro cases are very welcome.

## Overview of the Issue

A recursive CTE whose seed selects `*` from a table without authoritative column information panics during semantic analysis. The star never gets expanded, so column resolution finds a `StarExpr` where it expects only `AliasedExpr` entries. Semantic analysis runs before `operators.PlanQuery`, so it is outside the planner's `PanicHandler`; the panic travels to `VTGate.HandlePanic` and comes back to the client as an `uncaught panic` INTERNAL error, with a stack trace in the vtgate logs. Plain client SQL is enough to trigger it, e.g. whenever schema tracking is disabled, stale, or has not yet seen the table.

There are two shapes, with different panic sites:

1. **Without a declared column list** — `CTETable.getColumns` panics on the unexpanded star (`go/vt/vtgate/semantics/cte_table.go`, the `VT12001("should not be called")` branch) while resolving the recursive reference inside the definition.
2. **With a declared column list** — `extractColumnsFromCTE` (`go/vt/vtgate/semantics/real_table.go`) compares the declared list against the length of the *unexpanded* projection — one `StarExpr` — and hits the raw `panic("mismatch of columns")` while resolving columns at the CTE's use site. Because this is a string panic rather than an error-typed one, `operators.PanicHandler` would re-panic on it even where that handler is on the stack.

## Reproduction Steps

Sharded keyspace with a table the schema tracker has no authoritative column list for (`user_metadata` in `go/vt/vtgate/planbuilder/testdata/vschemas/schema.json` works in the planner test harness).

Shape 1:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE x AS (SELECT * FROM user_metadata UNION ALL SELECT id + 1 FROM x WHERE id < 10) SELECT id FROM x
```

Shape 2:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE x(a, b, c, d, e) AS (SELECT * FROM user_metadata UNION ALL SELECT a + 1, b, c, d, e FROM x WHERE a < 10) SELECT a FROM x
```

Both return `uncaught panic` to the client instead of planning (shape 1 today panics in `CTETable.getColumns`; shape 2 panics at the same place first, and at `extractColumnsFromCTE` once #20702 is applied). An unsharded pass-through does not reach the panic — the query is routed without ever resolving the CTE's columns.

## Analysis

Status against the two in-flight PRs in this area:

| Shape | main | after #20633 | after #20633 + #20702 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No declared list, star seed | panics (`getColumns`) | panics (`getColumns`) | ✅ plans as a single route |
| Declared list, star seed | panics (`getColumns`) | panics (`getColumns`) | ❌ panics (`extractColumnsFromCTE`) |

#20633 validates declared column list lengths but deliberately skips full validation when the projection still contains a star (a star expands to at least one column, so only `fewer names than select expressions` is provably wrong). That skip admits exactly the shape-2 combination: the declared list passes the check, `getColumns` no longer panics after #20702, and `extractColumnsFromCTE` then trips over the arity it compares against the unexpanded projection.

The likely fix for the remaining shape is to make `extractColumnsFromCTE` tolerate a star-containing projection the way `extractSelectExprsFromCTE` already does (return nil and fall back to non-authoritative resolution) instead of panicking, plus a regression test for the declared-list-over-star shape. Converting the raw string panic into a typed error would also stop this class of bug from escaping `PanicHandler` in the future.

Issue #4878: Threads Module

**“Threads” module** and a **feed** with hierarchical post-reply relationships, similar to the structure used in X (formerly Twitter). The module will allow posts and replies to behave as equal entities, capable of being parents or children, with efficient database queries and seamless user experience.

## **1. General Module Design**

The “Threads” module will enable users to:

• Create **standalone posts**.

• Reply to posts (or replies) to form nested **threads**.

• View threads in a **feed** that dynamically organizes posts and their relationships.

• Handle operations such as editing, deleting, or navigating through threads.

## **2. Post and Reply Logic**

**Key Principles:**

1\. **Equal Entity Structure**: Both standalone posts and replies are stored in the same database table and treated equally.

2\. **Parent-Child Relationship**: Each post or reply references its parent via a parent_id column.

• A **standalone post** has parent_id = NULL.

• A **reply** has parent_id = \[ID of the parent post\].

3\. **Root Post**: The first post in a thread (with parent_id = NULL) is referred to as the **root**.

4\. **Nested Replies**: Replies can have their own replies, forming a recursive hierarchy.

## **3. Database Design**

**Table: threads_posts**

**Column Name** **Data Type** **Description**

id INT (PK, AUTO_INCREMENT) Unique identifier for each post.

parent_id INT (FK, NULLABLE) ID of the parent post. NULL for standalone posts.

root_id INT (FK) ID of the root post in the thread.

user_id INT ID of the user who created the post.

content TEXT Content of the post.

created_at TIMESTAMP Time when the post was created.

updated_at TIMESTAMP Time when the post was last updated.

status ENUM(‘active’, ‘deleted’) Status of the post for soft deletion.

**Table: threads_feed**

**Column Name** **Data Type** **Description**

id INT (PK, AUTO_INCREMENT) Unique identifier for the feed item.

user_id INT ID of the user subscribed to the feed.

post_id INT (FK) ID of the post in the thread.

created_at TIMESTAMP Time when the feed item was created.

**4. Post Creation Logic**

**API Workflow:**

1\. **Create Standalone Post**:

• parent_id = NULL

• root_id = id of the created post.

2\. **Create Reply**:

• parent_id = ID of the post being replied to.

• root_id = root_id of the parent post.

**SQL Example:**

\-- Create a standalone post

INSERT INTO threads_posts (parent_id, root_id, user_id, content, created_at)

VALUES (NULL, NULL, 1, 'This is a standalone post.', NOW());

\-- Retrieve the newly created post ID

SET @post_id = LAST_INSERT_ID();

\-- Update the root_id to the same ID (self-referencing)

UPDATE threads_posts

SET root_id = @post_id

Issue #209: roar reproduce fails for lineages with a 'roar get' source step (wrong roar in venv + dropped destination)

## Summary

`roar reproduce --run` of a lineage whose source step is `roar get hf://datasets/...` fails at that first step, cascading to the whole pipeline. Two compounding problems.

## Problem 1 — reproduction venv installs the wrong `roar`

In the reproduce venv, `.venv/bin/roar` is a **Python-2** package (PyPI name collision), not `roar-cli`. When reproduce replays the source step as `roar run roar get ...`, the inner `roar get` invokes the broken py2 tool:

```
File ".venv/bin/roar", line 328
    print 'Invalid Port: %s' % options.serve
SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'.
```

→ Step 1 exits 1. Root cause: the reproduction venv resolves `roar` to the wrong distribution; `roar-cli`'s entrypoint isn't what ends up on PATH inside the venv.

## Problem 2 — `roar get` destination dropped from the replayed command

The replayed step is `roar get hf://datasets/yuanty/LIBERO-fastwam --force` — the original destination arg (`./data/libero_tarballs`) is gone. Even with Problem 1 fixed, `roar get` would fetch to a default location while downstream steps read the recorded path, so a path-based handoff fails:

```
tar: ./data/libero_tarballs/*.tar.gz: Cannot open: No such file or directory
```

## Impact

A pipeline that sources data via `roar get` (the recommended way to make data a tracked, reproducible input) cannot be reproduced end-to-end — steps after the get cascade-fail on missing data. This blocks the core reproducibility guarantee for any data-driven pipeline.

## Suggested fixes

1. Install/resolve `roar-cli` (not a colliding `roar`) into the reproduction venv, or drive replayed `roar get` steps via the same roar entrypoint running the reproduction rather than a venv-local `roar`.
2. Preserve `roar get` arguments (including destination) in the replayed command, or restore the fetched artifact to its recorded path before downstream steps run.

## Environment

roar 0.3.6 · `reproduce --run --lineage` · Hugging Face dataset source · Linux/conda

```go
case *Target:
```

```go

    var err error

    switch {
    case group.mode == DepModeParallel && group.collectAll:
        err = runGroupParallelAll(...)
    case group.mode == DepModeParallel:
        err = runGroupParallel(...)
    case group.collectAll:
        err = runGroupSerialAll(...)
    default:
        err = runGroupSerial(...)
    }
    ...
}
```

and every runner is a bare loop. `runGroupSerial` (`target.go:1031-1040`):

```go

    err := dep.Run(ctx)

        return err

}
```

`executeWithParents` (see `walkRoots`, `internal/core/run_env.go:781`, which constructs a fresh

**Memory arenas in Go** are an experimental feature (introduced in Go 1.20, behind `GOEXPERIMENT=arenas`) that lets you allocate many related objects from a contiguous block of memory and free them all at once, largely bypassing the garbage collector for those objects.

### How they work
- You create an arena with `arena.NewArena()`.
- You allocate values or slices from it with `arena.New[T](a)` or `arena.MakeSlice[T](a, len, cap)`.
- When you’re done, you call `a.Free()` (or rely on the arena becoming unreachable). The entire region is released together.

This is a classic **bump-pointer / region allocator**: a large chunk is obtained up front, a pointer is advanced for each allocation, and everything is discarded in one shot. There is little or no per-object bookkeeping and no individual GC tracking while the arena is live.

**Benefits** (when used appropriately):
- Lower GC CPU time and fewer GC cycles.
- Reduced heap memory pressure.
- Better locality (objects live close together).
Google reported up to ~15% CPU/memory savings in some large internal workloads that allocated many short-lived objects.

**Limitations and caveats**:
- Completely unsupported; the Go team has made no compatibility guarantees and has effectively put the public API on indefinite hold because of design concerns (it tends to “infect” APIs).
- An arena must not be used concurrently by multiple goroutines.
- After `Free()`, any remaining pointers into the arena become invalid (use-after-free is a hard error; on 64-bit the memory is typically unmapped so accesses fault).
- Best for bulk allocations on the order of MiB, not tiny one-off objects.
- Strings, interfaces, and some other values may still escape to the regular heap.
- You normally need separate code paths for arena vs non-arena builds.

Third-party pure-Go arena libraries also exist if you want something that doesn’t depend on the experimental flag.

# Auto-wire issue dependencies from a declared `Depends on:` line

Issues routinely declare their ordering in prose, and that declaration goes nowhere. #348's
body opens with *"Depends on #236 / #340 — file/land after that merges"*; #200 says
*"Sequencing: #199 (extract core) → framework map-step → Level B"*; #290 and #269 both carried
*"blocked on PR #N, which is still open"* in audit comments. None of it was machine-readable,
so the ordering lived only in whoever had read the thread.

GitHub now models this natively (`blocked_by` / `blocking`), and the six edges currently on
this repo were wired **by hand**. This issue proposes closing that gap at the source: a
workflow that reads a declared dependency line off an issue body and wires it.

## Scope

**In:** parse a strict, dedicated line from an issue body on `opened` / `edited`; wire missing
`blocked_by` edges; report anything it could not wire.

**Out:** inferring dependencies from free prose (that needs judgment — see Non-goals), removing
edges, cross-repo refs, and detecting *stale* blockers (an audit comment claiming
blocked-on-a-PR that has since merged). That last one is real and recurring — #269 and #290
both sat falsely-blocked for over a week — but it is a scheduled-audit problem, not a
trigger-time one, and belongs in its own issue.

## Trigger and placement

A **new file**, `.github/workflows/issue-dependencies.yml` — not a job in `ci.yml`. Two
reasons: the trigger is `on: issues:`, which `ci.yml` (push to main + pull_request) does not
carry; and `ci.yml`'s top-level `concurrency` group keys on `github.ref` with
`cancel-in-progress: true`, which is wrong for issue events (concurrent edits to different
issues would cancel each other).

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened, edited]
```


**Open risk, and the first thing to settle:** it is not established that `GITHUB_TOKEN` with
`issues: write` is accepted by the *dependencies* endpoints specifically — that API is newer
than the permission model's documentation, and every edge on this repo today was written with
a human PAT, not a workflow token. Establish it before building anything else:

```bash
# In a throwaway workflow on a scratch issue — do not reason about it, run it.
gh api -X POST repos/$REPO/issues/<N>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<ID>
```

If the workflow token is refused, the fallback is a fine-grained PAT in a repo secret with
`issues: write` — which is a materially bigger ask (a credential to rotate, and a token that
can edit any issue) and is worth weighing against the value before proceeding.

## Grammar — strict by design

The failure mode that matters is a **false positive**: silently wiring an edge nobody declared,
which is worse than wiring nothing, because a wrong `blocked_by` makes real work look blocked.
So the parser matches a dedicated anchored line, never prose.

```
Depends on: #236, #340
```

- Anchored `^Depends on:` at the start of a line, case-insensitive, one line.
- Comma-separated `#N` refs, same-repo only.
- Everything else is ignored — including `#306's first review finding`, `see #343`, and
  #348's own current bolded prose form, which would need rewriting to the strict form.

Deliberately **not** parsed: `blocked by`, `after X lands`, `follow-up to`, `split out of`.
Those appear all over the repo in senses that are *not* ordering — the full dependency pass
over 71 issues found `follow-up to` used for both real prerequisites and mere provenance.
Guessing between them is exactly the judgment this workflow should not attempt.

An optional second directive, `Blocks: #N`, is easy to add and lets an issue declare the
reciprocal side. Worth deciding whether to support it or keep one direction

Issue #32: bug: gc per-invocation startup (~9.5s) makes `gc event emit` unusable under subprocess budgets — brief.decided lost six-for-six

### Summary

A bare `gc` invocation spends ~9.5s in city-scoped startup before executing its subcommand (measured: `gc hook --help` 9,584ms — startup, not query). Any caller shelling `gc event emit` under a normal subprocess budget loses to that floor: mctl's typed adjudication path fires `gc event emit brief.decided` with a 10s timeout, and it timed out six-for-six on 2026-08-23 (23:41–23:43) — the event has plausibly never been successfully emitted from that path.

### Symptom

Six consecutive `briefs_adjudicate` applies each produced:
`MEVT_EMIT_FAILED — "gc event emit could not run: Command '['gc', 'event', 'emit', 'brief.decided', ...]' timed out after 10 seconds"`.
Systematic, not incidental. Consequence: every consumer triggered by the `brief.decided` event (rather than a file condition) silently never fires.

### Root cause

gc performs city-scoped work (city walk/config resolution) on EVERY invocation before it knows its subcommand — the same cost class previously measured at the claim window (hook startup 9,584ms vs an 11ms query). For an event-emit primitive whose useful work is milliseconds, the startup floor IS the cost. Downstream, callers size budgets (10s) without reference to that floor, but the defect to fix here is the floor itself: an emit primitive needs to be cheap or have a cheap path.

### Fix candidates

1. Fast path for `gc event emit` (and similar leaf commands): skip the full city walk; resolve only what an append to the event log needs.
2. General startup-cost reduction: lazy city resolution keyed on subcommand.
3. A long-lived emit daemon/socket so producers append without paying process startup — larger design.

### Environment / versions

macOS; gascity deployed binary (city ~/gt, 17 rigs). Downstream caller: mctl briefs adjudication (tdupu/mathcity — where this was originally filed as #216 before being re-homed here at the owner's direction; the 10s caller-side budget note lives there).

### Suggested priority

p1 — event-triggered automation downstream of adjudication is silently dead wherever emit runs under a bounded subprocess budget.

Issue #91: [Bug] Docker CLI can deadlock before start when wait acknowledgement is deferred

## Observed behavior

A Docker CLI `run --rm` uses the sequence:

1. attach
2. `POST /containers/{id}/wait?condition=removed`
3. wait for the HTTP response headers
4. `POST /containers/{id}/start`

The Engine implementation previously withheld the wait response until the
container reached the requested terminal state. Docker therefore waited for the
response before sending start, creating a liveness deadlock.

  successfully. Its trace proves `/wait?condition=removed` -> HTTP 200 ->
  `/start`; the Alpine workload printed its marker and exited 0.
- The candidate's debug-build performance warning was non-blocking. No hang
  occurred.

The fix is locally verified but not yet publishable through the ordinary
dependency graph. The normal Container pin still resolves Engine API 0.3.5,

Issue #521: feat: hub.rs native ACP cache invalidation — minimal-bandwidth event subscription

## Part of #516 — SourceHub ACP Performance & Proof-Validated Caching (Phase 3)

## Context

This is the hub.rs counterpart to #520 (Cosmos WebSocket invalidation). Because we control both ends — defra.rs and hub.rs — we can build a purpose-built invalidation channel that is:

- **Minimal bandwidth**: Only events relevant to this node's policies are transmitted
- **Proof-validated**: Events include cryptographic proofs against hub.rs module state
- **Exactly-once delivery**: Persistent log with consumer offsets (Kafka-like semantics)

## Approach

### Event Channel

hub.rs exposes a subscription API (see hub.rs #64, #67) where consumers register interest in specific policy IDs. The hub only sends events matching the subscription filter — no client-side filtering needed.

### Proof Validation

Each event includes a state proof against the hub.rs module store (see hub.rs #61). The defra.rs light client verifies the proof locally before applying the cache invalidation. This means a compromised or malicious event stream cannot trick the node into incorrect invalidation (or worse, into caching false "access granted" responses).

### Consumer Offsets

The subscription tracks offsets locally — on reconnect, the consumer resumes from its last confirmed offset. No events are missed, and no duplicate processing occurs. This is the "persistent log like Kafka" behavior Bruno described as a requirement.

### Integration with defra.rs

```
hub.rs validator
  → Filters ACP events by node's registered policy IDs
  → Sends proof-validated event stream
  → defra.rs light client:
      → Verify proof against known hub.rs state root
      → If valid: invalidate affected cache entries
      → If invalid: log warning, do NOT invalidate (fail-closed)
      → Update local consumer offset
```

### What This Enables

- **Surgical invalidation**: Only the specific `(identity, policy, resource, object, permission)` tuples affected by on-chain mutations are invalidated
- **Header-based cache age**: The light client knows how fresh its state is (the latest verified header). Combined with the Revocation SLA (#522), this provides a provable freshness guarantee.

## hub.rs Dependencies

- hub.rs #64 — WebSocket delivery mechanism
- hub.rs #67 — Delivery mechanism decision
- hub.rs #61 — Module state proof specifications
- ACP module emitting typed events on relationship mutations

## Depends on

- #517 (access cache)
- #514 (HubRsProvider — the transport this builds on)

## Related

- #520 (Cosmos path — same cache, different channel)
- #522 (revocation SLA)

However, that's not to say some finite amount of recursion isn't *useful*.  It's possible to come up with situations where a query should use some `type A` which contains `SomeField A[]`.  The recursion might be limited at some depth -- possibly 1, possibly 2; any finite number -- even 1 is significant.

```

  messages {
    ...CommentsRecursive
  }
}

fragment CommentsRecursive on Message {
  comments {
    ...CommentFields
    comments {
      ...CommentFields
      comments {
        ...CommentFields
      }
    }
  }
}

fragment CommentFields on Comment {
  id
  content
}
```

## Parent issue

This issue is part of:

> Support safe multi-module application from the Seed4J CLI

## Dependencies

This issue should be implemented only after completing:

- Add a read-only plan for applying multiple modules
- Define transaction, commit, and partial-failure semantics for multi-module application

## Goal

Execute a requested set of modules only after the complete set passes preflight validation.

Execution must reuse the same resolved plan shown by `--plan`, preserve deterministic ordering, and follow the previously defined commit and partial-failure contract.

## Proposed command

```bash
seed4j apply-set init maven-java prettier \
  --project-path .
```

Properties should use the same CLI options accepted by plan mode:

```bash
seed4j apply-set init maven-java \
  --project-path . \
  --project-name "Sample application" \
  --base-name sampleApplication \
  --node-package-manager npm \
  --package-name com.mycompany.sample
```

## Required behavior

Before applying the first module, the command must:

1. resolve all requested module slugs;
2. resolve the deterministic execution order;
3. validate module dependencies;
4. validate feature dependencies;
5. resolve the complete property set;
6. reject missing required properties;
7. reject any other predictable invalid state;
8. build an immutable or otherwise stable execution plan.

The command must then execute the modules from that validated plan.

It must not independently resolve a different order, property set, or dependency result after preflight validation.

## Dependency behavior

A dependency may be satisfied by:

- project history; or
- an explicitly selected module that appears earlier in the resolved execution order.

A feature dependency must continue to require an explicit provider.

The command must not silently add missing modules or automatically select a feature provider.

The output should make progress visible for each module.

```text
Applying module set:

[1/3] init
      Applied successfully

[2/3] maven-java
      Applied successfully

[3/3] prettier
      Applied successfully

Module set applied successfully.
```

When execution fails, the output must distinguish:

- modules successfully applied;
- the module that failed;
- modules skipped because of the failure.

The exact behavior for changes, commits, history, and events must follow the decision made in the transaction and partial-failure issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Execution is blocked when preflight validation fails.
- [ ] A preflight failure does not modify the project.
- [ ] A preflight failure returns a non-zero exit code.
- [ ] Execution uses the same resolved module order as plan mode.
- [ ] Execution uses the same resolved properties as plan mode.
- [ ] Modules are applied sequentially in deterministic order.
- [ ] A dependency can be satisfied by another selected module.
- [ ] Feature providers are never selected automatically.
- [ ] Progress is displayed for each module.
- [ ] Full success is clearly reported.
- [ ] Partial failure is clearly reported.
- [ ] Succeeded, failed, and skipped modules can be distinguished.
- [ ] Commit behavior follows the previously documented decision.
- [ ] Project-history behavior follows the previously documented decision.
- [ ] Event-dispatch behavior follows the previously documented decision.
- [ ] Exit codes follow the previously documented decision.
- [ ] Existing single-module `apply` behavior remains unchanged.

Issue #59: Cluster nodes depend on Pi-hole for DNS — circular dependency blocks power-failure recovery

All four k3s nodes resolve DNS via `192.168.1.250`, the Pi-hole LoadBalancer. **Pi-hole runs on the cluster that depends on it.** Any event that stops Pi-hole also removes the cluster's ability to pull the image needed to restart Pi-hole.

Demonstrated by the 2026-08-04 power failure: the entire house had no DNS for hours and the cluster could not self-recover. Required manual SSH intervention on every node.

## The deadlock

1. Pi-hole's **only** upstream is its own `cloudflared` sidecar (`FTLCONF_dns_upstreams=127.0.0.1#5053`, DoH). No fallback.
2. That sidecar is `crazymax/cloudflared:latest` with **`imagePullPolicy: Always`** — which forces kubelet to contact Docker Hub on *every* container start, even when a valid image is cached locally.
3. Reaching Docker Hub requires DNS. DNS requires Pi-hole. Pi-hole requires cloudflared. **Nothing recovers on its own.**

Symptom is misleading — the network is fine, nodes ping, k3s is `Ready`, but nearly every pod is `ImagePullBackOff` with `dial tcp: lookup registry-1.docker.io: Try again`.

## Compounding factor

Raspberry Pis have no battery-backed RTC. Three of four nodes came back with clocks up to **2m39s** off. NTP could not correct it (needs DNS), which skewed the Ceph mons:

```
health: HEALTH_WARN
        clock skew detected on mon.d, mon.e
        143 slow ops, oldest one blocked for 414 sec
```

That stalled PVC mounts, so Pi-hole could not start even once its image was available.

## Current state

Mitigated by hand: `nameserver 1.1.1.1` prepended to `/etc/resolv.conf` on all four nodes. **This is not persistent** — NetworkManager owns that file on these nodes (`systemd-resolved` and `dhcpcd` are both inactive) and rewrites it on reboot. **The next power failure will deadlock identically.**

## Options

These interact with the UDM DNS lockdown (port-53 DNAT to Pi-hole) — whichever is chosen likely needs a firewall exception for the four node IPs, or the fallback resolver is transparently redirected back to Pi-hole and provides no protection.

| # | Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NM static DNS: Pi-hole primary + public fallback — `nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" ipv4.ignore-auto-dns yes ipv4.dns "192.168.1.250 1.1.1.1"` | Persists reboots; keeps Pi-hole filtering primary; ~10 min | Needs DNAT exception; ~5s stall per lookup during failover |
| 2 | Point nodes at the router (`192.168.1.1`) | Router already has upstreams; no per-node drift | Node queries bypass Pi-hole filtering |
| 3 | Per-host DHCP option on the UDM for the 4 nodes | Centrally managed | UDM per-host DNS options are limited; still needs DNAT exception |
| 4 | Node-local caching resolver (dnsmasq/systemd-resolved), Pi-hole primary + public fallback | Fast failover, caches, graceful during Pi-hole restarts | Most moving parts |
| 5 | Pin cloudflared + `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` | Removes the common trigger; small in-git change | **Insufficient alone** — see below |

**Recommended: 1 + 5.** Option 5 removes the usual trigger; option 1 removes the failure class.

Option 5 alone is provably not enough: during this incident I set `IfNotPresent`, but ArgoCD reverted it once DNS returned, and separately the pod rescheduled onto `obiwan` which had **no cached image** — taking house DNS down a second time. Only `yoda` and `anakin` had the image; `obiwan` and `rey` never did.

## Tasks

- [ ] Pin `crazymax/cloudflared` to a release tag and set `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` (same class as #43)
- [ ] Decide and implement a node DNS option above
- [ ] Add the matching UDM firewall exception for the four node IPs if a non-Pi-hole resolver is used
- [ ] Consider an NTP fallback by IP so clock sync does not depend on DNS
- [ ] **Acceptance test:** pull node power, restore it, confirm the cluster returns to service with zero SSH intervention
