Issue #353: HIER: external validation — real ontologies at scale, PLL baseline, Neo4j/TigerGraph and TimescaleDB comparisons

## Summary
The HIER benchmark added in #344 runs on a **generated** dataset so it is reproducible from a clean checkout with no download and no licence gate. That covers the *shapes* — tree and multi-parent DAG, subtree sizes spanning four orders of magnitude — but it does not establish the constants on real data, and it has no cross-engine baseline at all. `benchmarks/hier/README.md` lists these under "Not yet covered"; this issue is that list, made actionable.

## 1. Real ontologies at scale
`examples/ontology_loader.rs` already reads the published formats — OBO, NCBI `nodes.dmp`, GeoNames `hierarchy.txt`, prefix-coded (ATC, MITRE ATT&CK), generic edge lists, generated calendar — and reports the probe verdict, encoding, space and build time. What is missing is running it on the full files and recording the numbers.

Targets, and what each is expected to show:

| Source | Size | Expected verdict |
|---|---|---|
| NCBI Taxonomy | ~1.3M nodes | tree → nested-set; the scale case for build time and 12 B/node |
| GeoNames hierarchy | ~330k | tree → nested-set |
| ATC | ~6.5k | strict 5-level tree; the clean prefix case |
| MONDO / HPO | ~25k / ~19k | mostly tree, some multi-parent |
| **Gene Ontology** | ~50k | **declines** — width approaches leaf count |
| MITRE ATT&CK + CWE | ~1k / ~1.4k | tree via prefix / edge list |

The Gene Ontology row is the one to publish loudest. A high-width DAG is where a 2-hop index is the right structure and OEH refuses to build, and reporting that on the real file is more credible than any speedup. Verified on a GO-shaped synthetic (width 500 > cap 179); the real file has not been run.

Licence note: everything above is open. UMLS/SNOMED stay behind `--i-have-a-licence` and no ontology data gets committed.

## 2. PLL / 2-hop baseline
The paper's claim is ~half the space and 6–7× faster build than 2-hop labelling *at query parity* on trees. Samyama has no PLL implementation, so this is **not reproduced** — `benchmarks/hier/README.md` says so. The reference repo `relationship-hierarchy-index` has a validated PLL in Python; porting it as a benchmark-only baseline (not engine code) would let us make or retract the claim on our own data.

This also matters for the decline path: above the width cap we tell users to go to a 2-hop index, and we should be able to show what that costs.

## 3. Cross-engine: Neo4j / TigerGraph
The corpus is Cypher and the dataset is generated, so porting the loader plus the H1–H8/H10 queries is mechanical. Home is `samyama-graph-competitor-benchmarks`. Worth doing precisely because the interesting classes are the ones where we are *not* obviously ahead (H1, H4, H6) — an external number tells us whether those are a Samyama planner problem or inherent to the shape.

## 4. TimescaleDB continuous aggregates for H10
The paper's head-to-head: the reference implementation matches TimescaleDB continuous aggregates to the unit (day 704,800; month 21,168,000) while also answering subsumption, which a continuous aggregate cannot. HIER class H10 is the same workload but has only been compared against Samyama's own expansion. Reproducing the TimescaleDB comparison in-engine would let us state the roll-up claim against the incumbent rather than against ourselves.

## Definition of done
`benchmarks/hier/README.md` "Not yet covered" shrinks, with committed CSVs for whatever was run and an explicit note for anything that stays unrun and why.

Issue #1059: Decide whether a composition body may declare its own source: it compiles and binds but cannot run

## Summary

A composition body may declare its own `type: source` node. The planner accepts it, binds it, and uses its schema to seed the body — but the executor has no path to ingest one, so a run that reaches it fails with an internal error. The limitation is already recorded in the test corpus; what is not decided is whether the surface should be wired or refused.

## What works and what does not

**Compile-time paths work.** `clinker run --lineage` is a static, plan-derived export that never enters the executor, and it handles a body-declared source end to end. The channel `sources:` patch mechanism addresses one with a `<composition>.<source>` key, and those tests pass.

**The run path cannot reach it.** The ingest pass iterates the top-level node list only and resolves each name against the top-level DAG, hard-erroring otherwise. Body entry additionally swaps the source-record map to an empty one on the grounds that "bodies declare ports, not top-level sources", and a body source that is neither port-seeded nor present in that map becomes an internal error.

Body *port* sources — the placeholders a call site feeds — are unaffected and work normally. This is only about a body that declares a source of its own.

The limitation is stated in the repo already: the channel-patch tests drive the compile-only `--explain` path with the comment that a body-declared source "binds (its schema seeds the body) but does not run today".

## Why it needs a decision rather than a fix

A recent review proposed that lineage should stop enumerating these nodes as input datasets, on the grounds that it declares an input the run can never read. That is the wrong end of the problem, for three reasons:

1. The lineage walk still resolves the node, so removing only the enumeration reintroduces a mid-walk failure against a key the author cannot bind.
2. Making the walk skip them instead deletes their column edges — the body source's contribution to downstream columns disappears — which is capability deletion with no replacement, and it also removes behaviour the local-diagnostic path has had since composition tracing landed.
3. Declaring the column edges while withholding the input dataset is the one clearly wrong option: a conformant consumer resolves a column-lineage input field only against the event's declared inputs, so the edges would be silently unreadable.

So lineage is reporting the pipeline accurately. The question is what the pipeline should be allowed to say.

## The decision

Either:

**(a) Wire it.** Give a body-declared source a real ingest path, so the shape the planner accepts is the shape the executor runs. This is the larger change and touches source discovery, the body-entry record map, and the ingest resolution pass.

**(b) Refuse it.** Reject a body-declared `type: source` at compile time with a diagnostic naming the composition, the body node, and the corrected form — presumably declaring the source at the call site and passing it through a port. This is small, honest, and immediately stops a pipeline that compiles from failing at run time.

Option (b) removes a surface that partially works today: `--lineage` on such a pipeline succeeds, and the channel `sources:` patch addresses it. Choosing (b) means accepting that those stop working, which is a deliberate call rather than an oversight — hence this issue rather than a patch.

There is no third option where the current state is correct: a configuration that compiles, binds, and produces lineage but cannot run is exactly the shape that costs an operator a production run to discover.

## Suggested acceptance criteria

- A pipeline with a body-declared source either runs, or is refused at plan time with a diagnostic naming the offending node and a corrected form the author can paste.
- If refused: the compile-only paths that accept it today are updated in the same change, and the tests that currently drive `--explain` because it "does not run today" are updated or removed wit

### Why `alien_signals`?

`alien_signals` (created by Johnson Chu, who also wrote Vue's reactivity system) implements a **push-pull hybrid algorithm** that combines the best of both worlds:
- **Push phase:** Dirty-marking propagates through the dependency graph immediately on write
- **Pull phase:** Values are recomputed lazily only when read

This is fundamentally different from Preact Signals' pure pull-based model, where updates only propagate on read.

The JavaScript ecosystem has already run this experiment, and the results are instructive.

Vue 3.4 shipped with a highly optimized reactivity system using a push-pull approach. Johnson Chu (the author) spent considerable time optimizing it, and it was considered state-of-the-art.

Vue 3.5 **switched to a pull-based algorithm similar to Preact Signals**. The idea was to simplify the system and reduce overhead. However, this change introduced **measurable performance degradation** in real-world scenarios. 

### Vue 3.6 — The Course Correction
Recognizing the regression, the Vue team **merged `alien_signals` into Vue 3.6** (PR: [vuejs/core#12349](https://github.com/vuejs/core/pull/12349)). Evan You explicitly tweeted: *"Just merged this into the branch for Vue 3.6. alien-signals 1.0 released! and signal performance looked impressive"* 

The benchmark results speak for themselves:
- **3–5× faster** than existing solutions 
- **~40% less memory allocation** overhead
- **Smaller bundle size** with zero dependencies

Issue #554: [ENHANCEMENT] RobotCode Language Server Performance Improvements

## Problem Statement

For large Robot Framework projects, the Language Server experiences noticeable delays that impact developer productivity:

### Startup Performance

**Library Loading**: Each library import spawns a separate Python subprocess for introspection. This process creation overhead compounds quickly when a workspace uses many libraries.

**Namespace Initialization**: While libraries and resources are cached to disk, namespaces (which contain resolved imports, keyword references, and variable definitions) must be rebuilt from scratch every time VS Code restarts. This is the primary bottleneck for large workspaces - users must wait for the entire workspace to be re-analyzed on every session start.

### Incremental Edit Performance

**Linear Lookups**: When a library or resource file changes, the language server iterates through ALL open documents to find which ones are affected. In large workspaces, this O(n) behavior creates noticeable delays during editing.

**Over-Invalidation**: Any import-related change currently invalidates ALL namespaces, even those that don't depend on the changed file. This causes unnecessary re-analysis work.

The goal is to make the Language Server feel instant for common operations, regardless of workspace size.


## Proposed Optimizations
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "Current Flow"
        A[VS Code Starts] --> B[Load Libraries]
        B -->|Per-lib process spawn| C[Init Namespaces]
        C -->|Rebuilt every restart| D[Ready]
    end

    subgraph "Optimized Flow"
        E[VS Code Starts] --> F[Load Libraries]
        F -->|Shared executor + parallel| G[Load Cached Namespaces]
        G -->|Disk cache hit| H[Ready]
        G -->|Cache miss| I[Init & Cache]
        I --> H
    end

    style C fill:#f99
    style G fill:#9f9
```

### Library Loading Optimization

- Reuse ProcessPoolExecutor instead of spawning new process per library
- Parallel loading with configurable workers (default: 4)
- Resource disk cache extending existing library cache

### O(1) Dependency Lookups

Replace O(n) document iterations with reverse dependency graphs:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Before: O(n)"
        A1[File Changed] --> B1[Iterate ALL docs]
        B1 --> C1[Check each import]
        C1 --> D1[Refresh affected]

Issue #3469: Call graph: name the space of relationship arcs (call-site modality vs propagated facts)

## Idea

The call graph today annotates a call site with `loop` (via `--loop` on Performance Triage). That is one instance of a much larger design space of **relationship arcs**, and it is worth naming the space before adding the second one ad hoc.

Two kinds of arc annotation look alike and are not:

### 1. Call-site modality — local, exact, cheap

A property of the edge itself, readable from the IL body with no fixpoint. `loop` is this.

- **in a loop** — invocation count unbounded (what makes `loop` interesting in the first place)
- **conditional / guarded vs unconditional** — "always runs" is a much stronger arc than "might run"
- **in `try` / `catch` / `finally`** — cost and failure semantics differ
- **back edge / recursion** — distinct from the existing `↩` marker, which means "already appeared earlier in this lowering", not "recursive"
- **dispatch certainty** — direct vs `callvirt` vs interface vs delegate vs reflection. The last two are edges that *cannot* be fully resolved; saying so is more honest than omitting them
- **call-site multiplicity** — one call site vs N

### 2. Propagated facts — global, fixpoint, approximate

A lattice flowed over the graph. Direction is the whole design decision.

| Direction | Reads as | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| callee → caller | "I inherit this from what I call" | throws, allocates, unsafe/pointers, blocking, async, `RequiresUnreferencedCode` / `RequiresDynamicCode`, touches IO, non-deterministic |
| caller → callee | "I inherit this from who calls me" | reachable from public API, reachable from `Main`, on a hot path, test-only, reachable from untrusted input (taint) |

Several of the callee → caller facts already exist in this repo as **node** facts — unsafe evidence, allocation facts, `MethodSignalAnalysis` copies/reflection signals. Turning a node fact into a propagated arc fact is the natural next step, and it runs over the same reverse graph the caller lens already builds.

## Two hazards, both already observed in this track

**Saturation.** "May throw" propagated over a framework-sized scope reaches essentially everything and carries no information. This is the same shape as the reverse-reference closure saturating on corelib (#3409, and again while wiring #3419: seeding the closure with a `netstandard`-derived alias selected all 182 shared-framework assemblies). A propagated fact is only useful if it is *rare*, or if the propagation is bounded by an explicit scope.

**May vs must.** With virtual dispatch, callee → caller propagation is an over-approximation. The lattice has to state which semantics it has. Per `AGENTS.md`, an arc that asserts "propagates unsafe" without naming its gate and its approximation direction is an unverified claim wearing the clothes of a verified one.

## Suggested first candidate

Trim/AOT safety (`RequiresUnreferencedCode` / `RequiresDynamicCode`) propagated callee → caller looks like the highest-value starting point:

- it is **rare**, so it does not saturate
- it is **attribute-declared** in the framework, so there is ground truth to validate the propagation against — a real gate, not a plausible-looking result
- "why is my app not AOT-safe, and which call chain causes it" is a question users actually ask, and a caller graph answers it well

## Status

Idea only — not scheduled, no design agreed. Filed to capture the framing while it is fresh. Part of the call-graph track (#3333).

Issue #212: 【Task.34】Deterministic Trajectory Replay - RFC

## 1. Background & Motivation

Intermittent production issues in reward, advantage, and loss are hard to reproduce with a full cluster. Relax's existing offline path (`--debug-train-only` + `--load-debug-rollout-data`, `relax/utils/arguments.py:2484`) only removes the SGLang side — the training cluster (Ray + Megatron) must still be fully launched. The two existing debug dumps (`relax/utils/training/train_dump_utils.py`) are raw `torch.save` pickle with no schema version; they can only be aligned at step granularity and lack a sample-level join key; loss scalars are never persisted at all; and they dump every step in full with no gating, so disk usage grows unboundedly with training (see §8 for item-by-item evidence).

A survey of slime, verl, OpenRLHF, AReaL, and NeMo-RL concludes: none of them implements a "zero-cluster portable replay bundle". Their four shared gaps: reward inputs are not stored for replay, single-sample replay is not supported, there is no schema versioning, and there is no regression test asserting replay == original run. These gaps are exactly this design's differentiation space.

## 2. Goals and Non-Goals

### Goals

1. During training, capture trajectories, reward inputs, reference tensors, and a config snapshot into a self-contained **Replay Bundle**; for **built-in computation paths**, copying the bundle is sufficient to replay offline on any machine; custom-code paths additionally require a code checkout with matching hashes on the target machine (§4.5).
2. Replay reward / advantage / policy-loss computation with **zero cluster, zero GPU dependency (CPU-capable), no Ray, no Megatron initialization, no model weights**.
3. Support selection of a single sample, a single prompt group, the whole batch, and a specific step; `--sample` aligns exactly with the original run under frozen-statistics substitution; `--group`/`--all` align per the tiered standard of §7 (recomputed parts under tight tolerance).
4. Tiered consistency acceptance + golden CI regression tests.
5. Field-level, actionable errors on schema incompatibility.

### Non-Goals (v1)

- **No model forward pass**: loss replay is tensor-level; single-machine real-forward replay is deferred to the L3 extension.
- **No replay of rollout generation**: GenRM/policy generation itself is not replayed — only its downstream computation.
- **No critic value-loss replay**: `value_loss_function` depends on the current critic forward output, which the v1 capture chain does not include; PPO **advantage** replay is supported by capturing the `values` input (§4.7).
- **Never execute custom code carried inside a bundle**: custom reward / TIS functions run only from the current checkout after hash verification (§4.5) — a security boundary.
- **No anomaly-triggered capture** (auto-promoting bundles on loss spikes) — see §11 Future Work.
- **The full SessionForest is not bundled**; agentic samples store only the flattened Sample + turn trace.
- **No eval-batch replay**; determinization of the `random` reward is out of scope (marked as non-deterministic in reports).

Issue #28: Sensitive values: three implementations, two uncovered paths, and a recomputed config-key link

Found while tracing the pipeline for `docs/pipeline-schema-and-state.md`.

Sensitive Terraform values are handled by three separate mechanisms, and two paths through the tool are not covered by any of them. This matters because the digest→stack-config link is how a real secret reaches Pulumi at all: the digest stores `(sensitive)` and records the config key holding the real value, and #22 resolves it from there when writing state.

## Three implementations

1. `redactSensitivePaths` (`pkg/module_map.go`) — replaces sensitive values in digest attributes with the literal string `(sensitive)`.
2. `BuildSensitivityMap` — schema-driven, **handles nesting**, and is currently unused.
3. The `tofu show -json` path (`pkg/generate_module_map.go:302`) — never reads `tfjson.SensitiveValues` at all.

## Two blind spots

- **Nested sensitive values are not redacted.** `redactSensitivePaths` handles top-level paths only. `BuildSensitivityMap`, which does handle nesting, already exists and is not wired up.
- **On the `tofu show -json` path nothing is redacted and no secret reaches stack config**, because sensitivity information is dropped before the digest is built. A migration that goes through that path silently has no secrets in config, and `#22`'s injection will fail to resolve them (correctly, but the cause will be opaque).

## A third, quieter problem

The digest↔config link is `flattenAddress`, recomputed independently at three sites, and only one of them applies the `_2`/`_3` dedup suffix for colliding keys. Where two attributes flatten to the same key, the mapping is not just wrong but unresolvable after the fact — the information needed to tell them apart is gone by the time anything downstream looks.

## Suggested shape

Compute the sensitivity map and the config key once, store both in the digest, and have every consumer read them rather than recompute. That removes the three-way divergence and makes the dedup suffix authoritative instead of site-dependent.

## Relationship to other work

#22 consumes this link when resolving `redactedAttributes` at injection time; its spec's Findings note that a sensitive **non-string** attribute makes the digest's `ctyjson.Unmarshal` fail, so the resource silently gets no injection state. Full trace in `docs/pipeline-schema-and-state.md`.

Issue #5: `next_key` eagerly downloads the entire enclosing storage map → runtime calls that iterate large maps hang

Hey Victor, 
I found a bug while testing forklift with bittensor. The bug is not bittensor specific so i think it's worth fixing.
Below is the full report about it, AI generated.

## Summary

When a runtime call iterates a storage map, forklift's `next_key` implementation fetches the **entire** enclosing map from the source in a single blocking `archive_storage` call, caches it, and marks the subtree exhaustive. On chains with very large maps (e.g. Bittensor / subtensor), the first `next_key` of the iteration triggers a network-wide map download that never completes in practice — the call hangs with no progress and no log output, and can exhaust memory.

Point queries (single-key `getStorage`) and non-iterating runtime calls work perfectly. Only calls that walk a map are affected.

## Environment

- `@polkadot-api/forklift` **0.4.0**
- `polkadot-api` 2.1.7
- Node.js v24
- Source chain: Bittensor mainnet (`wss://entrypoint-finney.opentensor.ai:443`), subtensor `spec_version` 424

## What works vs. what hangs

Forking Bittensor and querying it works for everything except map iteration:

| Operation | Result |
|---|---|
| Boot fork, follow blocks, serve `ws://localhost:3000` | ✅ |
| `System.Account(addr)` and other single-key storage reads | ✅ |
| Non-iterating runtime APIs (`Core.version`, `Metadata.metadata_versions`) | ✅ |
| Point runtime call `StakeInfoRuntimeApi.get_stake_info_for_hotkey_coldkey_netuid(hotkey, coldkey, netuid)` | ✅ |
| **Map-iterating runtime call** `StakeInfoRuntimeApi.get_stake_info_for_coldkey(coldkey)` | ❌ hangs indefinitely |

The workaround that confirms the data is reachable: replacing the single `get_stake_info_for_coldkey` call with N point calls (`get_stake_info_for_hotkey_coldkey_netuid` over each hotkey × subnet) returns correct results with zero errors. Issue #186: WPO: cross-function constant propagation over the call graph

## Motivation

Many Lisp programs contain "config-style" functions — small pure helpers that are
called throughout the codebase with the same literal arguments every time (flag
values, mode selectors, fixed numeric parameters). Today the optimizer sees each
call site in isolation and cannot eliminate the dead branches or constant
sub-expressions that would become obvious if it knew the actual argument values.
Cross-function constant propagation (CFCP) closes this gap: by walking the call
graph and tracking what values flow into each parameter, the optimizer can
specialize or inline-fold parameters whose values are always compile-time
constants, shrinking the residual code and enabling downstream passes (dead-code
elimination, constant folding) to fire on the specialized body. The payoff is
largest for config-style functions called with fixed flags.

## Technical Approach

The pass lives entirely in the Lisp optimizer layer (`lib/11-optimizer-vau.lisp`)
and is expressed as a transform over the IR produced by earlier passes, keeping
the Rust kernel unchanged.

**Inputs required:**

- `$CALL-GRAPH` — the caller→callee edge map produced by the existing call-graph
  pass. Each entry records the callee symbol and the argument expressions supplied
  at the call site.
- `PURE` plist annotation on function symbols — a purity certificate already
  planned/used by other optimizer passes. Only callees marked `PURE` (no
  observable side effects, no dependence on mutable globals) are eligible for
  specialization. Indirect calls, `APPLY` of an unknown, and all operatives
  (fexprs/macros) are treated conservatively and left unchanged.

**Algorithm (per callee):**

1. Collect all call sites in `$CALL-GRAPH` for the target symbol.
2. For each formal parameter, check whether every call site supplies the same
   literal constant (number, string, keyword, `NIL`, `T`). If so, the parameter
   is a *candidate constant*.
3. Rewrite the callee body substituting candidate constants for their formals,
   then run constant-folding and dead-branch elimination on the specialized body.
4. Replace the original call sites with calls to the specialized copy (or inline
   directly if the body is small enough after folding).

## Files Likely to Change

- `lib/11-optimizer-vau.lisp` — new CFCP pass and integration into the optimizer
  pipeline
- `lib/20-condensation.lisp` — may expose helpers for reading the call graph or
  purity annotations if not already public
- `tests/` — new integration test exercising a config-style function with fixed
  literal arguments, asserting the specialized form appears in the optimized output

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A pure function called with the same literal argument at every call site has
      that parameter folded away in the optimized IR.
- [ ] Impure functions, indirect calls, and operatives are left unmodified (no
      unsound specialization).
- [ ] All existing tests continue to pass (`cargo test`).
- [ ] The pass is guarded behind the same optimizer enable flag as other WPO
      passes; disabling the optimizer disables CFCP.
- [ ] Clippy and `cargo fmt --all` produce no new warnings.

Issue #81: Hoodini taxonomy mapping assumes superkingdom and mislabels valid NCBI taxonomy as unclassified

## Summary
Hoodini currently assumes that the top cellular taxonomic rank is superkingdom.  
That assumption is now outdated with recent NCBI Taxonomy changes, where the top cellular rank is represented as domain.  
ETE3 is correctly reflecting current NCBI taxonomy.  
Because Hoodini does not normalize or accept domain, records with valid taxid can be labeled unclassified.

## Concrete case: taxid 2
For taxid 2 (Bacteria), ETE3 returns a lineage including:

- root
- cellular root
- domain = Bacteria
- kingdom/phylum/class/order/family/genus/species as applicable

If internal logic only expects superkingdom, then domain is not mapped into the legacy top-rank slot.  
This causes valid records to appear as unclassified despite valid taxid and lineage.

## Diagnosis
- This is not an ETE3 bug.
- This is not an NCBI bug.
- This is a Hoodini rank-mapping mismatch against updated NCBI taxonomy semantics.

## Observed impact
- False unclassified labels for valid taxids.
- Distorted taxonomy summaries in reports and visualizations.
- Incorrect biological interpretation in downstream analysis.
- Regression risk for newer datasets aligned with current NCBI taxonomy.

## Expected behavior
Hoodini should correctly classify records when lineage uses domain, without defaulting to unclassified for valid taxids.

## Current behavior
Records with valid lineage can be labeled unclassified when top-rank is domain and the mapper only handles superkingdom.

## Recommended direction
- Align with NCBI Taxonomy as source of truth.
- Deprecate superkingdom as the canonical internal concept.
- Keep backward compatibility in outputs during transition.

## Transition plan
1. Short term (immediate fix):
   - Accept both domain and superkingdom.
   - Mapping priority: superkingdom if present, otherwise domain.
   - Never emit unclassified when a valid top-rank equivalent exists.

2. Mid term:
   - Make domain the canonical internal top-rank field.
   - Keep legacy output behavior for backward compatibility.

3. Long term:
   - Remove semantic dependency on superkingdom in pipeline and visualization logic.
   - Update docs and tests to match modern NCBI rank conventions.

## Suggested implementation
- Normalize ranks before taxonomy metadata assembly.
- Handle newer root labels where relevant:
  - cellular root
  - acellular root
- Avoid dropping lineage information by forcing legacy-only labels.

## Acceptance criteria
- Zero false unclassified records when taxid and lineage are valid.
- Backward-compatible outputs for existing downstream consumers.
- Tests cover both domain-based and superkingdom-based lineages.
- Taxonomy summaries remain biologically consistent with current NCBI data.

## Official references
- NCBI Insights: New ranks in NCBI Taxonomy  
  https://ncbiinsights.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2025/02/27/new-ranks-ncbi-taxonomy/

- NCBI Datasets docs: Taxonomy updates  
  https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/docs/v2/data-processing/taxonomy-processing/taxonomy-updates/

Issue #9088: make `*ast.Compiler` context-aware

## What is the underlying problem you're trying to solve?

Our use case for OPA involves accepting user-defined code through a REST API at runtime before evaluating it, which means we end up invoking the compiler on arbitrary, untrusted Rego code via `bundle.Activate()`. We pass a custom `*ast.Compiler` object already to handle print statements and restricting capabilities already, and `bundle.Activate()` itself takes a context. However, `*ast.Compiler.Compile()` itself takes no context, and none is available in [`compileModules()`](https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa/blob/54896f9f28515d14b31a93e6ef5737bb85866e30/v1/bundle/store.go#L993). As a result, a compilation process which takes a long time could hang a request indefinately, even after its context has been canceled. 

## Describe the ideal solution

OPA's compiler would accept a context and respect cancellation.

I believe we'll need to punch the context all the way down into the individual compile stages. We can pass it in where the stage gets invoked [here](https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa/blob/54896f9f28515d14b31a93e6ef5737bb85866e30/v1/ast/compile.go#L1963). Minimally, the context should be checked for cancellation before each stage runs. Some stages which have long running loops or which recurse should check each loop iteration or during each recursion step (e.g. `WalkRules()`).

API compatibility can be maintained by introducing new methods like `CompileWithContext()`. Existing methods can become wrappers that use `context.Background()`.

## Describe a "Good Enough" solution

As a stopgap, our current approach is to bound the size of the input bundle, but bundle size is an imperfect proxy for the time it will actually take to complete the compilation.

## Additional Context

I'm open to working on this but will need some guidance on the approach, I haven't worked much with the compiler, and this is potentially a cross cutting change.

Issue #707: [RRFC] Topological Sort

## Motivation ("The Why")

I got this idea from [a github issue](https://github.com/npm/feedback/discussions/579).

### Example

I am proposing that we add a sorting algorithm for ordering the graph traversal of npm commands that operate on the dependency graph express by a workspace.

A fully configured example in `package.json` might be as follows

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "workspaces/transitive-dependency",
    "workspaces/dependency",
    "workspaces/dependent"
  ],
  "workspaces-sort": {
    "algorithm": "topological-parallel",
    "include": [
      "dependencies",
      "bundleDependencies",
      "devDependencies",
      "optionalDependencies",
      "peerDependencies"
    ]
  }
}
```

And a user might use it at the command-line as follows

```shell
npm rn test --workspaces --workspaces-sort-algorithm=topological-parallel --workspaces-sort-include=dev,bundle,optional,peeru
```

### How
#### Current Behaviour

Currently, developers maintain a valid sort order manually in `package.json`, in the form of an ordered array in the `workspaces` key.

#### Desired Behaviour

Developers could list workspaces in any order, while still operating on packages in the order required for correctness.

### References
* [early draft](https://github.com/doug-wade/npm-rfcs/blob/topological-sort/accepted/0000-topological-sort.md)

Issue #378: feat(graph): track reverse import edges for impact analysis

## Problem

`memory_impact` cannot answer \"who imports this file/package?\" — the knowledge graph only tracks forward edges.

**Observed behavior** (tested live against nano-brain itself):

```
memory_impact(node="internal/watcher/filter.go::newFileFilter", max_depth=3)
→ {"count":1, "impacted":[{"node":"internal/watcher/filter.go", "edge_type":"contains"}]}
```

Only returns the containing file. Does not surface the 5 callers that actually import `internal/watcher`:
- `cmd/nano-brain/main.go`
- `internal/server/server.go`
- `internal/server/handlers/collection.go`
- `internal/server/handlers/reindex.go`
- `internal/server/handlers/workspace.go`

**Root cause:** The graph stores `file → imports → package` edges (outbound only). The `in` direction query returns 0 results for any file/package node because reverse edges are not stored.

## Use case

This is the core value proposition for multi-repo users:

> "I'm changing the redis key prefix from `latest:` to `later:` in repo A. Which other repos in my workspace use this key?"

Currently, `memory_impact` cannot answer this. `memory_search` can find text matches but doesn't traverse the dependency graph.

## Expected behavior

```
memory_impact(node="internal/watcher/filter.go", direction="in")
→ [
    "cmd/nano-brain/main.go",          -- imports watcher
    "internal/server/server.go",       -- imports watcher
    "internal/server/handlers/collection.go",
    "internal/server/handlers/reindex.go",
    "internal/server/handlers/workspace.go"
  ]
```

## Implementation sketch

During symbol extraction, when processing `file A` that contains `import "pkg/B"`, store **both** edges:
- `A → imports → B` (already done)
- `B ← imported_by ← A` (missing)

The `memory_impact` traversal (reverse lookup) then queries `imported_by` edges to find all dependents at each depth level.

This also enables cross-repo impact analysis when multiple repos are indexed under the same workspace (e.g. a monorepo root or a parent directory of related projects).

PoC PR #238 (`NivasSA:poc/tds-row-decode-optimizations`) reports **47.4% lower wall clock and ~65% lower CPU** on a 1.5M-row × 48-column scan. The wins are real and have since been independently reproduced. But it is a proof of concept, and it is not landable as-is.

What it is not: the PoC is often described as "adding sans-I/O". It is not. Its `buffered_slice` helper documents its own contract as *"Callers treat an empty slice as not enough data and fall back to the async path"* — the I/O-coupled decoder must still exist as a permanent fallback.

What makes it unlandable in its current form, beyond being +1516/−168 from an external fork with a pending CLA:

- a `POC_README.md` at the repo root
- PLP validation weakened from **6 checks to 2**, with the constants re-declared locally
- a third copy of the decode type switch
- a dead `decode_op_into`, and an NBCROW optimization that is only half-implemented (the bitmap fix exists *only* on the buffered fast path)
- pre-rebase benchmark numbers
- **zero tests** for its main fast path, against a repo that gates on 85% diff coverage

The wins are not one change. They are **four independent axes** with very different risk profiles, and separating them is the whole point of this issue.

|---|---|---|---|

Issue #4609: Property read cost depends on where the property sits in the record

## Problem

Two things about how a property is read make aggregation over a large expansion cost more than the data it returns.

**Read cost depends on where the property sits.** Fetching a property is not constant-time with respect to the record it lives in: a property stored later in the record costs measurably more to read than one stored earlier. On a node carrying eight properties, reading the last is around twice the cost of reading the first. Which properties are cheap is therefore an accident of the order they were first written, and users have no way to see or influence it.

**Nothing amortises across the properties a row actually reads.** A query reading three properties of one node pays three independent lookups, each starting from scratch. There is no cheaper path for "give me these three" than asking three times.

**Each value is built twice.** A read produces an intermediate representation which is then converted into the form the query evaluates. For a query over tens of millions of rows that is two constructions and two destructions per property per row, for values that are usually a number or a short string.

## Reproduction

1. Create nodes carrying 8 properties: a mix of strings, integers, doubles and a boolean.
2. Time `RETURN sum(n.first)` against `RETURN sum(n.last)` where `first` and `last` are the first and last properties written.
3. The second is materially slower, for identical work.
4. Time a query reading three properties against three queries reading one each; the combined cost is close to the sum, not below it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cost of reading a property does not depend on its position in the record
- [ ] Reading a set of properties of one node costs materially less than reading them one at a time
- [ ] A value is constructed once on the path from storage to expression evaluation
- [ ] No change to stored data format that would prevent an existing database from being opened, or a replica from following a main, without a migration step
- [ ] Results identical before and after, compared value by value, across all supported property types
- [ ] Memory per record does not increase
- [ ] Covered by benchmarks in the repository

## Notes

This underpins several of the other issues in the epic: batching reads (#4604) and reducing per-row work in aggregation (#4611) both get less valuable if an individual read stays expensive.

Property types worth explicit test coverage because they are easy to regress: temporal types with and without a named timezone, enums, points, lists and maps, and integers near the boundaries where their stored width changes.

Issue #83: [bug] Resource walk follows symlinks with no depth or visit budget: self-referential symlink hangs the build (OOM)

## Behavior

`PomChangeAnalyzer.scanDirectoryForPropertyRefs` uses `Files.isDirectory(entry)` without `LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS`, follows symlinks, and has no visited-set or depth cap.

Minimal repro: a PR that changes any `<properties>` value in a parent POM (so `changedProperties` is non-empty), marks a resource directory in a child module with filtering enabled, and adds a symlink `module-b/src/main/resources/loop -> .`. The walk enumerates `loop`, `loop/loop`, `loop/loop/loop` without bound; each level pushes new `Path` entries onto the stack, so it is unbounded CPU *and* unbounded heap, ending in OOM or a hung CI job. A symlink pointing at the filesystem root walks the entire runner filesystem instead.

Reachability: `hasFilteredResourcesWithChangedProperty` runs for any dependent module not already flagged whenever `changedProperties` is non-empty, so a completely ordinary "bump a property in the parent POM" PR reaches this code with PR-controlled directory contents. The `maxResourceFileSize` guard caps individual file reads and does nothing about traversal.

- Directory detection uses `NOFOLLOW_LINKS`, or the walk switches to `Files.walkFileTree`, which does not follow symlinks by default.

Issue #1064: flow(refine): emit a stack layout for ordered split children

## Problem

`/cenci:refine` already computes everything a stack needs and then throws the ordering away at the branch level. For an M/L ticket it produces numbered children as native sub-issues, links them with `gh issue edit --add-blocked-by`, writes a `Depends on #<n>` prose line into each dependent child's body, and appends an `### Execution Order` note to the parent when the children are not all independent.

That execution order *is* the stack order. Nothing currently records which branch each child should build on, so every child branches from `main` and the ordering is enforced by serialization instead.

## Goal

Have refine emit an explicit stack layout for ordered split children, so each child ticket carries the base it should be implemented on.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When a split's children have real ordering, refine records each child's base — the preceding layer's branch for a dependent child, `main` for the bottom layer.
- [ ] Children the split marks as independent are **not** stacked: they keep `main` as their base and remain genuinely parallel. Stacking a set of independent children would serialize work that is currently already parallel — a regression, not a feature.
- [ ] A design-only first child is never a stack layer — it produces a committed design spec, not a PR, so nothing can target its branch.
- [ ] Split depth stays one; a stack is a layout over existing children and never mints grandchild tickets (`docs/ticket-sizing.md`).
- [ ] The layout is visible to a human on the parent, alongside the existing `### Execution Order` note, not only in machine-readable form.
- [ ] The Confirmation Gate renders the proposed stack before any GitHub write, and declining performs zero writes — consistent with every other refine write path.
- [ ] When the `gh stack` capability probe reports absent, refine emits no stack layout and the split behaves exactly as it does today.
- [ ] Tests cover: an ordered split producing a layout, an all-independent split producing none, a design-first split, and the capability-absent path.

## Dependencies

Gated on the spike's decision doc and on the base-ref plumbing (the layout has nowhere to be consumed until a ticket can carry a base). Pairs with the Blocked-Dependency Gate's stackable path — the layout is what that gate reads.

## Size estimate

M — one new output from an existing split computation, plus the gate's rendering and the four test paths.

```
I love org.as3commons.reflect.*.  But, I do not love the way it manages type 
information.

It seems that type information is parsed and cached "en masse" -- that is, all 
type information for the entire .swf is loaded and then sits like a lump in 
memory.  Apparently, the only methods for managing the cached information are 
ByteCodeType.fromXxx() and ByteCodeTypeCache.clear().  (At least, it seems this 
how ByteCodeTypeCache works.)

I have very large project which uses ByteCodeType in many different places and 
at different times in the application life-cycle.  I call 
ByteCodeType.fromLoader() at startup to fill the cache with type information.  
Afterwards, ByteCodeTypeCache.clear() is not fine-grained enough to manage the 
cache -- performance would suffer if the type information was loaded and 
cleared en masse again and again as my application ran.  On the other hand, my 
application doesn't make use of *all* the type information for the entire .swf, 
so it is a great waste of memory for all the ByteCodeType-related objects (and 
strings!) for every possible type in my application to sit in memory.  It is 
also a great waste of time...  it takes several seconds for my application to 
start (while ByteCodeType.fromLoader() runs, loading the universe).

So, this issue to ask you to please consider the following:

1) Parsing type information more "on-demand", perhaps loading each type only 
when it is asked for (for example, when Type.forInstance() or 
ByteCodeType.forClass() is called).  Or, take it to the next level, and even 
parse individual member info on-demand (for example, when an instance of Method 
or Variable is needed).

2) Caching all type information using SoftReferences, so unused type 
information will naturally "fall out" of memory when no longer needed (i.e., 
let the application's actual set of references control what stays cached).

Ideally, an application should be able to freely use instances of Type and 
ByteCodeType and only pay the costs to parse, load, and store the type 
information that is actually used.

Perhaps calls such as ByteCodeType.fromLoader() should simply do some 
lightweight "cursory" parse (maybe just build a list of the type names and 
offsets to where the type information is), and leave the more detailed parsing 
until later (on-demand).

It would also be extremely desirable for any time-consuming functionality to 
operate asynchronously, providing an event or callback notification when the 
result is available.  (By "asynchronous", I meant dividing up the work and 
processing it in "slices", never taking longer than some caller-specified 
duration per slice.)

### The Risk

The `delete_file` (recursive), `modify_file` (regex-replace), and `write_file` tools expose powerful filesystem operations to LLM agents. This creates a risk for **Indirect Prompt Injection** attacks:

1. An attacker places a crafted `.txt` file in a monitored directory
2. The AI agent reads the file during a legitimate operation
3. The injected instructions trigger `delete_file` with recursive flag, or `modify_file` to alter config files

This is classified as **OWASP LLM05 (Insecure Output Handling)** — the LLM output (file operations) is not validated against the user's original intent.

### Suggested Mitigations

- Add a security disclaimer to the README warning users about prompt injection risks
- Implement a confirmation step before destructive operations (delete recursive, modify system files)
- Add path allowlisting beyond the current directory validation
- Consider rate limiting and audit logging for write/delete operations

### Our Scan Results

We scanned mcp-filesystem-server with ClawGuard Shield (120 patterns, 12 languages, F1=97.4%) and found patterns matching data exfiltration and insecure output handling risks.

Related reading: [6 Real MCP Security Breaches](https://prompttools.co/blog/6-real-mcp-security-breaches) — documented incidents from WhatsApp, GitHub, Asana, and Smithery that show why MCP security scanning matters.

Happy to share the full scan report if helpful. This is not a CVE filing — just a heads-up from the security community.

## Recommended implementation shape

- `project_sources/collector/tools/run_powershell_unused_function_report.py`

## Detection guidance

The analyzer should classify functions rather than produce a simple pass/fail list. Suggested classes:

- `entrypoint`: known collector entrypoint or manifest/runtime entry function that should not be flagged merely because it is called externally.
- `referenced`: function has a literal call/reference from maintained collector runtime source.
- `likely_unused`: function has a definition but no literal reference after excluding comments, strings, here-strings, and documentation-only text.

- PowerShell function names are case-insensitive.

## Problem Statement

LandForger’s Maps, Map Folders, Pins, and Reference Canvas still live in a browser-local deferred cache even though Worlds and Pages now persist through the Go API. A worldbuilder can arrange a Map Library, place Pages as Pins, build a Map hierarchy, narrow Pins by Era, or fill a Reference Canvas, but that work is tied to one browser. Switching devices, clearing site data, or opening the same World elsewhere loses the spatial organization and moodboard state.

The backend contract already describes most of the M2 HTTP surface, but the server returns empty Maps, Pins, and Map Folders, unimplemented operations fall through to 501, and the frontend deliberately intercepts these features before they reach the API. The result is a split World whose core content is durable while its spatial model is not.

## Solution

Make Postgres authoritative for Map metadata, Map Folders, Pins, chart assignments, and the World-scoped Reference Canvas, while making R2 authoritative for Map chart image bytes and preserving the existing product behavior:

- A World’s full response includes its Maps, Map Folders, Pins, Root Map, and Reference Canvas.
- Map creation, editing, hierarchy changes, Root Map changes, and deletion are durable and account-scoped.
- The Map Library’s independent folder tree is durable, cycle-safe, and promotes contents when a folder is deleted.
- Pins are durable placements at percentage coordinates, inherit their Page’s Eras, support multiple placements, and retain the established Timeless/Active Era visibility semantics.
- Reference Canvas JSON is saved to the World in Postgres rather than the browser-local deferred cache.
- Existing browser-local M2 data is imported without silently discarding it, and the frontend’s existing `WorldRepository` remains the single application data seam.

Issue #1554: Epic: Agent tool-surface hardening — gaps exposed by a live "watch a page" task

> **Principle: Penny's own operations get the same discipline as her data — structural state, foreign keys, one source of truth — so that acting, inspecting, and dismantling her mechanisms are reads and cascades, never guesses.** The model keeps the work that genuinely needs a model (reading the messy world); everything decidable is decided in Python from structured fields.

A user asked Penny to **monitor a web page for a value change and alert them on change**, then later to **tear the watch down**. Setting it up, running it, and tearing it down each surfaced distinct, reproducible failures.

A forensic pass over the full session — every user message, tool call, model reasoning trace, and reply, ~100 runs classified atom-by-atom — showed Penny was mostly **acting rationally given the surfaces she was handed**. The failures cluster not in her reasoning but in the **tool surface** and her **self-model**.

**Root theme.** The primitives she builds with — `collection` / `collector` / `schedule` / `skill` / `log` — overlap and blur, and the surface lacks **identity/resolution, non-lossy editing, a unified inventory, honest state read-back, and operational self-grounding**. So one simple intent shattered across several mechanisms she then couldn't reliably **address, inspect, edit, or dismantle**.

The children are not independent fixes — they build **one thing**, an *operational spine*, in five moves:

1. **A registry** (what exists): every long-lived mechanism is a row with provenance (`source_message_id`, `created_by_run_id`), configuration, and lifecycle (incl. `expires_at`); archived rows stay visible with status. → #1566
2. **A ledger** (what happened): runs, emissions, and mutations closed under provenance — from any event to its cause and its entity; from any entity to its events. State stays materialized in registry flags (audit trail, **not** event sourcing). → #1560
3. **A complete collector**: every background task decomposes along seven structured axes — **trigger / target / procedure / state / gate / emission / lifecycle** — and the model keeps exactly one (procedure: read/extract). 4. **One emission channel**: a single send surface with honest receipts; every autonomous emission carries the identity of its cause and is novelty-key gated at the channel (policy on the channel, not the mechanism). → #1557, #1568
5. **The ambient inversion**: the system prompt surfaces Penny's own operational state (rendered from the registry/ledger — deterministic facts) and relegates speculative user-content recall to on-demand lookups. Self-side lookups are unanchored — what isn't ambient won't be fetched. → #1555, #1558, #1559

Issue #7515: [Feature Request] In-place materialize of base-referenced files (promote a shallow clone / branch to independent without deep_clone)

## Summary

Add an operation to **materialize a dataset's `base_paths`-referenced files into its own storage in place** — copy the referenced data (and index) files local, rewrite the referencing `DataFile`s to `base_id = None`, and drop the now-unreferenced `BasePath`s. This is the in-place counterpart to `deep_clone` (which only produces a **new** dataset) and the missing **remove** half of base-path management (`UpdateBases` only adds). It is what lets a shallow clone — or, with #7263, a branch that adopted another branch's fragments — become self-contained so the source can be safely deleted (#7185).

## Motivation

After a `shallow_clone` (or a future branch merge / rebase, #7263), a dataset/branch holds `DataFile`s whose `base_id` points into another base. To make it independent — so the source dataset/branch can be vacuumed or deleted without orphaning it (the hazard in #7514) — those files must become local. Today the only way is `deep_clone`, which copies to a **new** URI and refuses if a dataset already exists at the target (`Dataset::deep_clone`, `rust/lance/src/dataset.rs`). There is no way to re-home the base-referenced files of an *existing* dataset/branch in place, keeping its version/lineage chain.

## Background: base references today

- `Manifest.base_paths: HashMap<u32, BasePath>` + `DataFile.base_id: Option<u32>` resolve a file relative to a registered base, or to the dataset root when `base_id` is `None` (`rust/lance-table/src/format/manifest.rs`, `rust/lance-table/src/format/fragment.rs`).
- `Manifest::shallow_clone` and `Operation::UpdateBases` **add** bases — `UpdateBases` is add-only (proto `new_bases`; apply in `rust/lance/src/dataset/transaction.rs` only inserts).
- `compact_files` re-homes only the fragments it happens to rewrite; `DataReplacement` swaps a single fragment's `DataFile`. Neither is a complete "materialize all base-referenced files and drop the bases" sweep.

So there is a shallow-clone path (reference) and a `deep_clone` path (full copy to a new dataset), but no **in-place shallow → independent** transition.

## Proposed mechanism

```
materialize_bases(dataset):
  1. for each DataFile with base_id = Some(_):
       object-store copy the file into the dataset's own data dir
       (and index files under _indices/), preserving fragment ids + row-id meta
  2. commit DataReplacement (data) / re-commit CreateIndex with base_id = None (indices),
       rewriting the DataFiles to base_id = None  (rows + fragment ids unchanged)
  3. drop the now-unreferenced BasePaths
       (the remove half of UpdateBases — currently missing)
```

Preserving fragment ids and row-id meta keeps index `fragment_bitmap`s valid, so indexes don't need rebuilding (a `base_id`-carrying index can be re-homed by copying its files and re-committing the `IndexMetadata` with `base_id = None`). The result is a dataset with no `base_paths`, identical contents, on the same version chain — at which point the source it cloned from can be deleted (#7185) with no dangling references.

Related: #5249 (`deep_clone`, the new-dataset alternative), #4864 (the add-bases API; this is the remove half), #7263, #7185, #7514.

Issue #3233: P2PROD: ant-zookeeper: replace static pipeline templates with per-revision deployment DAGs

## Problem

The current pipeline system has two fundamental issues:

1. **Static templates, manually created.** `init_pipelines` must be run before
   any deployment can happen. Pipeline stages ("build", "deploy") are declared
   upfront in the database and shared across all revisions of a project. Adding
   a new deployment step (e.g. config delivery in #3228) requires extending the
   static stage schema and rerunning `init_pipelines`.

2. **The "build" stage is a runtime graph that accumulates artifacts.** The DAG
   starts at `upsert_revision` time and blocks on `Pending` nodes until all
   architecture artifacts arrive. The pipeline exists before the build is done,
   the event log fills with partial state, and tests must drive iteration ticks
   while uploading artifacts one at a time.

## Proposed design

### Pipelines are per-revision and ephemeral

A pipeline is created **once per revision**, at activation time (when all
architecture artifacts are registered at the same version), and never reused.
It has no required name. `init_pipelines` is deleted.

There is no "build" stage. Artifacts accumulate as today. When the revision
activates, the full deployment DAG is created synchronously inside a single
serializable transaction:

```
activate_revision()          -- sets activated_at
create deployment_pipeline   -- linked to revision_id
insert deployment_node rows  -- one per step
insert deployment_edge rows  -- adjacency list encoding ordering and parallelism
```

If DAG creation fails, the transaction rolls back and the build system gets a
500 on the last artifact upload. It retries.

### New schema

**Removed:**
- `deployment_pipeline_stage`
- `deployment_pipeline_stage_edge`
- `deployment_pipeline_stage_host_group`
- `deployment` (completed-event log — replaced by node state)

**Changed:**
- `deployment_pipeline`: add `revision_id FK`, make `name` nullable, add
  `UNIQUE(revision_id)`. Created at activation, not by `init_pipelines`.
- `deployment_job`: replace `(revision_id, deployment_event TEXT)` with
  `deployment_node_id FK`. Add `error TEXT`. Remove `is_retryable`.

**Added:**
```sql
CREATE TABLE deployment_node (
  deployment_node_id     TEXT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT ('dn-' || random_string(10)),
  deployment_pipeline_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES deployment_pipeline,
  event                  TEXT NOT NULL,
  state                  TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  -- state: pending | executable | in_progress | finished | failed | surpassed
  created_at             TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  finished_at            TIMESTAMPTZ,
  attempts               INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  UNIQUE (deployment_pipeline_id, event)
);

CREATE TABLE deployment_edge (
  from_node_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES deployment_node,
  to_node_id   TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES deployment_node,
  PRIMARY KEY (from_node_id, to_node_id)
);
```

### State machine

```
pending → executable → in_progress → finished
                                    ↘ failed → executable  (manual retry)
                       surpassed  (newer revision already owns this step)
```

**Promotion:** when a node transitions to `finished`, run inside a serializable
transaction:

```sql
UPDATE deployment_node SET state = 'executable'
WHERE deployment_node_id IN (
  SELECT e.to_node_id FROM deployment_edge e
  WHERE e.from_node_id = $1
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM deployment_edge e2
      JOIN deployment_node dep ON e2.from_node_id = dep.deployment_node_id
      WHERE e2.to_node_id = e.to_node_id

)

```

Issue #30: Implement filesystem watching for automatic cache invalidation

## Background

Currently, the MCP server caches app metadata with a 15-minute TTL. This creates UX friction:
- **New apps installed** aren't discoverable until cache expires (up to 15 min delay)
- **Apps uninstalled** may still appear in metadata for up to 15 minutes  
- **SDEF file changes** (app updates) aren't reflected until cache refresh

**Current workarounds**:
- Restart the MCP server
- Wait up to 15 minutes for automatic expiration

## Proposed Solution

Implement filesystem watching to automatically invalidate cache when apps are installed/uninstalled or updated.

### Architecture Options

**Option 1: Watch /Applications directories**
```typescript
import { watch } from 'fs/promises';

// Watch for .app bundle changes
const watcher = watch('/Applications', { recursive: true });
for await (const event of watcher) {
  if (event.filename?.endsWith('.app')) {
    invalidateCache();
  }
}
```

**Option 2: Watch specific app bundle SDEF files**
```typescript
// Only watch discovered apps' SDEF files
const sdefPaths = apps.map(app => app.sdefPath);
for (const path of sdefPaths) {
  watchFile(path, () => invalidateCache(path));
}
```

**Recommendation**: Start with Option 1 (directory watching) for broader coverage.

## Implementation Plan

1. **Add filesystem watcher to JITD discovery module** (2-3 hours)
   - Use Node.js `fs.watch()` or `chokidar` library
   - Watch /Applications, /System/Applications, ~/Applications
   - Debounce events to avoid thrashing

2. **Invalidate cache on app changes** (1 hour)
   - Call existing `invalidateCache()` function
   - Log cache invalidation events (debug level)

3. **Handle watcher lifecycle** (1 hour)
   - Start watcher during server initialization
   - Clean up watcher on server shutdown
   - Handle watcher errors gracefully

4. **Add configuration option** (30 min)
   - `enableFilesystemWatching: boolean` in server options
   - Default: true
   - Allow disabling for testing/debugging

5. **Test edge cases** (2-3 hours)
   - App installation/uninstall
   - App updates (SDEF file changes)
   - Permission errors
   - Watcher crashes

## Benefits

- ✅ **Instant app discovery** - No 15-minute wait for new apps
- ✅ **Accurate metadata** - Removed apps disappear immediately
- ✅ **Better UX** - Users see real-time updates
- ✅ **Reduced confusion** - No stale app metadata

## Risks & Mitigations

**Risk 1: Performance overhead**
- Mitigation: Debounce events (500ms-1s delay before invalidation)
- Mitigation: Use efficient recursive watching (native OS events)

**Risk 2: Watcher crashes**
- Mitigation: Graceful degradation (fall back to TTL-based cache)
- Mitigation: Log errors, continue server operation

**Risk 3: Too many invalidations**
- Mitigation: Selective invalidation (only affected apps)
- Mitigation: Rate limiting (max 1 invalidation per second)

## Dependencies

- Requires: Existing cache invalidation mechanism (already present)
- Optional: `chokidar` library for more robust watching

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Filesystem watcher monitors app directories
- [ ] Cache invalidates when apps installed/uninstalled
- [ ] Cache invalidates when SDEF files change
- [ ] Watcher lifecycle managed properly (start/stop)
- [ ] Configuration option to disable watching
- [ ] Tests cover installation, updates, removal scenarios
- [ ] No performance degradation under normal load

## References

- PR #28: https://github.com/jsavin/iac-mcp/pull/28
- Cache limitation documented in PR description
- Planning doc: `planning/CACHE-INVALIDATION-IMPROVEMENTS.md`

**Priority: P1** - High priority UX improvement
**Estimated effort**: 1-2 days

Issue #185: refactor(locations): migrate from tag-based storage to dedicated locations table

## Background

Locations are currently stored as tags with `tag_type ∈ {country, city, address}` (introduced in #184). This works for the CRUD MVP but will not scale to location-based queries.

## Problem

When we add "assign location to item" and need queries like _"find all items in Kraków or any address in Kraków"_, the tag-based approach requires a recursive walk up the tag hierarchy:

```sql
-- current approach — fragile and slow on large datasets
SELECT DISTINCT i.* FROM items i
JOIN item_tags it ON it.item_id = i.id
JOIN tags t ON t.id = it.tag_id
WHERE t.id = :city_id
   OR t.parent_tag_id = :city_id
   OR t.parent_tag_id IN (SELECT id FROM tags WHERE parent_tag_id = :city_id)
```

## Proposed schema

```sql
CREATE TABLE locations (
    id        TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id   TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    name      TEXT NOT NULL,
    address   TEXT,
    type      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(type IN ('country', 'city', 'address')),
    parent_id TEXT REFERENCES locations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

CREATE INDEX idx_locations_user ON locations(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_locations_parent ON locations(parent_id);

CREATE TABLE item_locations (
    item_id     TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES items(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    location_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES locations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (item_id, location_id)
);
```

With a recursive CTE, the subtree query becomes clean and indexable:

```sql
WITH subtree AS (
    SELECT id FROM locations WHERE id = :root_id
    UNION ALL
    SELECT l.id FROM locations l JOIN subtree s ON l.parent_id = s.id
)
SELECT DISTINCT i.* FROM items i
JOIN item_locations il ON il.item_id = i.id
WHERE il.location_id IN (SELECT id FROM subtree);
```

## Migration plan

1. Add `locations` and `item_locations` tables (new migration)
2. Migrate existing location tags → `locations` rows (one-time data migration in the same migration file)
3. Remove location tag types from the tag system
4. Update domain, server fns, and MCP tools to use the new table
5. Update `/locations` CRUD page to call new server functions

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `locations` and `item_locations` tables exist with proper FK constraints and indexes
- [ ] Existing location data migrated from tags
- [ ] Location CRUD page works as before
- [ ] Item detail page allows assigning one or more locations
- [ ] Query "items in location X (including descendants)" returns correct results

Issue #6: v3: Wiki support — structured pages with link graph

## Problem
Wiki has been requested multiple times. Without entry relationships, a wiki is just a pile of disconnected pages.

## Solution
With v3 relationships (issue #2), wiki becomes a convention on top of existing infrastructure:

### Convention
- Wiki entries use `wiki/` namespace prefix
- Key format: `wiki/{slug}` (e.g. `wiki/breefs-audio-pipeline`)
- Value: markdown or HTML content
- Tags: `["wiki", "category:ops"]` for categorization

### Link graph
- Use `references` relationships to link wiki pages
- `GET /memory/{key}/relationships` returns linked pages
- Traversal: start from a wiki page, follow references to build the graph

### Ingestion (future, not v3)
- Auto-convert raw documents into wiki entries
- Extract headings as separate entries with parent relationships
- Build link graph from cross-references in content

### REST
- `GET /wiki` — list all wiki entries (shortcut for `GET /memory?namespace=wiki`)
- `GET /wiki/{slug}` — get wiki page (shortcut for `GET /memory/wiki/{slug}`)
- `GET /wiki/{slug}/links` — get linked pages (shortcut for `GET /memory/{key}/relationships`)

### MCP
- `memory_wiki_list` — list wiki pages
- `memory_wiki_get` — get wiki page + its links

### No schema change needed
This is all convention + relationships. The wiki is just entries with a namespace prefix and reference relationships.

Issue #53: Stack overflow: chained redefinition inside an anonymous redefining usage never resolves

## Summary

`SymbolIndex::resolve_all_type_refs` never terminates on a chained redefinition nested inside an unnamed redefining usage. The process dies with `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW`. It also dies on a 256 MB stack, so this is an infinite loop rather than legitimate deep recursion.

## Minimal repro

```sysml
part :>> s {
    :>> pwrCmd.x;
}
```

```rust
let mut host = AnalysisHost::new();
host.set_file_content("cycle.sysml", source);
host.rebuild_index(); // stack overflow
```

The file parses with zero errors. Any API that triggers index building hits the loop too, for example `host.model()`.

Official examples shipped in this repo trigger it: `tests/sysml-examples/Timeslice and Snapshot Examples/TimeVaryingAttribute.sysml` and the `Vehicle Example` folder. The construct there is a snapshot redefining a lifecycle feature while also redefining a member of a sibling item through a feature chain:

```sysml
part def Transport2 {
    out item pwrCmd : PwrCmd;
    timeslice :>> portionOfLife {
        snapshot :>> start {
            :>> pwrCmd.pwrLevel = 0;
        }
    }
}
```

## Mechanism

Verified on `v0.5.1-alpha`. The cycle sits in `src/hir/resolve.rs`:

1. The anonymous usage `part :>> s` registers in the visibility maps under its base name `s`, so its own redefinition target `s` resolves to the symbol itself.
2. The nested anonymous member `<:>>pwrCmd.x#1@L1>` likewise registers under `pwrCmd`, so its chain head `pwrCmd` also resolves to the symbol itself.
3. Pass 2 of `resolve_all_type_refs` resolves the chain part `x` via `resolve_feature_chain_member`, which asks `get_member_lookup_scope` for the member scope of that self resolved symbol.
4. `get_member_lookup_scope` sees a redefinition target equal to the symbol and calls `infer_type_from_parent_feature`. The parent `s` resolved its supertype to itself as well, so `find_member_in_scope("s", "pwrCmd")` returns the same anonymous member again, and `infer_type_from_parent_feature` calls `get_member_lookup_scope` on it. Neither function tracks visited symbols, so the pair recurses forever.

Trace with debug prints at both function heads:

```
GMLS  sym=s::<:>>pwrCmd.x#1@L1>
ITFPF sym=s::<:>>pwrCmd.x#1@L1> feature=pwrCmd
GMLS  sym=s::<:>>pwrCmd.x#1@L1>
ITFPF sym=s::<:>>pwrCmd.x#1@L1> feature=pwrCmd
...
```

`find_member_in_subsetting_chain_internal` and `find_member_in_scope_internal` already guard against exactly this with a visited set. `get_member_lookup_scope` and `infer_type_from_parent_feature` predate that pattern and lack it.

## Suggested fix

Thread a visited set through `get_member_lookup_scope` and `infer_type_from_parent_feature`, mirroring `find_member_in_scope_internal`. On a revisit, fall back to the symbol's own qualified name as the member scope, which is the existing behavior for untyped symbols. PR with fix and regression tests follows.

Issue #387: Reduce per-element database calls during element hierarchy traversal

## TL;DR

`IModelExporter` discovers an element hierarchy by calling `queryChildren()` once for every visited element. Large exports pay for thousands of source-database lookups even though the required depth-first order can be produced in one recursive query. We need a set-based traversal that preserves the exporter’s existing ordering, filtering, callback, and child-pruning behavior.

## Current behavior

- `exportModelContents()` selects top-level elements in ID order.
- Each accepted element eventually calls `exportChildElements()`, which performs another `queryChildren()` lookup.
- A hierarchy with N visited elements therefore performs roughly N child lookups.
- Consumers can override or skip child traversal, so replacing the loop is not only a query change. The existing callback scope and pruning behavior are part of the compatibility boundary.

Current implementation: [`IModelExporter.exportChildElementsImpl()`](https://github.com/iTwin/imodel-transformer/blob/9112135f1e25d1ccd3f07b8b4d473b2bc256422f/packages/transformer/src/IModelExporter.ts#L1049-L1064)

## Why address it

A deterministic 100,000-element mixed hierarchy measured about 330 ms for hierarchy discovery before element materialization and import work. The cost is not dominant in every transformation, but it scales with element count and creates avoidable TypeScript-to-database calls.

> The less calls between TS and native the better.

The replacement must not trade the lookup cost for unbounded TypeScript memory, unstable sibling order, or changed exporter behavior.

## Exit criteria

- Characterization tests pin down root order, sibling order, depth-first traversal, child suppression, explicit child traversal, filtering, yielding, and failure cleanup.
- The selected implementation returns the same ordered element digest as the current traversal on deep, wide, and mixed hierarchies.
- A same-run A/B comparison reports hierarchy-discovery time, end-to-end transformation time, and peak worker RSS without a material regression.
- Any dependency on SQLite recursive-query behavior is documented and tested against the supported iTwin.js core range.
- If the best remaining design needs a core/native API, that work is recorded separately rather than hidden in the transformer change.

Introduction

Most users at one time or another have dealt with hierarchical data in a SQL database and no doubt learned that the management of hierarchical data is not what a relational database is intended for. The tables of a relational database are not hierarchical (like XML), but are simply a flat list. Hierarchical data has a parent-child relationship that is not naturally represented in a relational database table.

For our purposes, hierarchical data is a collection of data where each item has a single parent and zero or more children (with the exception of the root item, which has no parent). Hierarchical data can be found in a variety of database applications, including forum and mailing list threads, business organization charts, content management categories, and product categories. For our purposes we will use the following product category hierarchy from an fictional electronics store:

These categories form a hierarchy in much the same way as the other examples cited above. In this article we will examine two models for dealing with hierarchical data in MySQL, starting with the traditional adjacency list model.

The Adjacency List Model

Typically the example categories shown above will be stored in a table like the following (I’m including full CREATE and INSERT statements so you can follow along):

CREATE TABLE category(
        category_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
        name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
        parent INT DEFAULT NULL
);

INSERT INTO category VALUES(1,'ELECTRONICS',NULL),(2,'TELEVISIONS',1),(3,'TUBE',2),
        (4,'LCD',2),(5,'PLASMA',2),(6,'PORTABLE ELECTRONICS',1),(7,'MP3 PLAYERS',6),(8,'FLASH',7),
        (9,'CD PLAYERS',6),(10,'2 WAY RADIOS',6);

SELECT * FROM category ORDER BY category_id;
+-------------+----------------------+--------+
| category_id | name                 | parent |
+-------------+----------------------+--------+
|           1 | ELECTRONICS          |   NULL |
|           2 | TELEVISIONS          |      1 |

What is better to store hierarchical data: nested sets model or adjacency list (parent-child) model?

First, let's explain what all this means.

Adjacency list

Hierarchical relations (not to be confused with hierarchical data model) are 0-1:0-N transitive relations between entities of same domain.

For instance, ancestor-descendant relation is:

  • Transitive:
    • If A is an ancestor of B and B is an ancestor of C, then A is an ancestor of C
  • Antisymmetric:
    • If A is an ancestor of B, then B is never an ancestor of A
  • Irreflexive:
    • A is never an ancestor to itself
  • 0-1:0-N
    • A can have zero, one or many children. A can have zero or one parents.

These relations can be represented by an ordered directed tree.

Tree is a simple directed graph (that with at most one directed edge between two different vertices) and relational model has means to represent simple graphs.

Two vertices are considered related (and therefore their primary keys forming a row in the table) if and only if they are connected with an edge.

This table along with the table defining the vertices identifies a graph completely by defining pairs of vertices connected by the edges. Each record in the table defines a pair of adjacent vertices, that's why this representation is called adjacency list.

Adjacency lists can represent any simple directed graphs, not ony hierarchy trees. But due to the fact that this structure is most commonly used to define the parent-child relationships, the terms parent-child model and adjacency list model have almost become synonymous. However, they are not: adjacency list model is much wider and parent-child model is one of its implementations.

Now, since we have a tree here which implies 0-1:0-N relationship between the vertices, we can define the relation as a self-relation: the table defines both the entity and the relationship. Parent is just a one attribute among other attributes with a FOREIGN KEY reference to the table itself.

Since multple items can have no parents (and therefore be the roots of their trees), it's sometimes useful to convert this tree into an arborescence: make a single fake root that considered a parent of all entries that have no actual parent.

This is a nice and elegant model, but until recently it had one drawback: it could not be used with SQL.

SQL, as we all know, deals with relational tables which can be transformed by the means of relational algebra.

It provides a way to do number of operations including relational multiplication, projection, sum etc.

However, earlier versions or SQL lacked recursion which is required to do certain operations efficiently. Namely, recursion is required to operate upon the adjacency list structure.

The most common operations are:

Introduction

Most users at one time or another have dealt with hierarchical data in a SQL database and no doubt learned that the management of hierarchical data is not what a relational database is intended for. The tables of a relational database are not hierarchical (like XML), but are simply a flat list. Hierarchical data has a parent-child relationship that is not naturally represented in a relational database table.

For our purposes, hierarchical data is a collection of data where each item has a single parent and zero or more children (with the exception of the root item, which has no parent). Hierarchical data can be found in a variety of database applications, including forum and mailing list threads, business organization charts, content management categories, and product categories.
