## Summary

Add `Store<V>`, the per-kind reflector store with tombstones and an atomic staging swap at
`Event::InitDone`, plus `watch_config(kind)`, the decided `watcher::Config` for every watched kind, plus
`apply_event`, the one function in this crate that is allowed to match on a `watcher::Event` variant.
Resync is zero and there is no option to change it. There is no `StoreUpdater` type: the updater is the
pair of free functions `apply_event` and `apply_meta_event` plus `spawn_kind`, and `watch/stores.rs` is
the module the `no-event-variant-branch` lint exempts by exact path.

## Context

This issue owns the milestone's central invariant:

> **INVARIANT L1.** No code in `irontraffic-k8s` may branch on the *variant* of a `watcher::Event` to
> decide what the world looks like. `Apply`, `Delete`, `InitApply` and `InitDone` may only update the
> store and mark dirty. All decisions are made by reading the store.

kube-rs's `watcher::Event` is `Apply(K) | Delete(K) | Init | InitApply(K) | InitDone`
(`kube-runtime/src/watcher.rs:55-84`). The documentation on `InitDone` says it "can be used as a signal
to replace buffered store contents atomically" and that "Any objects that were previously `Applied` but
are not listed in any of the `InitApply` events should be assumed to have been `Deleted`". The `Delete`
variant carries the source warning: "This should not be used for managing persistent state elsewhere,
since events may be lost if the watcher is unavailable. Use Finalizers instead." That warning, written by
the library authors, is the whole edge-triggered-is-a-bug argument.

Why edge-triggered logic is a defect, in this system's terms:

1. **Events are lost.** A watch that dies and relists after an HTTP 410 Gone (an etcd compaction)
   delivers `Init` / `InitApply*` / `InitDone` with no delete events for the objects that vanished while
   we were disconnected. An edge-triggered handler leaks those routes into the data plane forever. A
   level-triggered one recomputes and they are gone.
2. **Events are coalesced.** Our own scheduler collapses a create-then-delete inside the debounce window
   into nothing at all. Correct for level, catastrophic for edge.
3. **Events across kinds have no relative order.** A route can arrive before its Gateway, its Service,
   its EndpointSlice and its ReferenceGrant, in any permutation. Edge logic must then encode a state
   machine per arrival order; level logic has one code path.
4. **Restarts.** A controller that restarts has seen no events at all and must be correct immediately.

Issue #48: Handle inverse and sub-properties (normalize inverses at ingest, expand sub-properties at query time)

## Summary

Design notes for handling **inverse properties** and **sub-properties** in GrEBI. These feel like one problem but want different solutions. Recommendation up front:

- **Inverse → ingest-time canonicalization** (normalize each inverse pair to one predicate + direction)
- **Sub-property → query-time type-union expansion** (expand a requested predicate to itself + its transitive sub-predicates)

Both share one new build artifact — a **predicate-metadata table** (sub-property closure + inverse pairs) — which can be derived from the ontology datasource added in #47.

## Two different problems

**Inverse properties** — e.g. `biolink:has_phenotype` ⇄ `biolink:phenotype_of`. Different sources assert different directions of the same fact. This is a *normalization* problem: we want one canonical way to express each relationship.

**Sub-properties** — `rdfs:subPropertyOf` chains, e.g. `biolink:causes` ⊑ `biolink:contributes_to` ⊑ `biolink:related_to`. A query for the general predicate should also match the specific ones. This is a *closure/expansion* problem, structurally identical to the subclass `redundant`/`nonredundant` trick in #47.

## Current state

- Edges become Neo4j relationship types verbatim — `grebi_make_neo_csv` (`dataload/06_create_neo_db/grebi_make_neo_csv/src/main.rs`) writes `edge.edge_type` straight into the `:TYPE` column.
- Query templates hard-code single predicates, e.g. `-[:`biolink:related_to`]->` in `query_templates/hello_world.yaml`.
- The only predicate normalization today is `additional_equivalence_groups` in `configs/subgraph_configs/src/shared.py`, which merges *synonymous* predicates (e.g. `ols:directParent` = `rdfs:subClassOf`) but does **not** handle property hierarchy or inverses.

## The big lever from #47

PR #47 ingests Ubergraph/ontologies as data, so **the property hierarchy and inverse axioms are now in the graph as facts** — `rdfs:subPropertyOf` and `owl:inverseOf` edges between predicate entities. We don't need to hardcode a mapping from the Biolink YAML; we can *derive* the predicate-metadata table from the ontology datasource itself, the same source of truth the rest of the pipeline already trusts. This is the foundation for both halves below.

## Inverse: normalize at ingest, not query time

For inverses, query-time is the wrong place — if both directions stay live, every query must consider both forever. Instead, canonicalize each inverse pair to **one predicate + one direction** during ingest (a cheap relabel in `grebi_link` or earlier — no graph growth). Pick the canonical member from the inverse-pair table.

Caveat: if a source genuinely asserts both directions as distinct provenance, canonicalizing merges them — but edges already carry `grebi:datasources` as a **set**, so the merge is lossless for provenance.

## Sub-properties: expand at query time

Query-time is the right call here, and the contrast with subclass is instructive. Subclass closure is *materialized* (redundant graph) because nodes are queried by hierarchy constantly. Property closure materialized as duplicate edges would multiply **edge** count by predicate-tree depth × every source — expensive and baked-in at load.

Instead, expand the predicate at query-build time. Neo4j matches a union of relationship types efficiently via the rel-type index:

```cypher
// query asks for related_to; expand to its sub-property descendants
MATCH (gene)-[assoc:`biolink:related_to`|`biolink:causes`|`biolink:contributes_to`|...]->(disease)
```

Mechanically:
1. At ingest, walk `rdfs:subPropertyOf` edges from the ontology datasource and precompute a **closure table**: predicate → all transitive sub-predicates. It's tiny (hundreds of entries) — load it into the API like the existing `PrefixService`/prefix map, **not** into Neo4j.
2. In `GrebiCypherRepo` (`webapp/grebi_api/.../repo/GrebiCypherRepo.java`), expand each predicate in the Cypher fragment to the `|`-union of itself + descendants before sending to the cypher service.

# RFC: Minimal immutable prefix checkpoint tree for Flash KV reuse

## Status

Revision 5 after terminal-boundary, atomic-lifecycle, and eviction-policy clarification.

**Recommendation: conditional Go**, delivered as three independently gated slices:

1. **P0a — engine proof:** exact split/capture/restore, no server lookup and no durable cache.
2. **P0b — RAM-only token-text tree:** usable prefix reuse under a hard global memory budget.
3. **P0c — immutable disk persistence:** FIFO writer, restart scan, shared disk budget, and leaf-only GC.

The proposed object remains one narrow immutable **prefix tree**, not a generic DAG, radix database, paged-KV system, or new protocol state machine. Every node has exactly one parent and contains:

- the compressed/indexer rows added since that parent; and
- the exact terminal frontier required to continue inference at this node.

KVC v1 remains the fallback and correctness oracle until P0c has passed the full matrix.

Revision 5 makes three operational rules explicit:

1. every real prompt terminal is an exact, variable-length capture candidate, even when it is only a few tokens after its parent;
2. a node's history delta and terminal frontier have one atomic publication, persistence, and deletion lifecycle in P0;
3. RAM-only pruning and durable deletion are leaf-only; RAM payload offload may target an internal node only when a durable copy remains available.

## Why a tree is sufficient

Given cached branches:

```text
[SYSTEM][A][B][C]
[SYSTEM][A][B][D]
[SYSTEM][A][B][E]
```

a new prompt ending at `[SYSTEM][A]` can reuse a checkpoint only if one was captured at or before that prefix. A later child cannot be "truncated" by slicing tensors: raw SWA rows are a logical ring and the compressor/indexer recurrent state is position-specific.

The reusable structure is nevertheless simple:

- compressed/indexer history is append-only;
- raw SWA, recurrent compressor/indexer state, counters, logits, and exact tokens form the terminal frontier;
- siblings share an immutable parent path;
- restore walks exactly one root-to-leaf chain.

No sibling merge or arbitrary substring reuse is causally valid. A tree therefore supplies the needed sharing without DAG machinery.

## Evidence and remaining unknown

Local M2 Ultra measurements with the 262,144-context MXFP4 Flash model found:

| State | Size | Synchronous time |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Existing full KVC at ~2K | 49.93 MiB | median 56.3 ms |
| Existing full KVC at ~8K | 130.62 MiB | median 135.1 ms |
| Existing full KVC at ~32K | 453.35 MiB | median 468.0 ms |
| Exact terminal frontier, warm RAM | 22.88 MiB | p50 0.561 ms, p95 0.639 ms |
| Exact terminal frontier, first touch | 22.88 MiB | 2.7–4.3 ms |
| 23 MiB write plus `fsync` | 23 MiB | 5.1–6.3 ms |

At 2,048-token cadence, 128 conservative frontiers are about 2.86 GiB. Unique F32 compressed history is about 3.36 GiB, for roughly 6.22 GiB for one full 262K path. At the current natural 4,096-token Metal prefill cadence, frontier overhead is about 1.43 GiB.

These numbers justify an experiment. They do **not** measure the full node capture path. P0a must still prove that copying the unique compressed/indexer delta plus frontier regresses linear prefill by less than 5%.

## Goals

1. Restore the globally deepest compatible saved prefix no longer than the incoming prompt.
2. Share immutable compressed/indexer history across branches.

## Buyer-visible gap

mightyETL can now accept, execute, discover, poll, conditionally validate, and cancel durable ETL jobs. Failed or deliberately cancelled work, however, cannot be safely retried by an operator after the terminal payload has been cleared. Enterprise operations need an explicit replay resource that creates new work, preserves the original terminal evidence, proves the exact payload being replayed, and never mutates history.

This issue becomes implementation-ready only after PRs #121, #122, #129, #130, #131, and #133 integrate in order. Do not create a parallel feature PR while that stack is open.

## Proposed bounded vertical slice

Add an authenticated owner-scoped replay action:

```http
POST /api/etl/jobs/{source_job_record_id}/replays
Authorization: Basic <credential>
Idempotency-Key: "new replay key"
Content-Type: application/json

[{"id":"record_alpha","name":"accepted"}]
```

The request supplies the complete candidate payload again because terminal source jobs retain only `request_digest`, not raw payload. The service must validate the bounded JSON through the existing intake contract and require its SHA-256 digest to equal the immutable source `request_digest` before creating any new job.

A successful first replay returns RFC 9110 `202 Accepted`, a new `PENDING` job resource, `Location`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, and `Idempotency-Replayed: false`. Repeating the same source, principal, semantic key, and byte-identical payload returns the same new job with `Idempotency-Replayed: true`.

## Immutable lineage

The source job remains unchanged. The replay creates a new row with descriptive multi-word `snake_case` lineage fields:

```text
replay_source_job_record_id
replay_root_job_record_id
replay_generation_count
```

Required invariants:

- `replay_source_job_record_id` identifies the immediate terminal source;
- `replay_root_job_record_id` identifies the first job in the lineage;
- a first replay has generation 1;
- a replay of a replay increments the generation exactly once;
- generation is bounded, initially 1 through 100;
- the root row has all replay fields null;
- a replay row has all replay fields non-null;
- source and root rows belong to the same principal scope;
- source and root references cannot point to the new row itself;
- a terminal source can never be rewritten to `PENDING`;
- the lineage can be exported as W3C PROV `prov:wasDerivedFrom` without changing the relational authority.

The first slice may use nullable self-referencing foreign keys only when migration and deletion/retention behavior are explicit. Silent cascade deletion of replay history is prohibited.

- `FAILED`;
- `CANCELLED`.

Rejected source states:

- `PENDING` and `RUNNING`: active work is not replayable;
- `SUCCEEDED`: replay could duplicate target effects and requires a separately authorized duplicate-processing workflow;
- missing, malformed, or foreign-owned identifiers: one owner-safe `404 etl_job_not_found` surface.

Issue #81: Topological sort silently produces an incomplete order for cyclic graphs (not currently reachable, but a latent correctness gap)

## Found via
Writing #5's test suite made me think about what \`topologicalSortSteps\` does on a graph with a cycle, since Kahn's algorithm (which it implements) is only defined for DAGs.

## Bug
\`topologicalSortSteps\` (src/visualizers/graph/steps/topological.ts) never checks whether every node was actually dequeued. If the input graph has a cycle, the nodes in that cycle keep a non-zero in-degree forever and are never enqueued/visited - the algorithm just stops with a queue that permanently empties out early. \`useGraphDerivedState\`'s \`deriveTopoOrder()\` builds the "Topological Order" output purely from \`mark-visited\` steps, so the output panel would silently show an order with only some of the nodes - no error, no cycle indicator, and \`order.length < graph.nodes.length\` is never checked anywhere.

## Why this isn't urgent
Not currently reachable: the graph visualizer only offers fixed presets (\`GRAPH_PRESETS\`, no user-editable graph), and the \`dependency\` preset used for Topological Sort is a genuine DAG. So no user can trigger this today.

## Fix (when it matters)
Worth guarding before any future work makes the graph user-editable (a custom-graph input, an example picker with more presets, etc.): after the main loop, compare how many nodes got \`mark-visited\` against \`graph.nodes.length\`, and either push a distinct \`cycle-detected\`-style step or otherwise surface that the order is incomplete, rather than silently truncating it. Also worth adding a cyclic-graph test case to #5's topological-sort tests once that guard exists.

`OutageORM.sla_status` (`app/models/orm/outage.py`) is a JSON column read in `_orm_to_pydantic` (`app/repositories/outage_repository.py`) and exported by `app/utils/exporter.py`, but no code path ever writes it:

...

- **Every outage payload claims "no SLA status"**: `GET /outages/{id}`, list views, and CSV/JSON exports always carry `sla_status: null` even for resolved, computed outages — the field exists in the public model (`Outage` in `app/models/outage.py`) and the frontend outage detail page has no data to render.
- **Schema/behavior drift**: the column, the DTO, the exporter, and the SLA computation all know about the concept, but the persistence link is missing — exactly the kind of half-wired field that silently misleads consumers.
- **Duplicated truth**: `sla_results.is_latest` already holds the authoritative status; `sla_status` was presumably meant as a denormalized copy, but without a writer it is dead weight and a future confusion source.

## Root cause

The column was added to the model/exporter before the SLA pipeline existed; when the pipeline landed, nothing backfilled the denormalized field.

## Why this is archititionally hard

1. The fix is either (a) write `sla_status` from `sla_results` on resolve/recompute and keep both in sync (needs transactional updates in `resolve_outage` and `recompute_sla`), or (b) remove the column/DTO field and have `_orm_to_pydantic` join `sla_results` for the status — a schema removal migration versus a denormalization decision.
2. Exports (`exporter.py`) and the frontend `outages` types (`src/types/outages.ts`) reference `sla_status`; choosing (b) changes the public response shape and requires a coordinated frontend change.
3. Historical data has no `sla_status` values; any writer must backfill from `sla_results` for consistency, which is a data migration with its own test.

## Proposed design

Prefer (b): drop the `sla_status` JSON column and derive status via a join to `SLAResultORM` (latest per outage) in `_orm_to_pydantic`, or if (a) is chosen, write it atomically on resolve/recompute and backfill existing rows. Update exporter and the frontend types accordingly.

Frontend `src/types/outages.ts` and outage detail view; OpenAPI snapshot regenerated via `make openapi-update`.

### Service
- [ ] Outage responses report the SLA status of the latest SLA result (or explicitly `null` when none exists).
- [ ] No dead `sla_status` column remains if (b) is chosen.

### Tests
- [ ] A test resolves an outage, computes SLA, and asserts the outage payload carries the status.
- [ ] Export output includes the status.

The KPI aggregation semantics and analytics caching.

Issue #354: lib: reify construct-level `node.addDependency` into resource `depends_on`

### Description

CDKTN inherits the `constructs` library's `node.addDependency()` API, but nothing in the framework ever reads `node.dependencies`. As a result, a construct-level dependency declared on an L2/L3 construct is silently dropped at synth time — it never becomes `depends_on` in the generated Terraform.

Today the only way to express ordering is to pass `dependsOn: ITerraformDependable[]` on each individual L1 `TerraformResource`/`TerraformDataSource`. That works, but it forces every abstraction author to manually plumb dependencies through their construct API down to every leaf resource, and it makes `constructs`' `IDependable`/`DependencyGroup` (the standard way to model "logical readiness" that doesn't map to a single resource) unusable.

**This is a silent failure.** `myConstruct.node.addDependency(otherConstruct)` compiles, runs, and produces plan output with no warning — it just has no effect on the generated configuration. Users reasonably expect it to work, because it does in AWS CDK, from which the construct programming model, `Aspects`, and much of the surrounding API were ported.

#### What's missing

`packages/cdktn/src/terraform-dependable.ts` is still the empty marker interface, and `TerraformResource`/`TerraformDataSource` only consume an explicitly-passed `dependsOn` array. There's no pass anywhere in `TerraformStack` or `StackSynthesizer` that walks `node.dependencies` and reifies it into resource-level `depends_on`. (`TerraformStack.addDependency()` is a separate, stack-to-stack deploy-ordering mechanism and doesn't help here.)

#### Prior art: AWS CDK

AWS CDK solves this generically during the prepare/synth phase, in [`core/lib/private/deps.ts`](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/packages/aws-cdk-lib/core/lib/private/deps.ts):

```ts
/**
 * Turn all dependencies added via `source.node.addDependency(target)` into concrete dependencies.
 *
 * The semantics are that every construct underneath the source construct
 * depends on every construct underneath the target construct, ...
 */
export function reifyConstructDependencies(root: IConstruct) { ... }
```

Mechanically it:
1. Walks the tree DFS-preorder collecting every construct with a non-empty `node.dependencies`.
2. Resolves each entry via `Dependable.of(dependable).dependencyRoots` — this is what makes `DependencyGroup` fan out to multiple targets.
3. Finds all L1s under source and under target (`findCfnResources()`, a DFS filtered by `CfnResource.isCfnResource`) and applies `sourceResource._addResourceDependency(targetResource)` for **every pair**.

That cross-product is exactly the design question @jsteinich raised in #785 — *"Would that add `depends_on` to every resource within the custom construct?"* — and yes, N×M is the semantic AWS CDK actually shipped and has lived with for years. Issue #26: Fix circular dependencies across packages

## Summary

Circular dependencies exist in the codebase and are flagged as urgent. In Metro/React Native environments, circular deps can cause undefined imports at runtime — modules that appear correctly imported resolve to `undefined` because the dependency cycle hasn't finished initializing when the import is evaluated. This is a correctness hazard, not just a warning.

## Goals

* Eliminate all circular dependency cycles in `packages/client/src/`
* Ensure no runtime `undefined` imports caused by initialization order
* Establish a clear, acyclic dependency direction between layers (API → managers → stores → builtins)

## Scope

### Audit
* Use `bun` or `madge` to visualize the full dependency graph and identify all cycles
* Map the dependency direction between key modules: managers, API, stores, builtins
* Document which cycles cause actual runtime issues vs. which are benign (type-only imports)

### Common culprits
* Managers importing from API which imports back from managers
* Stores importing from builtins which import back from stores
* Shared utility modules that pull in heavy dependencies creating indirect cycles

### Resolution strategies
* Restructure modules to enforce a strict layered dependency direction
* Introduce lazy imports (`require()` inside function bodies) where restructuring is too invasive
* Create intermediary modules to break specific cycles
* Extract shared types/interfaces into leaf modules with no upstream deps

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Dependency graph tooling (madge or equivalent) reports zero circular dependencies
- [ ] No runtime `undefined` import errors caused by initialization order
- [ ] Dependency direction is documented (which layer may import from which)
- [ ] No lazy `require()` hacks unless explicitly justified with a comment

## Out of scope

* Refactoring module public APIs beyond what is needed to break cycles
* Cross-package (monorepo-level) dependency changes
* Performance optimizations unrelated to circular deps

Issue #313: Implementation Gap: Location-based Encounter Proximity Queries

## Implementation Gap: Location-based Encounter Proximity

**Source:** `docs/plugins/CHARACTER-ENCOUNTER.md`
**Identified:** 2026-02-06

## Summary
Integrate with location hierarchy to find encounters "near" a location via ancestor/descendant queries. Currently, `QueryByLocationAsync` only returns encounters at the exact location specified.

## Investigation Findings

### Code Analysis
Current implementation in `CharacterEncounterService.cs` line 801-868:

```csharp
// Line 807: Current exact location query
var encounterIds = await GetLocationEncounterIdsAsync(body.LocationId, cancellationToken);
```

The service only queries the `loc-idx-{locationId}` index for exact matches. To support hierarchy queries:
1. Add `ILocationClient` dependency (Location is L2, CharacterEncounter is L4 - allowed)
2. Call `GetLocationAncestorsAsync` for ancestor encounters (e.g., "all encounters in this city including its neighborhoods")
3. Call `ListByParentAsync` recursively for descendant encounters (e.g., "all encounters in this room and all sub-rooms")
4. Aggregate results from multiple location indexes

### Integration Points
- **New dependency:** `ILocationClient` from lib-location (L2)
- **Location APIs available:**
  - `GetLocationAncestorsAsync` - Returns all ancestors of a location
  - `ListByParentAsync` - Returns immediate children of a location (would need recursive calls for all descendants)
- **State stores:** Uses existing `loc-idx-{locationId}` pattern - would query multiple locations

### TENET Considerations
- **Schema changes needed:** Add to `QueryByLocationRequest`:
  ```yaml
  includeAncestors:
    type: boolean
    default: false
    description: Include encounters at ancestor locations
  includeDescendants:
    type: boolean
    default: false
    description: Include encounters at descendant locations
  maxDepth:
    type: integer
    minimum: 1
    maximum: 10
    default: 5
    description: Maximum hierarchy depth to traverse
  ```
- **Service hierarchy:** CharacterEncounter (L4) → Location (L2) is allowed direction

## Open Questions

The following questions require human judgment before implementation:

1. **Performance limits**: A location with depth 10+ or 100+ descendants could result in many Location service calls and many index lookups. Should there be a hard `maxDepth` limit in config, or leave it to the request?

2. **Descendants recursion strategy**: For `includeDescendants`, should we:
   - Traverse ALL descendants (could be thousands in a realm)? No "get all descendants" endpoint exists.
   - Only immediate children (one level)?
   - Limit to `maxDepth` levels of recursion?

3. **Which direction is more useful?**: 
   - Ancestors seems more useful for "all encounters in this city, including its neighborhoods"
   - Descendants seems more useful for "all encounters in this building, including every room"
   - Should we implement one first, or both together?

4. **Caching location hierarchy**: If querying the same location hierarchy frequently, should we cache the location tree separately to avoid repeated Location service calls? The Location service likely already caches its data.

5. **Result size limits**: A query with `includeAncestors=true` could return encounters from many locations. Should pagination be per-location or combined across all locations?

## Recommended Next Steps

1. Decide on recursion strategy for descendants (immediate children, maxDepth levels, or all)
2. Decide if implementing ancestors only is sufficient for initial release
3. Add `ILocationClient` dependency to CharacterEncounterService
4. Update schema with new request fields (schema-first)
5. Implement ancestor query path first (simpler - single API call)
6. Implement descendant query path with chosen recursion strategy
7. Add configuration for default/max depth limits

Issue #218: Improve source-edit rebuild granularity for large strict projects

## Summary

Profile-separated build roots for debug/release are a big improvement: repeated checks and mode switching can now stay hot, and no-change debug/release builds can fall through to Ninja with no work. The remaining pain point is source-edit rebuild granularity for large strict projects that still hit the broad generated project/main unit.

In the v2 compiler project, some source edits still cause a very large rebuild fanout even when the semantic change is narrow. To really make edit-time development fast, Simple C++ needs project-unit decomposition / dependency-grouped generated C++ so Ninja can rebuild only the affected generated units and link.

## Concrete evidence

Recent v2 compiler measurements from `compiler/v2/src`:

```text
# Earlier baseline before profile-separated roots / grouped checks
debug build after source edits: 455.59 s
release/O3 build after source edits: 707.98 s
no-change build: about 10-11 s
```

After the profile-separated-root work, repeated debug/release mode checks are much better, but a project-graph/source edit still did this:

```text
XDEBUG_MODE=off SCPP_NINJA_JOBS=16 php ../../../vendor/simple_cpp/bin/scpp.php build --no-stan
Transpiled PHP files: 422, skipped unchanged: 0
Generated Ninja file: .prism/build/build.ninja
Using build mode: debug
ninja: Entering directory `.prism/build'
[1/423] ...
...
Build completed: .prism/build/main
```

A follow-up body-only correction in one PHS file showed the shape we want more often:

```text
XDEBUG_MODE=off SCPP_NINJA_JOBS=16 php ../../../vendor/simple_cpp/bin/scpp.php stan
Source units: 423
Analyzed: 1
Reused cache: 422
Warnings: 68

XDEBUG_MODE=off SCPP_NINJA_JOBS=16 php ../../../vendor/simple_cpp/bin/scpp.php build --no-stan
Transpiled PHP files: 1, skipped unchanged: 421
ninja: Entering directory `.prism/build'
[1/2] CXX compile/incremental/resident_source_unit_frontend_payload_tables.o
[2/2] LINK main
Build completed: .prism/build/main
```

That second run completed in about 17 seconds from the Codex tool wall clock. The first broad run took several minutes. The important conclusion: when Simple C++/Ninja can isolate the touched source unit, the workflow is already much better; the remaining issue is avoiding unnecessary project-wide invalidation and generated-unit fanout.

## Proposed direction

Please consider extending the current project generation model so large strict projects can be split into dependency-grouped generated units instead of one broad project/main dependency surface.

Possible shape:

- Let STAN/project discovery compute source-unit dependency groups and stable public-surface/body hashes.
- Generate multiple project unit headers/translation units, for example `__project_units_*.hpp` plus matching `.cpp` files, grouped by dependency/component or source path/module bucket.
- Make each generated `.cpp` include only the project units it actually needs, rather than pulling one monolithic `__project_units.hpp` surface everywhere.
- Keep public API/signature/layout changes separate from body-only changes so a body edit can rebuild the owning object and link, while public-surface changes still invalidate dependents correctly.
- Preserve the profile-separated roots from the recent work: `.prism/build/debug`, `.prism/build/release`, etc.
- Add `explain-build` visibility for broad rebuilds: which source unit, public hash, body hash, generated header, or dependency group forced the fanout.

## Desired behavior

For a large strict project like the v2 compiler:

- A body-only edit in one `.phs` file should normally transpile one source unit and rebuild one generated object plus link.
- Adding a private helper/body implementation should not regenerate/recompile hundreds of unrelated generated objects.
- Adding or changing exported structs, layout, public signatures, or shared metadata may still fan out, but the reason should be explicit and inspectable.
- Debug and release modes should remain independent and hot after the first build.

Issue #76611: Matrix crypto-store: state only persisted on 60s timer + sync stop helpers do not await final persist (E2EE decryption breaks across restarts)

## Summary

Two related defects in the Matrix crypto-store persistence lifecycle that together can cause an OpenClaw Matrix bot to silently lose its ability to decrypt inbound E2EE messages over restart cycles, even with a fully-bootstrapped recovery key, server-side key backup, and verified cross-signing.

### Defect A — Crypto state is only persisted on a 60s timer

`initializeCryptoIfNeeded` schedules `setInterval(() => persistIdbToDisk(...), MATRIX_IDB_PERSIST_INTERVAL_MS)` (default 60s) and provides no event-driven flush in addition. When the rust crypto SDK establishes a new Olm session, decrypts an incoming Megolm key, finishes a key backup restore, or completes cross-signing rehydration, that state lives only in fake-indexeddb in process memory until the next 60s tick.

If the process exits inside that window (npm update, crash, OOM, manual restart), the just-negotiated Olm session is lost. The peer's Element keeps encrypting outbound to-device events with the same Olm session key the bot no longer has, producing repeating `InvalidMAC(MacError)` errors and "Established new Olm sessions" loops on the same `sender_key` until manual recovery (key request, reverify, or backup-restore CLI) is run.

### Defect B — Some shared-client stop APIs start final persistence but do not await it

`MatrixClient.stop()` correctly initiates final persistence (writes `syncStore.markCleanShutdown()`, kicks off `persistIdbToDisk` + `syncStore.flush()`, stores the resulting promise as `this.stopPersistPromise`; `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/sdk.ts:666-694`). `stopAndPersist()` awaits that promise.

However, the **synchronous** shared-client stop helpers do not:

- `stopSharedClient()` (`shared.ts:268-273`)
- `stopSharedClientForAccount()` (`shared.ts:275-282`)
- `stopSharedClientInstance()` (`shared.ts:294-299`)

All three call `client.stop()` and return `void`. They start the final persist promise but do not give callers a way to await it. The `releaseSharedClientInstance(..., "persist")` path (`shared.ts:301-322`) does correctly `await client.stopAndPersist()`, and the monitor cleanup path uses it (`monitor/index.ts:243`), so monitor-driven shutdowns are clean. Other call sites (e.g. one-off CLI flows, abort cleanup) using the synchronous variants can return before the persistence promise resolves.

Defect A means recently-acquired keys are not yet on disk. Defect B means whichever shutdown path uses the synchronous helpers does not wait for the in-flight final persist. Together, this is the slow-burn E2EE-decryption-broken pattern.

## Summary

The topological sort implementation in `ApplicationsRegistry.resolve_dependencies()` has O(N² + NE) time complexity due to a nested loop pattern. While this performs adequately for HARP's typical use cases (<10 applications), it could be optimized to O(N + E) by building a reverse dependency graph.

## Current Implementation

**File:** `harp/config/applications.py:319-323`

```python
# Find apps that depend on this node
for app_name in original_order:  # O(N) iteration
    if node in graph[app_name]:   # O(E) check for each
        in_degree[app_name] -= 1
        if in_degree[app_name] == 0:
            queue.append(app_name)
```

**Current Complexity:** O(N² + NE)
- For each processed node (N iterations in while loop)
- We iterate through all applications (N iterations)
- Checking if node is in dependencies list (up to E checks)

## Proposed Optimization

Build a reverse dependency graph upfront:

```python
# Build reverse dependency graph (add after line 295)
reverse_graph = defaultdict(list)  # dependents_of[dep] = [apps that depend on dep]
for app_name in self._applications:
    for dep in graph[app_name]:
        reverse_graph[dep].append(app_name)

# Then replace lines 319-323 with direct lookup:
for dependent in reverse_graph[node]:
    in_degree[dependent] -= 1
    if in_degree[dependent] == 0:
        queue.append(dependent)
```

**Optimized Complexity:** O(N + E)
- Building reverse graph: O(N + E) - iterate apps and their deps once
- Processing queue: O(N + E) - each app and dependency processed once

## Why This Isn't Critical

**Current Performance:**
- Typical HARP usage: <10 applications, <20 dependencies
- Current implementation: <1ms startup overhead (measured in #802)
- With N=10: N² = 100 operations ≈ 0.05-0.1ms

**This optimization would save:** ~0.05ms at startup (unmeasurable)

**Why defer:**
- One-time startup operation, not in hot path
- Current implementation is correct and well-tested
- No user-facing performance issues
- Optimization would require re-testing all 33 dependency tests

## When to Implement

This optimization becomes relevant if:
1. HARP supports 50+ applications in a single system (unlikely)
2. Startup time becomes a bottleneck (currently not an issue)
3. Someone wants to contribute a "good first issue" (learning opportunity)

Issue #143: Async agent delegation with cascading pause/resume/cancel

## Problem

Today `AgentDelegationTool` and `A2AAgentTool` block the parent agent synchronously until the child task reaches a terminal state (or the 120s timeout fires). This means:

- Parent agent cannot do other work while a child runs.
- Parent cannot fan out N delegations in parallel and wait on all of them.
- No way to peek at a child's status mid-flight.
- No native Temporal back-channel — the parent polls instead of being notified.
- Pausing a parent task does not propagate to delegated subtasks (children keep running, which usually isn't what the user means when they pause a *task*).

## Proposed design (Option B — sibling workflow + signal-back)

Keep each task as an independent top-level workflow. Add a back-channel via Temporal external signals.

### 1. Pass parent context to child

When `AgentDelegationTool` submits a task, include `parent_task_id` and `parent_workflow_id` in the child's task metadata.

### 2. Child signals parent on completion

At the end of `AgentExecutionWorkflow`, if `parent_workflow_id` is set:

```python
workflow.get_external_workflow_handle(parent_workflow_id) \
    .signal(\"delegation_completed\", task_id, result, status)
```

Wrap in try/except for \`WorkflowExecutionAlreadyCompleted\` (parent may be canceled/done).

### 3. Parent state and signal handler

Parent maintains `self._pending_delegations: dict[task_id, ChildRef]` and `self._delegations: dict[task_id, DelegationResult]`. New signal handler:

```python
@workflow.signal
def delegation_completed(self, task_id: str, result: str, status: str):
    self._delegations[task_id] = DelegationResult(result=result, status=status)
    self._pending_delegations.pop(task_id, None)
```

Signals are processed even while the workflow is paused, so results queue up correctly.

### 4. New agent-facing tools

- `delegate_to_<agent>(message, mode=\"sync\"|\"async\")` — `sync` is today's blocking behavior (default, backwards compatible). `async` returns immediately with `{task_id}`.
- `wait_for_delegation(task_id, timeout)` — `await workflow.wait_condition(lambda: task_id in self._delegations, timeout=timeout)` then return result.
- `wait_for_delegations([id1, id2, ...], timeout)` — fan-in.
- `check_delegation(task_id)` — return status without blocking; useful for periodic peeks.

### 5. Cascading pause/resume/cancel (defaults to tree)

Pausing a *task* should pause its descendants by default. Same for cancel and resume.

API additions:

- `POST /v1/agents/{a}/tasks/{t}/pause` — body `{\"scope\": \"tree\" | \"self\"}`, default `tree`.
- `POST /v1/agents/{a}/tasks/{t}/resume` — same.
- `DELETE /v1/agents/{a}/tasks/{t}?scope=tree|self` — default `tree` (matches today's expectation).
- `GET /v1/agents/{a}/tasks/{t}` — include `parent_task_id` and `child_task_ids` for tree rendering.

Mechanics: parent's `pause_execution` / `resume_execution` / cancel handlers iterate `self._pending_delegations` and forward the signal to each child workflow. Each child runs the same handler, so propagation is recursive without explicit depth tracking.

Per-delegation override (advanced, can defer):

```python

```

`isolate` means the child runs independently of parent's pause/resume — for genuine fire-and-forget background work.

Issue #316: Feature Request: Incremental Index Updates for Large Documents

## Problem

Currently, PageIndex appears to rebuild document indexes as a whole when a document is reprocessed.

This works well for static documents, but it can become expensive for large documents that undergo small updates.

For example:

* A 500-page policy manual receives a 2-page revision.
* A contract receives a minor amendment.
* A compliance document is updated in a single section.

In these cases, rebuilding the entire hierarchical index may require regenerating summaries and tree structures for large portions of the document even though only a small subset changed.

## Proposed Enhancement

Introduce incremental index updates that can:

1. Detect changed sections between document versions.
2. Rebuild only affected branches of the document tree.
3. Recompute summaries only along impacted paths.
4. Optionally maintain document version history and change tracking.

At a high level, this could be achieved through node-level content hashing and selective subtree regeneration.

## Benefits

### Reduced Indexing Cost

Only modified sections would require reprocessing, significantly reducing LLM and indexing costs for large documents.

### Faster Updates

Small document revisions could be indexed much faster than full document rebuilds.

### Better Enterprise Support

Many enterprise workflows involve:

* Policy revisions
* Regulatory updates
* Contract amendments
* Documentation versioning

Incremental updates would make PageIndex more practical in these environments.

### Foundation for Future Features

This capability could also enable:

* Document version comparison
* Change history visualization
* Impact analysis of document updates
* Audit and compliance workflows

## Example

Current workflow:

Document v1
→ Build full tree

Document v2 (2 pages changed)
→ Rebuild full tree

Proposed workflow:

Document v1
→ Build full tree

Document v2 (2 pages changed)
→ Detect changed nodes
→ Rebuild affected subtree only
→ Update parent summaries as needed

## Discussion

Has incremental indexing already been considered for the roadmap?

It seems like a natural fit for PageIndex's hierarchical tree architecture and could provide significant performance improvements for large, frequently updated documents.

Support additive, inspectable metadata for:

- model/Class identity and inheritance/generalization
- stored members and their backing Collection path/column/key/index
- primary and alternate identities

Every exposed Class member must be classified as one of:

1. **Stored writable member** — maps to an explicit supported mutation on an authoritative backing Collection.
2. **Writable bounded-view member** — writable only within the bounds and mutation surface of a specific collection view.
3. **Stored read-only member** — persisted but immutable through this ORM contract.
4. **Derived/computed member** — evaluated from state or a query and never directly assignable unless an explicit setter operation exists.
5. **Prototype/inherited member** — resolved through the Class definition; writable only if an explicit instance mutation contract maps it to backing state.
6. **Method/action** — executable, not assignable.
7. **Relationship member** — mutation follows its declared foreign-key/link/through-collection operation and cardinality rules.
8. **Unsupported/opaque member** — inspectable only to the degree authorized; mutation fails explicitly.

Member lookup follows the accepted Class resolution order, but mutation authority comes from the resolved instance/backing-collection contract—not merely from a prototype containing a name.

## Mutation semantics

- Assignment must compile to a canonical explicit mutation plan; do not implement local Python-object mutation as if it were authoritative.
- Validate Class identity, member classification, type, bounds, schema revision, capability, and backing Collection support before dispatch.
- Use the existing kernel-owned transaction lifecycle.
- Preserve collection-specific semantics such as keys, uniqueness, indexes, bounds, sparsity, shape/dtype, writable views, compare-and-set/version checks, and supported update operators.
- Never broaden a bounded view or materialize an entire Collection to perform a member update.
- Derived, method, immutable

Issue #226: feat(flock): recursive CTE lineage traversal for SYNTHESIZE depth

## Current limitation
SYNTHESIZE queries look at flat cluster membership — `WHERE cluster_id = ?`. A synthesis produced in round 1 has `parent_ids` linking to its source findings, but this lineage is never traversed. Round 2's SYNTHESIZE cannot discover that synthesis S1 shares ancestry with findings in cluster 12.

## What DuckDB enables
Recursive CTEs (`WITH RECURSIVE`) can walk the full `parent_id` DAG:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE lineage AS (
    SELECT id, fact, parent_id, 0 as depth
    FROM conditions WHERE id = ?
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.id, c.fact, c.parent_id, l.depth + 1
    FROM conditions c JOIN lineage l ON c.parent_id = l.id
    WHERE l.depth < 10
)
SELECT * FROM lineage;
```

## What this enables
**Recursive synthesis** — the Flock generates meta-syntheses from its own prior syntheses:
- Round 1: Synthesize findings in cluster 7 → produces synthesis S1
- Round 2: Recursive CTE discovers S1 shares parent ancestry with cluster 12 findings
- SYNTHESIZE combines S1 + cluster 12 → second-order synthesis S2
- This is the architecture's core promise: the ConditionStore IS the intelligence, and recursive SQL IS the reasoning

## Implementation
- Replace flat cluster query in SYNTHESIZE section with recursive CTE that walks `parent_id` chains
- Limit recursion depth to prevent runaway (10 hops)
- Add `synthesis_depth` metadata to track how many synthesis layers deep a finding is
- Higher-depth syntheses get priority boost (they represent more integrated knowledge)

Issue #1: Why ddx uses a SQL rewrite, not a Substrait plan round-trip (recursive CTEs & DML unsupported)

## Why `ddx` uses a SQL rewrite, not a Substrait plan round-trip

`ddx` differentiates `grad()`/`jvp()`/`vjp()` as a **plan-time rewrite** (they are
markers that must be rewritten away before execution — see
[`docs/design.md` §3.1](../blob/main/docs/design.md)). One approach we evaluated
and rejected — the intermediate design in the
[xarray-sql prototype PR #192](https://github.com/xqlsystems/xarray-sql/pull/192)
(commit `672e7d0`) — round-tripped the **entire DataFusion `LogicalPlan` through
Substrait** to apply the rewrite in a separately-linked copy of DataFusion:

> produce `LogicalPlan` as Substrait → rewrite `grad()` → re-produce Substrait →
> consume & execute.

That approach was deleted (PR #192 commit `14b26971`) because Substrait's producer
cannot represent the query shapes that make in-SQL training loops interesting.
This issue records a **fresh, reproduced** account of the limitation and is the
reference for [`design.md` §3.2 and §6](../blob/main/docs/design.md) (Substrait is
off the critical path; we rewrite `grad()` as SQL text before planning instead).

### Reproduction (datafusion 54.0.0)

```python
import datafusion
from datafusion import SessionContext
from datafusion.substrait import Producer

ctx = SessionContext()
ctx.from_pydict({"x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]}, "t")

def produce(label, sql):
    try:
        plan = ctx.sql(sql).logical_plan()
        Producer.to_substrait_plan(plan, ctx)
        print(f"{label}: OK")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{label}: FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)[:160]}")

produce("control (projection)", "SELECT x + 1.0 AS y FROM t")
produce("recursive CTE",
        "WITH RECURSIVE r(step, v) AS ("
        " SELECT 0 AS step, CAST(1.0 AS DOUBLE) AS v UNION ALL"
        " SELECT step + 1, v / 2 FROM r WHERE step < 5) SELECT v FROM r")
produce("scalar subquery", "SELECT x, (SELECT max(x) FROM t) AS mx FROM t")
produce("DML (INSERT...SELECT)", "INSERT INTO t SELECT x + 1.0 FROM t")
```

Output:

```
control (projection):  OK
recursive CTE:         FAILED -> RuntimeError: NotImplemented("Unsupported plan type: RecursiveQuery { name: \"r\", ... }")
scalar subquery:       OK
DML (INSERT...SELECT): FAILED -> RuntimeError: NotImplemented("Unsupported plan type: DmlStatement { table_name: ... op: Insert ... }")
```

### What's still blocking vs. what has been fixed upstream

| Query shape | `to_substrait_plan` (datafusion 54.0.0) |
| --- | --- |
| Plain scalar projection | ✅ works |
| **Recursive CTE** (`WITH RECURSIVE`) | ❌ `Unsupported plan type: RecursiveQuery` |
| **DML** (`INSERT … SELECT`) | ❌ `Unsupported plan type: DmlStatement` |
| Scalar subquery | ✅ works (this **was** a limitation at [xarray-sql#197](https://github.com/xqlsystems/xarray-sql/issues/197) time; fixed since) |

Recursive CTEs and DML are precisely the shapes needed to express a **training
loop in one query** (e.g. gradient descent / Newton's method in a `WITH
RECURSIVE`, or `INSERT`-ing updated parameters), so their absence is
disqualifying for a Substrait-plan-transport design.

### Root cause

- `datafusion-substrait`'s producer does not (yet) support the `RecursiveQuery` or
  `DmlStatement` logical-plan nodes. Upstream tracking:
  [apache/datafusion#16248 (Substrait conversion issues epic)](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/16248).
- The deeper reason a bridge was needed at all: the native extension statically
  links its **own** copy of DataFusion, so it cannot share `Expr`/`LogicalPlan`
  objects with `datafusion-python` — forcing Substrait serialization as the
  transport, which makes Substrait's representational limits the bottleneck.

### Design consequence (what `ddx` does instead)

Rewrite `grad()`/`jvp()`/`vjp()` as a **SQL source-to-source transform before
planning** (`ddx-core::rewrite_sql`): parse with a dialect-aware parser
(`sqlparser`), differentiate the marker's argument on the AST, unparse, splice
back. This works for *every* query shape the parser accepts — recursive CTEs, DML

Issue #1343: Detect aliased requirement include cycles

## Problem

[`read_requirements`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ecosystem-pypi/src/mirror/selection.rs#L149-L174) tracks lexical paths in one global `seen` set. **Assignee:** Himanshi | **Labels:** `bug`, `backend`, `reliability` | **Domain:** AI/ML


**Description:** `backend/src/modules/team/repository.js` has three separate `WITH RECURSIVE` queries walking the manager hierarchy, none of which cap recursion depth — unlike the near-identical query in `backend/src/utils/hierarchy.js`, which correctly includes `AND chain.depth < 100`.

**Current code (one of three, same pattern repeated):**
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE team AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM users WHERE manager_id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT u.id, u.manager_id, t.depth + 1
  FROM users u INNER JOIN team t ON u.manager_id = t.id
  WHERE u.deleted_at IS NULL
  -- no depth cap
)
```

**Compare to the correctly-guarded sibling:**
```sql
-- hierarchy.js
WHERE u.deleted_at IS NULL AND chain.depth < 100
```

**Impact:** If a `manager_id` cycle ever exists in the data (data-entry bug, direct DB edit, or a race condition around the very cycle-check query this file itself uses), these recursive queries would loop until Postgres's internal safety limits kick in with an error, rather than terminating gracefully. Ironically, the third occurrence is itself the pre-write cycle-detection check meant to *prevent* a cycle from being created — if a cycle already exists from before this check existed, the check meant to catch it would itself hang/error instead of detecting the problem.

**Expected fix:** Add a `depth < 100` (or similar sane bound) column and `WHERE` guard to all three recursive CTEs, matching the pattern already established in `hierarchy.js`.

Issue #1298: Avoid scene-graph traversal on every render

On CPU bound systems, large scene, with many objects, traversing the scene on each call to render to create a flatscene is rather costly. On lower end CPUs, this is my bottlekneck especially if you use nested groups to keep track of the geometry transforms for me.

So sometimes, I'll have one group, with an optional object, so that the group can always exist, but we can "cleanup" the object (image or line) from the GPU.

I think we could prebuild this flatscene at the same time we build the scene graph. 

I worked with AI to create a proof of concept. Happy to share, but I wanted to see if such a overhaul would be welcome.

If it is welcome, I could cleanup the AI code and ensure it fits with your style.

<details><summary>AI generated details</summary>

Every call to `WgpuRenderer.render()` constructs a `FlatScene`, which walks the entire scene graph (`FlatScene._iter_scene`) to bucket objects into lights by type, shadow casters, and renderables, and to propagate `group_order` from each `Group` ancestor. This walk runs at frame rate — typically 60+ times per second — and its cost scales with the size of the scene, not with what's actually changing. For interactive applications with large or deep scenes (CAD models, scientific visualizations with many small objects, deeply nested rigs), this traversal becomes a measurable share of the per-frame CPU budget even when nothing about the scene topology has changed since the previous frame.

The fundamental issue is a mismatch between the rate at which scene structure changes and the rate at which we re-derive information from it. Scenes are mutated rarely (typically once at setup, occasionally during animation/picking) but rendered constantly. Recomputing categorization, ancestor lookups, and visibility chains on every render means we pay an O(N) Python-level recursion cost — with `isinstance` checks per node — to recompute information that was already correct. In a focused micro-benchmark of just `FlatScene` construction (no GPU work), I see this cost dominate small/deep scenes: e.g. a 500-deep `Group` chain takes ~2.4 ms per render purely for the categorization walk, which is most of a 16.7 ms frame budget at 60 FPS.

The scene-graph mutation API (`WorldObject.add` / `remove` / `clear`, plus the `visible` / `geometry` / `material` / `cast_shadow` setters) is the right place to maintain these derived structures incrementally. Doing the bucketing once at mutation time and reading flat lists at render time keeps render-path complexity bounded by what's actually being drawn rather than by total scene size. As a proof-of-concept I prototyped this on a branch (each `WorldObject` keeps a per-subtree categorized index, plus cached `_effective_visible` and a weakref to the closest `Group` ancestor) and measured **1.1×–1.3× speedup on flat/grouped scenes and 2×–6× on deep hierarchies** in the `FlatScene` micro-benchmark — happy to open a draft PR if there's interest in this direction.
</details>

A native Codex subagent was created through `collaboration.spawn_agent` for a bounded read-only research audit of a GitHub repository. It was asked to inspect current-Codex compatibility, worker/subagent design, risks, and return an adopt/borrow/reject recommendation. The subagent nevertheless attempted an out-of-scope local smoke installation. Its cleanup command used `$home` as a temporary variable in Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
$home = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'isolated-codex-home'
if (Test-Path $home) { Remove-Item $home -Recurse -Force }
```

PowerShell variable names are case-insensitive, so `$home` collided with automatic read-only `$HOME`. The assignment produced a non-terminating `VariableNotWritable` error. Execution continued, `$home` still resolved to the actual user profile, and the recursive deletion ran until tool timeout.

## Summary

Improve the performance, memory footprint, and correctness of **bulk recursive deletes**, especially **service-level hard deletes** of large catalogs. Recursive hard delete of a service with hundreds of thousands of descendants (e.g. a `databaseService` with ~1M tables) could take **hours** and OOM the server, and could leave **orphaned relationship rows**.

## Root causes

In the bulk subtree-delete path (`EntityRepository.bulkHardDeleteSubtree`):
1. **Unbounded memory** — each tree level was hydrated whole (`loadForBulk(ids, ALL)`), so a 1M-table service loaded ~1M entities into the heap at once.
2. **O(N) per-entity work** — for every descendant: a per-entity search dispatch (snapshot + lane submit) plus per-entity `field_relationship` / `tag_usage` / `usage` cleanup. The round-trip/dispatch count, not row volume, dominated the wall-clock.

## Done (PR #29322)

- **Bounded-memory chunking** of `bulkHardDeleteSubtree` (`BULK_HARD_DELETE_TXN_CHUNK_SIZE`): peak heap is now ~`chunk × tree-depth`, not a whole level.
- **`descendantsCoveredByAncestorCascade` capability flag** (constructor-set like `supportsSearch`): for FQN-nested service/container-rooted asset trees, the bulk path skips the per-entity search dispatch and per-entity `field_relationship`/`tag_usage` deletes, relying on the root's `deleteOrUpdateChildren` (`service.id`) search cascade + the root `cleanup()` FQN-prefix delete. Enabled for database, dashboard, messaging, pipeline, mlmodel, search, storage, drive, and api trees. Default `false` keeps flat-FQN (Team/User/Role/Policy) and reference types (Tag/GlossaryTerm/Domain/DataProduct/TestSuite) on the safe per-entity path.
- **id-set `usage` batching** (`UsageDAO.deleteByIds`); fixed a latent `apiService` search-cascade gap.
- **Result (local, 1 GB heap, 100k tables under one schema):** recursive `databaseService` hard delete **1643 s → 59 s (~28×)**, peak heap **546 → 493 MB** (no OOM), `entity_relationship` 100088 → 86 (orphan-free), search index clean.
- Tests: `EntityRepositoryRestoreTest` (chunking + skip logic) and a shared `BaseServiceIT` recursive-delete regression (no orphan relationships + search clean) across all flagged service trees.

## Remaining tasks

- [ ] **Per-chunk transactional atomicity** — wrap each chunk's reference + row deletes in one `flushInOneTransaction` (`DeadlockRetry.execute(() -> jdbi.inTransaction(...))`, #28675 infra) so a crash/deadlock mid-chunk can't leave a live entity stripped of its dependencies (or orphan satellite rows); deletes are idempotent so retry is safe. Today the chunk purge is per-DAO-call autocommit.
- [ ] **Chunk soft-delete + restore** — `bulkSoftDeleteSubtree` and `bulkRestoreSubtree` share the same whole-level `loadForBulk(ids, ALL)` OOM ceiling.

Issue #93: Implement Adapton-style demand-driven incremental computation

**Priority:** P3

**Problem Statement:**
When a file changes, librainian currently must decide what to recompute eagerly. Overly aggressive recomputation (rebuild everything) is too slow. Overly conservative recomputation (skip too much) produces stale results. Adapton's demand-driven model solves this: mark dependent computations as dirty (lazy), recompute only when queried, use early cutoff (if the result is identical, stop propagating dirty marks).

**Evidence:**
research-temporal-graphs.md: "Adapton DCG (lazy dirty marking, early cutoff). Dirty marking without eager recomputation. Early cutoff optimization: if result unchanged, no downstream propagation." research-temporal-graphs.md: "Salsa red-green algorithm: RED = stale, GREEN = clean, early cutoff if result hash unchanged." Both implement the same core insight: demand-driven computation with result-hash-based early cutoff.

**Comparative Context:**
- **Salsa** (Rust): `salsa::query` derives a demand-driven computation graph; used by rust-analyzer for incremental IDE features
- **Roslyn** (C#): green/red tree model — immutable trees with structural sharing; only changed nodes are re-parsed

**Proposed Approach:**
1. Implement dirty marking in `librarian.sqlite`: add a `dirty BOOLEAN` column to context packs, graph edges, and embeddings
2. When a file changes: mark all dependent context packs and edges as dirty (BFS from changed nodes in the dependency graph)
3. At query time: if a context pack is dirty, recompute it; if the new result hash equals the old result hash, mark GREEN (no downstream dirty propagation needed)
4. Eager recompute only for the query path; unqueried dirty nodes remain dirty until needed

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Changing a leaf function (not called by others) marks only that function's context pack as dirty; parent module's pack is not marked dirty
- Early cutoff: if a function body is reformatted but semantically identical, the pack hash is unchanged and downstream dirty marks are not propagated
- Incremental recompute after 1-file change runs in < 1 second (dirty walk + selective recompute)

**Risks and Tradeoffs:**
- Result hash comparison requires deterministic LLM output for context pack synthesis — LLMs are not deterministic; use a structural hash of the input (function body hash) rather than the output (pack content hash)
- Dirty marking graph traversal can be slow for highly connected graphs (utility functions with 200+ callers); bound the dirty walk depth

Issue #2780: Implement SBOM Merkle tree for minimal storage requirement of component dependencies table

# Proposal: Content-addressed (Merkle) SBOM storage

## Problem

The current `SBOMGraph` model (`normalize/sbom_graph.go`) stores all artifacts
in one shared node/edge map, keyed by component ID (PURL). `MergeGraph` uses
"last write wins" semantics on a component's outgoing edges — see the comment
in `MergeGraph`:

> Whichever scan most recently touched a given node's declared children is
> authoritative for that node's entire edge set from here on

This means two artifacts sharing a component (e.g. `circl@v1.6.3`) **cannot
disagree** about that component's transitive dependencies. A rescan of one
artifact silently rewrites the dependency tree seen by every other artifact
that shares the node.

## Proposed solution

Replace the mutable `(component_id, dependency_id)` edge table with a content-addressed
one. Components (PURL, license, name, etc.) are unchanged. An edge points at
the hash of the child's entire subtree (`direct_dependency_subtree_hash`),
and a component's own `subtree_hash` is `hash(component_id + all children's
subtree hashes)`. Two artifacts that disagree about a shared component's
children produce different `subtree_hash` values rooted at that component,
so both edge sets coexist as separate rows; where they agree, the rows are
identical and collide on the primary key, so nothing is duplicated. **This deduplication works across a whole devguard instance - never storing information twice** 

This builds on the existing `SBOMMerkleEdge` model added in
[14bcc64](https://github.com/l3montree-dev/devguard/commit/14bcc64d9b7e7c51d860382173f1d64d6c6e57d2).

## Schema

```sql
-- existing, reused as-is
CREATE TABLE sbom_merkle_edge (
  subtree_hash                  TEXT NOT NULL,
  component_id                  TEXT NOT NULL, -- PURL, or 'ROOT'
  direct_dependency_subtree_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (subtree_hash, component_id, direct_dependency_subtree_hash)
);

-- new: index for upward (vuln -> affected artifacts) traversal
CREATE INDEX idx_merkle_edge_child
  ON sbom_merkle_edge (direct_dependency_subtree_hash);

-- new: one row per asset version + SBOM origin (replaces synthetic
-- artifact:/infosource: nodes)
CREATE TABLE asset_version_sbom_source (
  asset_id           TEXT NOT NULL,
  asset_version_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  origin             TEXT NOT NULL, -- e.g. "sbom:package-lock.json"
  root_subtree_hash  TEXT NOT NULL,
  updated_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (asset_id, asset_version_name, origin),
  FOREIGN KEY (asset_version_name, asset_id) REFERENCES asset_versions (name, asset_id)
);
```

Component metadata (license, name, etc.) stays in the existing `components`
table, keyed by PURL — unchanged, no duplication.

## Core queries

**Ingest a new/updated SBOM source:**
1. Build in-memory graph for the source (existing `normalize` build logic,
   unchanged).
2. Compute `subtree_hash` bottom-up (existing `computeSubtreeHashes`).
3. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` all edges — new subtrees insert,
   already-seen subtrees no-op.
4. Upsert `artifact_sbom_source.root_subtree_hash` for `(artifact, source)`.

**Which artifacts contain vulnerable PURL `X` (upward walk):**
```
seed:   rows WHERE component_id = X
walk:   recursive join on direct_dependency_subtree_hash = subtree_hash
        (memoize visited subtree_hash to bound fan-in blowup)
stop:   component_id = 'ROOT'
result: join stopped subtree_hash against artifact_sbom_source.root_subtree_hash
```

**Which components does artifact `A` depend on (downward walk):**
Recursive CTE starting at `artifact_sbom_source.root_subtree_hash`, joining
`subtree_hash -> direct_dependency_subtree_hash` downward.

Issue #6335: Make WITH RECURSIVE behaviour more consistent across dialects

We should consider how to make recursive CTEs behave more consistently across dialects.

Key differences:
- Syntax keyword: Some engines require WITH RECURSIVE (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite), others use plain WITH for recursive CTEs.
- Column list rules: Some engines require an explicit column list for recursive CTEs (Oracle is the common case).
- Recursion limits: Most engines have a default recursion cap you can change (MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server). Hitting the limit fails the query.
- Cycle handling: Some engines have built-in cycle helpers; others don’t, so you must add your own stop condition.
- Ordering: Ordering inside the CTE body is often restricted; stable ordering should happen in the outer SELECT.
- Type inference: Column types usually come from the anchor part; some engines need explicit casts.

Related issue
- #3779: "position of with/CTE (top-level or together with subquery)". It reports that MySQL allows WITH inside subqueries, but MSSQL requires WITH at the top level. It also notes that some MySQL compilers don't include with() for update, so users monkey-patch it. This matters here because any cross-dialect plan for recursive CTEs must decide where WITH is allowed and how the compiler should place it per dialect.

Goal (if we ever do this)

Make results more consistent, or at least make the differences very clear, so the same recursive query behaves as close as possible across dialects.

Possible dialect-specific approach (high level)
- PostgreSQL:
  - Keep WITH RECURSIVE.
  - If no column list is provided, infer from the anchor query (current behaviour is fine).
  - Keep as the reference dialect for docs and examples.

- MySQL 8+ / MariaDB 10.2+:
  - Use WITH RECURSIVE explicitly.
  - Expose or document the recursion limit (`cte_max_recursion_depth`) so users know why a query might fail.
  - Encourage adding a termination condition in the recursive part.

- SQLite 3.8.3+:
  - Use WITH RECURSIVE.
  - Be clear about performance limits and planner differences.

- MSSQL:
  - Use WITH (no RECURSIVE keyword).
  - If the user doesn’t provide a column list, consider adding one when needed.
  - Note the default recursion limit and how to override it.

- Oracle:
  - Use WITH (no RECURSIVE keyword).
  - Always require or inject an explicit column list for recursive CTEs.
  - Make sure the anchor part and recursive part have compatible types (cast if needed).

Potential follow-up
We can add a capability matrix and a small dialect adapter for recursive CTEs, or at least tighten the docs with these differences.

Issue #8562: [Bug] visit [-->] never terminates on cyclic graphs — osp_visit has no visited set

### What's wrong

`visit [-->]` on a graph with a cycle re-enqueues nodes unconditionally — traversal never terminates and burns CPU printing until killed. The OSP kernel's `osp_visit()` tracks only `scope.ignores`; there is no visited set. A self-loop is enough to hang any program.

### Minimal repro

```jac
# cycle.jac
node N { has tag: str; }
walker W {
    can start with Root entry { visit [-->]; }
    can go with N entry { print(here.tag); visit [-->]; }
}
with entry {
    a = N(tag="A");
    root ++> a ++> a;   # a has an edge back to itself
    root spawn W();
}
```

```
timeout 5 jac run cycle.jac
```

### Expected vs actual

Expected: each node visited once per traversal (or termination per documented revisit policy); program exits after printing `A`.

Actual: prints `A` thousands of times per second forever (killed via timeout after ~3400 lines in 5s). Any user graph containing a cycle makes `jac run` spin at 100% CPU with no diagnostic.

### Suggested direction

One coherent fix for the revisit question in `osp_kernel.jac` `osp_visit()`, not two ad-hoc rules:

- Track a per-traversal visited set of edge/node anchors so each node is enqueued once by default.
- Note the same mechanism currently dedupes duplicate parallel edges between the same pair, so whatever policy lands must preserve that behavior.
- If revisiting is ever wanted, make it explicit opt-in (e.g., a `visit` modifier), never implicit.

Related but distinct: #6636 covers the *native* stopgap gate where a node-in-list cycle guard silently evaluates False — this report is the kernel-level missing visited-set in dev-mode Python runtime.

### Environment

- jac 0.16.7 (dev mode), main@844ea3ea5
- Linux x86_64

Graphs Basics

Before we dive into interesting graph algorithms, let’s first clarify the naming conventions and graph properties.

A graph is a data structure where a node can have zero or more adjacent elements.

The connection between two nodes is called edge. Nodes can also be called vertices.

The degree is the number of edges connected to a vertex. E.g., the purple vertex has a degree of 3 while the blue one has a degree of 1.

If the edges are bi-directional, then we have an undirected graph. But, if the edges have a direction, then we have a directed graph or di-graph for short. You can think of it as a one-way street (directed) or two-way street (undirected).

Vertex can have edges that go to itself (e.g., blue node), this is called self-loop.

A graph can have cycles which means that if you traverse through the node, you could get the same node more than once. The graph without cycles is called acyclic graph.

Issue #488: parser: generated DeepCopy is not cycle safe and overflows the stack

## Summary

The generated deep copy recurses without tracking what it has already copied, so a document whose pointer graph contains a cycle overflows the stack instead of returning a copy. This is true for every type the generator emits, not one of them.

Decoding cannot produce a cycle, since neither JSON nor YAML can express one, so this only reaches documents assembled in Go: the builder, tests, and anything constructing a document programmatically before handing it to another package.

## Reproduction

A schema that contains itself:

```go
s := &parser.Schema{Type: "object", Properties: map[string]*parser.Schema{}}
s.Properties["self"] = s
_ = s.DeepCopy()
```

```
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
```

The same holds for an encoding nested under itself, and for a media type that reaches one:

```go
e := &parser.Encoding{Encoding: map[string]*parser.Encoding{}}
e.Encoding["self"] = e
_ = e.DeepCopy()

mt := &parser.MediaType{Encoding: map[string]*parser.Encoding{"part": e}}
_ = mt.DeepCopy()
```

## Where it bites

The joiner treats cyclic pointer graphs as possible: `SchemaRewriter.rewriteSchema` and `rewriteEncoding` both keep a visited set precisely so a cycle terminates the traversal. Copying has no equivalent, so a document the rewriter handles fine can still crash the copy.

Reached today from:

- `joiner`, which deep copies a top level entry before rewriting its references (#480), so a cyclic document that also needs a rename crashes where it previously rewrote successfully
- `joiner`, which deep copies a document handed in at two positions (#481)
- anything else calling the generated methods on a Go assembled document

## Expected

`DeepCopy` returns a copy whose cycles are preserved as cycles, or the codebase states that cyclic documents are unsupported and the callers that guard traversals stop implying otherwise.

## Fix direction

The generator would thread a visited map through `DeepCopyInto`, keyed by source pointer and holding the copy already made, so reaching a node twice returns the existing copy rather than recursing. That preserves cycle structure rather than just avoiding the crash, and it matches what the rewriter's visited sets already assume about these graphs.

The cost is one map allocation per top level copy and a lookup per node. Worth measuring on the corpus specs, since deep copy sits on the joiner's rewrite path.

## Notes

`internal/driftguard` reflects over parser structs to catch a new field missing one of its homes. Whatever shape the fix takes, the visited threading is another home a new pointer-bearing field has to reach.

## Environment

- oastools 758dc34, reproduced on go1.26.5 darwin/arm64

A maintainer on the project cq27-dev/rag-rat (Rust) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #105: Architecture-metrics queries: cycles, coupling, treasure, lost, complexity ranking, shortest-path

Borrowed from prior art: [butttons/dora](https://github.com/butttons/dora) exposes a crisp suite of whole-repo architecture metrics on top of its dependency graph that rag-rat doesn't have as first-class tools. We already have the underlying graph (edges, `find_callers`/`trace_callees`, `repo_clusters`, `repo_brief`) — these are mostly new *queries* over data we already index, not new indexing.

## Candidate metrics (dora's set, mapped to rag-rat)
- **cycles** — bidirectional/circular dependencies (A imports/calls B, B imports/calls A), at file and/or module granularity. We have the edge graph; this is cycle detection over it.
- **coupling** — file/symbol pairs with high shared-symbol or cross-edge density (`--threshold N`).
- **treasure** — most-depended-on files/symbols (highest fan-in). We already compute fan_in for `repo_brief` load-bearing list; generalize it.
- **lost** — defined symbols with zero in-corpus references (dead-ish code candidates). Note our honest caveat: "zero references" must account for unresolved/external edges so we don't mislabel (provenance — surface coverage like the graph tools already do).
- **complexity ranking** — files ranked by change risk (size × churn × fan-in). We have churn (git history) + fan-in + size already in `repo_brief`; expose a ranked view.
- **adventure / shortest-path** — shortest dependency path between two files/symbols (graph BFS over edges).

## Why it fits
`repo_brief` and `repo_clusters` already surface spine/churn/god-modules/ownership — this is the same family, extended to cycles/coupling/shortest-path/dead-symbol. It's high-value for agents doing refactor/impact reasoning and cheap to build on the existing edge + git + symbol tables.

## Caveats to honor
- **Provenance/coverage**: rag-rat's edges carry resolution confidence and a meaningful unresolved/external fraction. Every metric here must surface that (e.g. "lost" candidates flagged when fan-in is only unresolved edges; cycles built only from resolved edges) — otherwise we'd ship confident-looking-but-wrong architecture claims, which is exactly what our provenance discipline exists to prevent.
- Decide CLI commands vs MCP tools vs both; likely both (mirror the existing `repo_brief`/`repo_clusters` pattern).

Issue #7309: feat(server): indexed session query — replace the linear substring scan in conversation-search.js

Part of #7304 (Tranche B — loop/runtime hardening).

## The current behaviour

`packages/server/src/conversation-search.js:111`:

```js
const idx = lower.indexOf(queryLower)
```

Session search is a linear, case-folded substring scan over conversation content. That is fine for a handful of short sessions and degrades linearly with the transcript corpus — which, on a daemon that has been running for months across many projects, is the normal case rather than the edge case.

It also constrains what search can *mean*. A substring scan cannot rank, cannot do phrase or prefix queries, cannot scope by relationship (this session's fork parent, its subagent children), and cannot answer "which session touched this file".

## What DeepSeek Harness does

`dsh` splits this into a seam: `ctx.sessionQuery` (`packages/session-query/session-query`) owns the provider-independent vocabulary — exact reads, source precedence, relationship tracing, semantic extraction, and filters — and `session-query-sqlite` owns the concrete full-text index lifecycle. The definition is deliberately live-preferred: it queries the in-memory session corpus first and falls back to the index, so a search never misses the turn that just happened.

That live-preferred detail is the part most likely to be got wrong on a reimplementation, and it is the reason their design is worth following rather than just "add FTS".

## Proposal

Keep the current call sites; replace the backend.

1. Define a query interface covering: full-text with ranking, filters (session, project, provider, time range, role), and relationship traversal (fork parent/child, subagent lineage).
2. Back it with SQLite FTS5, indexed incrementally as session events are appended rather than rebuilt on read.
3. **Live-preferred reads** — the in-memory store answers for the current session; the index answers for the corpus. A message written one second ago must be findable.
4. Index rebuild path for an existing install, and a corruption-recovery path that rebuilds rather than failing search entirely.

Note that `session-query-sqlite` also gives `dsh` the "@-mention a prior thread" capability that Zed's context picker has — this issue is a dependency of the context-picker issue in Tranche C.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Full-text search over the session corpus with ranked results, backed by an index
- [ ] Search latency is flat, not linear, in corpus size — benchmarked against a synthetic corpus large enough to show the difference, with the before/after numbers in the PR
- [ ] A message appended during the current turn is findable immediately (live-preferred read)
- [ ] Filters: session, project, provider, role, time range
- [ ] Index rebuild for existing installs; corrupt index rebuilds rather than breaking search
- [ ] Tests pass a temp `stateFilePath` and write only under a temp config dir (#4633)

- https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/master/docs/subsystems/session-query.md
